We had succeeded in seeing Madagascar's extraordinary wildlife without joining a tour. But you never really travel "independently" here. Every national park guide who helped us track lemurs, the pisteurwho pointed the way andthe villagers who hauled us from the mud had made the journey possible. --

item.title: Inside the places that shaped Dolly Parton
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.22
'Everything about her was East Tennessee': The places that shaped Dolly Parton From her Appalachian childhood to Nashville and Dollywood, a journey through the Tennessee she loved – and transformed in return. On a sunny day on 24 June 2026, hundreds of travellers, locals and Dolly Parton fans from across the US gathered in the small rural community of Cornersville, less than an hour's drive south of Nashville, for the unveiling of her Tennessean Travel Stop. It was the country star's last public appearance before her death just two months later. Wearing her signature fringe and rhinestones and a grin as bright as that Tennessee morning, Parton cut the ribbon and welcomed travellers to the new roadside stop, complete with a Southern meat-and-three restaurant, live music and – of course – a Dolly-themed gift shop. It was a fitting final chapter for an artist whose life and career were inseparable from Tennessee. From crooning about the Smoky Mountains to investing in rural East Tennessee where she grew up, Parton spent decades sharing her home state with the world – and transforming it in return. Explore Parton's Tennessee mountain home In 1964, US President Lyndon B Johnson launched the War on Poverty, a federal effort to reduce poverty and expand economic opportunity across the United States. Southern Appalachia, one of the nation's poorest regions, was thrust into the national spotlight. Media portrayals often depicted its residents as backward and destitute, reinforcing the caricature of the "hillbilly", a stereotype that had persisted since the 19th Century. But when Dolly Rebecca Parton came into the spotlight, this daughter of Appalachia who grew up in a two-room cabin with 11 brothers and sisters offered the world a different view of her home: one of joy, dignity and talent. Follow Dolly Parton's story across Tennessee Sevierville: See the bronze statue of Parton outside the Sevier County Courthouse and The Pines, where she performed for a paying audience for the first time at just 10 years old. RCA Studio B, Nashville: Visit the legendary recording studio on Music Row where Dolly Parton and other iconic artists like Elvis Presley recorded some of their greatest hits. The Country Music Hall of Fame, Nashville: A must-visit Nashville institution that chronicles the history of country music through artefacts, exhibits and the stories of the artists who trailblazed the genre. Dollywood, Pigeon Forge: Set in the Smoky Mountains that Parton loved so dearly, Dollywood takes guests on a journey through the singer's roots, from an exact replica of her childhood two-room cabin to the Dolly Parton Experience, which displays childhood memorabilia. "Dolly Parton told a new story about Appalachia that was rooted in her very particular experience," said Dr Jessie Wilkerson, a history professor and Appalachian scholar at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. "Yes, her family was poor, but they weren't desperate or hopeless, and they took care of one another. There was a lot of love and beauty in the place where she grew up, and so we get a different story about Appalachia through her." In the title track of her 1973 album, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Parton describes her Appalachian home as "peaceful as a baby's sigh". The landscape around her childhood home on the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains, along with Appalachia's storytelling traditions and bluegrass heritage, inspired much of Parton's music. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, a blue-grey mist that gives the Smokies its name settles over the peaks and valleys and waterfalls tumble through the forest. The 522,000-acre expanse is threaded with hiking trails and scenic overlooks, with autumn bringing a canvas of brilliant jewel tones and spring a kaleidoscope of wildflowers to the lower slopes. The landscape was a reoccurring muse, from the mountain blooms that inspired her 1987 ballad Wildflowers to the fog-covered peaks evoked in Blue Smoke, the title track of her 2014 album, and the pastoral idyll captured in My Tennessee Mountain Home. In nearby Sevierville, the main town serving rural Locust Ridge, where Parton grew up, the region's pride in its local legend is evident. A bronze statue on the courthouse lawn depicts her as a young girl playing guitar. Down the street is the Wings of Wander mural, inspired by her hit song Love Is Like a Butterfly, and the Red's Cafe mural, another larger-than-life depiction of Parton as a child, this time getting a cheeseburger from her favourite childhood restaurant. "People in East Tennessee really, really adore her, and it's something that's been important for the region to have someone who's really proud of coming from there, and who's a positive representation of Appalachia, when historically the representations of the region are the opposite," Wilkerson said. Retracing Parton's path in Nashville On the day Parton graduated from high school in 1964, she boarded a Greyhound bus headed west for the neon lights of Nashville. In a letter home shortly after arriving, feeling homesick and uncertain, she wrote, "Nashville isn't what I thought it was gonna be, but I think I'll like it once I get used to it." "When she came to Nashville, she came with a very distinct East Tennessee identity and made that very clear in both her music and her accent," said Robert K Oermann, co-author of her memoir Dolly Parton: Songteller, My Life in Lyrics and a longtime collaborator. "Everything about her was East Tennessee and mountain, and I think that was the message she brought to Nashville." Nashville looks very different today from when Parton first stepped off that bus 62 years ago, but visitors can still trace Parton's path from her early days fresh out of Sevier County to her rise as a country music icon who never lost the Appalachian sound of home even as she became one of Nashville's biggest stars. On Music Row, the city's historic record-industry district, visitors can step inside RCA Studio B where a blue X marks "The Sweet Spot" where Parton recorded hits including Jolene and I Will Always Love You – both of which she wrote on the same day. Nearby, the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum is featuring Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker, an exhibition spanning her career and featuring memorabilia like her Gibson five-string banjo and handwritten music drafts. A few blocks away, the historic Ryman Auditorium is where a 13-year-old Parton made her Grand Ole Opry debut in 1959 and earned three encores. Murals of Parton dot the city in her honour, museum exhibits display her stage costumes and in the wake of her passing, fans have left flowers on her star on the Music City Walk of Fame. Visiting Parton's Appalachia Nashville, however, was never the end of Parton's journey. The further her career carried her from the mountains to Nashville and eventually Hollywood, the more firmly she seemed to plant her roots at the centre of her story. In 1982, she told Barbara Walters in an interview about her dream of opening a "mountain Disneyland" in her Appalachian home region. More like this: Today, that "mountain Disneyland" is Dollywood, a major tourist destination in Sevier County that invites visitors into the version of Appalachia Parton spent her career sharing with the world. Beyond the thrill rides and water park are shows featuring Parton's music, some performed by members of her own family. But to Parton, Dollywood was also a way to give back to the mountains and the community that nurtured her. "I think we owe a lot to Dolly Parton for Tennessee tourism and the kind of goodwill that she's helped create for the state," says Dr Celeste Carruthers, an economics professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. According to Carruthers, Dollywood draws millions of visitors and supports tens of thousands of tourism-related jobs in Sevier County, generating an estimated $1.8bn in direct economic impact annually. But Parton's investment in her home region extends well beyond tourism. In 1995, she launched the Imagination Library through the Dollywood Foundation in tribute to her father, who never learned to read or write. The programme's mission was to put a book in the hands of every child in Sevier County, with it later expanding around the world. "We really feel there's a responsibility going forward, that it's about more than just a theme park," says Andrew Wexler, CEO of Herschend, the family-owned entertainment company that co-founded Dollywood with Parton. "It's about the principles and values that Dolly had of family and love, generosity, community, faith and the idea that people's best experiences are shared with the people that matter most to them." --

item.title: How to Boil Potatoes (and How Long to Boil Them)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.37
So many potato recipes start with the same instruction: “Boil the potatoes.” Simple enough—until you’re wondering whether to start them in cold or boiling water, how much salt to add, or how long the potatoes actually need to cook. The short version: Start potatoes in cold, well-salted water, bring it to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer until tender. That’s it! Depending on their size and what you’re making, the actual cooking time could range from 8–40 minutes. A baby potato destined for smashing needs far less time than a big chunk of russet headed for mashed potatoes. Want to know more? Here’s how to get it right every time. How to boil potatoes The essential rule for boiling potatoes: Start them in cold water. When you drop potatoes into water that’s already boiling, the outsides overcook before the centers turn tender. Starting them cold lets the potatoes and water heat up together so they cook more evenly. Ingredients - 2 lb. potatoes, scrubbed, prepared as desired (more on that in a minute) - 1 cup Diamond Crystal or ½ cup Morton kosher salt - Place 2 lb. potatoes, scrubbed, in a large pot. Baby, small, and medium potatoes can stay whole; cut large potatoes into evenly sized pieces. Peel them first if your recipe calls for it. - Cover the potatoes with 3 qt. cold water and add 1 cup Diamond Crystal or ½ cup Morton kosher salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, stirring occasionally. Reduce the heat to maintain a simmer and cook until the potatoes reach the desired tenderness (more on that below). - Drain in a colander and let cool for 10 minutes, or proceed as directed in your recipe. Potatoes are dense, so seasoning only the exterior after boiling won’t give you the same deeply seasoned result. For 3 quarts of cold water, we recommend 1 cup of Diamond Crystal or ½ cup of Morton kosher salt (Morton is denser than Diamond Crystal, so you need less). Most of that salt goes down the drain with the cooking water, but the concentrated salt bath gives the potatoes a chance to absorb the seasoning as they cook. The time it takes to boil potatoes depends primarily on their size and how you plan to use them. Small potatoes can be ready in less than 15 minutes; larger pieces destined for mashed potatoes, gnocchi, or dumplings may need 30 minutes or more. | How long to boil potatoes for: | Smashed Potatoes | Potato Salad | Mashed Potatoes | Gnocchi and Dumplings | |---|---|---|---|---| | Fingerling potatoes | 8–12 minutes | 15–20 minutes | n/a | n/a | | Baby potatoes | 8–12 minutes | 10–15 minutes | n/a | n/a | | Medium potatoes | 18–22 minutes | 20–25 minutes | 30–35 minutes | 30–35 minutes | | Large potatoes (cut into 2" cubes) | n/a | 15–20 min | 20–25 minutes | 35–40 minutes | Large potatoes should be cut before boiling so they cook evenly—a whole russet may still be firm in the center by the time its exterior is overcooked. The exact dimensions matter less than consistency: Cut the pieces roughly the same size, and they should finish cooking at about the same time. Baby and other small potatoes can generally be boiled whole. Consider these time ranges as guidelines rather than deadlines. Start checking your potatoes at the low end of the range and let their texture—not the timer—tell you when they’re ready. How to tell when boiled potatoes are done “Fork-tender” is the usual cue: A fork, cake tester, or paring knife should pierce the potato easily. Exactly how tender you want it depends on what you’re making. A knife or cake tester should slide easily into and out of the potato. You want the potatoes fully tender all the way through, without any firm or crunchy spots. A knife or tester should slide in easily but meet a little resistance on the way out. The potatoes should be tender without falling apart when you toss or dress them. The best potatoes for boiling You can boil just about any potato, but the best variety depends on what you plan to do with it afterward. Idaho, russet, and other high-starch potatoes cook up fluffy and readily break down with a ricer or food mill, making them a classic choice for mashed potatoes. They’re also more prone to becoming waterlogged if overcooked, so keep an eye on them. New potatoes, Red Bliss, fingerlings, and other waxy varieties have a dense texture and hold their shape particularly well after boiling. That makes them a good choice for potato salad, niçoise, and other dishes where you want distinct, intact pieces. Yukon Golds land somewhere between starchy and waxy potatoes, with enough starch to make a creamy mash but enough structure to hold their shape. They’re the Test Kitchen favorite for ultra-creamy, buttery mashed potatoes—and a reliable all-purpose choice. Boiled potato FAQs Do you need to peel potatoes before boiling? Not necessarily. Thin-skinned potatoes like Yukon Golds, red potatoes, fingerlings, and baby potatoes can be boiled with their skins on after a good scrub. Whether you peel thicker-skinned potatoes like russets depends on the dish you’re making; peel them when you want an especially smooth final texture. Can you boil potatoes whole? Yes. Baby, small, and medium potatoes can be boiled whole. Large potatoes should be cut into evenly sized pieces so their centers cook through before their exteriors become overdone. Can you overboil potatoes? Yes. Cook potatoes too long and they can become waterlogged or start falling apart. Starchy potatoes like russets are particularly prone to breaking down, while waxy varieties tend to hold their shape better. Start checking for doneness at the low end of the suggested cooking-time range. Editor’s note: This article was originally published online in June 2019. It has been expanded and updated for style with further reporting by Zoe Denenberg and Hannah Lee Leidy.

item.title: Parker House Rolls
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.93
With burnished tops, buttery layers, and a sprinkle of flaky sea salt, Parker House rolls are the classic American dinner roll. Created at Boston’s Parker House Hotel in the 19th century, the soft, fluffy yeast rolls are sometimes called pocketbook rolls due to their signature folded shape. Serve them alongside Thanksgiving turkey or holiday ham, then pry open any leftovers to slather with honey or jam for breakfast. Adapted from The Fannie Farmer Baking Book, this Parker House roll recipe is straightforward enough for novice bread bakers: The dough is easy to knead by hand (though a stand mixer works too). Brushing each piece with melted butter before folding creates the rolls’ characteristic shape, while a second swab after baking gives them their sheen. Parker House rolls FAQ What makes a Parker House roll different from a regular dinner roll? It’s all in the fold. Instead of shaping the dough into balls, Parker House rolls are shaped into rectangles, brushed with butter, and folded over themselves. The result is their distinctive pocketbook shape and a buttery seam that makes them easy to pull apart. Can I make Parker House rolls ahead of time? Yes. Dough can be mixed 8 hours ahead. Cover and refrigerate. Once shaped, the rolls can be covered and refrigerated for at least 30 minutes and up to 6 hours before baking. You can also bake them earlier in the day. Remove them from the oven about 5 minutes before they are done (they should be puffed and cooked through but not yet golden). Finish baking when ready to serve. Why did my Parker House rolls turn out dense? Too much flour or insufficient rising can produce dense rolls. For the most accurate measurement, weigh the flour rather than scooping it by volume and let the dough rise until doubled in size before shaping. Unfortunately, overproofing can also create a dense roll. To get it just right, use the poke test to determine when your rolls are ready to bake. Can I freeze Parker House rolls? Yes. Freeze baked and then cooled Parker House rolls up to a month. Thaw and rewarm them in a low oven to restore their soft texture. A spritz of water on top of the rolls will keep them plush and prevent them from becoming too dark. You can also freeze the risen, unbaked rolls for up to a month. Bake straight from the freezer, adding about 5 minutes of extra cooking time. This recipe was adapted for style from ‘The Fannie Farmer Baking Book’ by Marion Cunningham. Buy the full book on Amazon or ThriftBooks. Recipe information - Total Time 55 minutes plus chilling - Yield Makes 36 Ingredients 1 1 ¼ 3 1½ 1 3½ 4 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Whisk one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) and ¼ cup warm water (110°–115°) in a small bowl; let sit until foamy, about 5 minutes. Step 2Heat 1 cup whole milk in a small saucepan over medium until just warm. Combine ¼ cup vegetable shortening, 3 Tbsp. sugar, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Pour in warm milk, whisking constantly to blend and break up shortening into small clumps (it may not melt completely). Add yeast mixture and 1 large egg, room temperature, and whisk to combine. Add 3½ cups (438 g) all-purpose flour and stir vigorously with a wooden spoon until a dough forms. Step 3Turn dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead with lightly floured hands until smooth, about 5 minutes. Lightly coat a large bowl with vegetable oil; transfer dough to bowl and turn to coat. Cover loosely with plastic wrap. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in size, about 1½ hours. Do Ahead: Dough can be mixed 8 hours ahead. Cover and refrigerate, dough will rise more slowly as it chills. Step 4Lightly brush a 13x9" baking dish with some of the 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted. Punch down dough; divide into 4 equal pieces. Working one at a time, roll out pieces on a lightly floured surface into 12x6" rectangles. Cut each rectangle lengthwise into three 2"-wide strips; cut each strip crosswise to make three 4x2" rectangles (9 total per piece). Brush half of each rectangle (about 2x2") with melted butter, then fold unbuttered side up and over buttered side, leaving ¼" uncovered at the end. Starting in a corner of prepared dish, place rolls, flat side down, so folded edge is against a short side of the dish. Add rolls side by side to form a long row. Repeat with remaining rolls, facing folded edge toward rolls in previous row, until you have 4 rows total. Brush tops of rolls with melted butter, loosely cover with plastic wrap, and chill at least 30 minutes and up to 6 hours. Step 5Preheat oven to 350°. Bake rolls until golden and puffed, 25–35 minutes. Brush with more melted butter and sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Let cool slightly before serving. Editor’s note: This Parker House roll recipe was first printed in the 1984 edition of the ‘Fannie Farmer Baking Book,’ and appeared in our November 2012 Thanksgiving issue. Head this way for more of our best Thanksgiving recipes →

item.title: How to Build a Knife Set
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.63
For years we’ve been convinced that the best knife sets are made, knife by knife, by considering what you cook, how you cook, and the size of your space. Knife sets have their place, but really, we think of them as a stopgap as you assemble your own personal knife roll. Building a knife collection is extremely personal—the look, feel, and utility of each knife will read differently from person to person. And after all my time testing knives, the blades that became my go-tos have surprised me. I never expected a nakiri knife to be one of my daily drivers, and I never expected myself to own different styles of chef’s knives for different tasks. Not everyone is going to keep a gyuto around just to slice meat, but I was able to perfectly cut the flatiron steak I grilled the other week into thin strips that almost melted in my mouth because I had one. So this guide walks you through all the different categories of knives we’ve tested and how necessary they’re likely to be in your kitchen. Even though there’s a case to be made that you only need three knives, I think you should give yourself the opportunity to be surprised by some of the incredibly useful blades out there, just like I was. The essential knife You’re going to need a chef’s knife. Full stop. Many people prefer the durability of a Western chef’s knife, but some people might want the precision and steel quality of a Japanese chef’s knife. Most people will pick one or the other, but it’s also common for many home cooks to have one of each. Chef’s Knife The chef’s knife is the do-it-all star of any professional or home kitchen. This versatile blade can chop, slice, dice, even peel and core if you’re in a pinch. Generally defined by its tall heel, curved belly, and fine point, a good chef’s knife should be one of the first purchases you make for your kitchen. But because they have some of the most varied designs in the knife world, my full review of chef’s knives breaks down a large variety of top picks to help you find exactly what type of chef’s knife works best for you. Western chef’s knives tend to be sturdy, heavy, and made with slightly softer and more forgiving steel; Japanese chef’s knives (known as a gyuto), on the other hand, are designed to be sharp, nimble, and excellent slicers. Gyutos have finer edges made from harder steel, which helps them stay sharper longer but also makes them more vulnerable to chipping. If you’re looking for more precision and don’t mind a bit more maintenance, you might snag a Japanese chef’s knife for your daily use. Important knives you’ll use constantly: No matter how good your chef’s knife is, it won’t cut bread as well as a serrated knife. It will also feel ungainly for peeling or coring. That’s work for a paring knife. Bread knife Serrated knives cut bread without squishing it, which chef’s knives really can’t pull off. The best serrated knives are sharp, long enough to tackle big loaves, and sturdy enough to cut through a defined crust. They’re also useful for delicate tasks, like slicing tomatoes, and their overall size can help with big tasks, like splitting or peeling a watermelon. Paring knife Paring knives are great for coring and peeling, and their short blades give the user more control over small movements than a full-size chef’s knife or even a mid-size utility knife. They’re also useful for ultra-small tasks like slicing and hulling berries. But not all paring knives are designed the same, some have longer handles, some have narrow blades, some really can’t be sharpened. We tested and reviewed a wide variety of shapes, sizes, and price points to help you snag the type of paring knife you’ll find most useful. Useful knives you may not own: Adding a mid-size specialized knife to your kit, like a santoku, nakiri, or petty knife, brings more versatility while taking some workload off your other knives (meaning they’ll stay sharper longer). Most home cooks won’t need all three; most knife enthusiasts couldn’t imagine their collection without them. Santoku knife Named after the “three virtues,” santoku knives are great at chopping, slicing, and dicing. Their shape takes inspiration from a trio of other knives: the straight edge of the nakiri, the overall length of a petty knife, and the slight curve of a gyuto. They also have extremely pronounced sheep’s foot tips for precision point work. Santoku knives are great for a large variety of tasks and are often prized for their daily use for things like slicing cheese, cutting an apple, breaking down an onion, or chopping herbs. Nakiri knife Nakiri knives are traditional Japanese vegetable cleavers that feature a sturdy spine and a straight edge. These knives are great for breaking down tough vegetables like sweet potatoes and hard-skinned squash, and the straight edge is ideal for matchsticking carrots and cucumbers because the entire edge cuts all the way through to the cutting board (unlike the curved edge of a chef’s knife). If you have a fine-edged gyuto for an everyday chef’s knife, you might want a nakiri with its sturdy spine and heftier weight to handle some tougher jobs. Petty knife Petty knives are small Japanese utility knives that are great for precision work and slicing. Shaped like a gyuto, but with blades just a smidge longer than a paring knife, a petty knife is great for tasks like breaking down a whole chicken because they can easily fit between joints. The length of the blade gives you more freedom to tackle everyday tasks, and while they’re ideal for small tasks like dicing a shallot or cutting hard cheese, their nimbleness also makes them adept at slicing a steak. Nice-to-have knives: You may not ever need a heavy-duty meat cleaver, but you might be surprised at how versatile a Chinese cleaver is. Neither is essential in a kitchen, but both are great to have on hand when you need one. Same goes for the boning knife: You might not always bring home an entire striped bass, but on the occasion you do, you’ll be glad you have a boning knife on hand. Meat cleavers and Chinese cleavers Heavy-duty cleavers tend to be blunter than most knives, but that’s on purpose. Their edges are designed to crack through bone, so don’t expect them to slice through a delicate steak easily. Chinese cleavers, on the other hand, are thin and sharp, designed for precision push cuts. Our review breaks down the difference between the two in detail, while also showcasing why you might need one or the other more than you think. Boning knife Many home cooks get by just fine asking their butcher counter to portion their meat and fish, but more intrepid folks might find that breaking down a whole chicken, filleting a fresh-caught sea bream, or portioning a T-bone gives them more control over the meal they want to cook. A good boning knife is nimble, sharp, and easy to maneuver—it may be a specialized knife, but it excels at the task it was designed for. And don't forget… You’ll probably want to pick up a knife sharpener and honing rod to keep your knives pristine.

item.title: Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf Cake
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.48
Something about having a loaf of lemon poppy seed cake on the counter makes you feel like the star of a sitcom. As if you might drink your coffee from a thick-walled mug and scratch your cat under the chin just before you leave for work, a slice of said cake in your hand as you dash to the bus stop. Whether that rings true or not, know that this is a main character cake, worthy of its own show. Tall and hefty with a gentle tang and the crunchy burst of poppy seeds in every bite, it is completely unfussy yet still elegant. The bright loaf cake sings of sunny lemons thanks to the zest as well as juice. With the addition of oil and the insulating cap of snow-white glaze, it keeps nicely for a couple of days. Find more cheerful bakes here: Chocolate Guinness Cake; Apple Cider Doughnut Loaf Cake; and Preserved Lemon Tea Cake. Recipe information - Total Time 1½ hours - Yield one 9x5" loaf Ingredients Cake 2¼ 1½ 1½ ¾ 1½ 5 2 2 3 ¾ ¼ Glaze and Assembly 1 1–2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - CakeStep 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Generously coat a 9x5" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray or unsalted butter, room temperature; line with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Whisk 2¼ cups (281 g) all-purpose flour, 1½ tsp. baking powder, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Step 2Beat zest of 3 large lemons, ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, 5 Tbsp. vegetable oil, 2 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract on medium speed in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with paddle attachment until light and creamy, about 5 minutes. Step 3Add 3 large eggs, one at a time, beating after each addition to combine before adding the next one (batter may look curdled at this point). Scrape down sides of bowl with a rubber spatula, add half of dry ingredients, and beat on low speed just to combine. Add ¾ cup whole milk and remaining dry ingredients and mix until batter is smooth and creamy, about 1 minute. Add ¼ cup poppy seeds; scrape down bottom and sides of bowl and fold batter with spatula a few times to ensure it’s evenly mixed. Step 4Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. (If your pan looks more than three quarters full, transfer excess batter to a greased small ovenproof container and bake alongside cake as a cook’s treat). Generously coat the blade of a small paring knife with nonstick spray; run knife lengthwise through center of batter to make a shallow cut (this will help cake split cleanly along line as it bakes rather than cracking randomly). Step 5Bake cake until golden brown all over, it springs back when gently pressed, and a tester inserted into the center comes out with only a few moist crumbs attached, 60–65 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and let cake cool slightly in pan, about 15 minutes. Step 6Run a small offset spatula around edges of cake to loosen, then invert out onto rack. Turn cake right side up and let cool completely. - Glaze and AssemblyStep 7Stir 1 cup (110 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and a pinch of kosher salt in small bowl, adding up to 1 Tbsp. additional lemon juice as needed, until thick but pourable. Pour glaze over cake, letting it drip down sides. Top with poppy seeds and thin strips of lemon zest if using while glaze is still wet; let sit until glaze is set, at least 45 minutes. Do Ahead: Cake can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

item.title: 3-Ingredient Curry Pumpkin Soup
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.99
This dead simple three-ingredient soup houses a wealth of flavor with a shockingly trim ingredient list. Made by sizzling curry paste in oil, then adding a can of pumpkin purée and coconut milk, this cozy soup is a celebration of simplicity, creating something that tastes far more complex than it was to make. For the best flavor, I like to use the Maesri brand curry paste, leaning on its warm intensity to lend the soup its depth, but the ubiquitous Thai Kitchen, sold in almost all grocery stores, is also nice, producing a gentle heat. It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: The 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Soup You’ll Fall For. Recipe information - Total Time 30 minutes - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 1 1 2 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Transfer a couple of spoonfuls or so of one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, stirred well, to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Heat 1 Tbsp. unrefined coconut oil or other oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 2 Tbsp. red curry paste and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, 2–3 minutes. Add one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, remaining coconut milk in can, and 1½ cups water. Increase heat to high and bring soup to a simmer. Remove pot from heat. Taste soup and season with kosher salt if needed. Ladle into bowls and drizzle some reserved coconut milk into each bowl.

item.title: Lasagna-Vibes Zucchini Skillet
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.56
For years, one of my go-to dinners in the summer was zucchini lasagna, where zucchini is used in place of noodles. It’s delightful, but it’s also very labor-intensive, requiring you to slice the zucchini into long, thin planks, salt each individual plank, wipe each individual plank, and then layer the zucchini “noodles” with ricotta, sauce, and mozzarella. Now I have far too many children to be salting individual planks of zucchini—so I make this. It’s a dump-and-go skillet meal that has all of those favorite flavors in a way, way quicker and easier format. Read More: Finding My Way Back to the Kitchen After Giving Birth Recipe information - Total Time 15 minutes - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 2 1 3 1¾ 1 2 1 ½ 1 4 4 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground turkey and cook, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until mostly cooked through with only a little pink remaining, about 4 minutes. Add 3 medium zucchini (about 20 oz.), halved lengthwise, sliced crosswise ⅛" thick, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt; season with freshly ground black pepper. Increase heat to high and cook, stirring often, until meat is cooked through and no longer pink and zucchini is tender, 6–8 minutes. Step 2Reduce heat to medium and stir in one 14.5-oz. can tomato sauce, 2 tsp. Italian seasoning, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. onion powder, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and half of 1 cup thinly sliced basil leaves. Taste zucchini mixture and season with more salt and pepper if needed. Swirl in spoonfuls of 4 oz. whole-milk ricotta (about ½ cup), then sprinkle 4 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over. Reduce heat to low, cover pan, and cook until mozzarella is melted, about 4 minutes. Step 3Top zucchini mixture with remaining basil and crushed red pepper flakes (if using) to serve.

item.title: What Are Budget-Friendly Recipes I Can Make for My 60-Person Wedding?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.39
There are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook. Tell us about it! Dear Bon Appétit is an advice column where we answer your culinary conundrums with handpicked recipes and well-seasoned advice. Submit a question here. My 60-person wedding is going to be a DIY affair at a small inn-turned-Airbnb. The big meals are going to be handled by professionals, but there’s a couple meals—Friday breakfast and lunch, Saturday breakfast—that we’re hoping to cobble together ourselves in the inn’s commercial kitchen. While we regularly host groups of 20ish at our apartment, 60 people feels like an entirely different beast. How can we (simply! not-too-expensively!) scale up and make sure everyone is well-fed? We’re nominating some friends to help prep and serve food for each meal, but where do we start with the menu? How do you think about how much food you need? —I Do Congrats are in order! Thanks for writing in about your big day—I’m honored. This is a great size for a guest list. My husband and I invited a similar range (scandalous in pre-pandemic times) and the room was overflowing, bountiful, raucous at times. The funny thing about a small wedding is…it’s still a lot of people. And you’re right, it’s an entirely different beast than your everyday dinner party. I applaud you for tapping in friends. Delegation is—begging my editor to let me keep italics here—of the utmost importance. Not just because, unless you are a Top Chef contestant, feeding 60 people should not be a one-person endeavor. But also because, ahem, you’re the one getting married! As corny as it sounds, I hope that the top item on your to-do list is: Have fun. Everything else can wait, or should be someone else’s problem. Okay, speech over, taking a sip of pét-nat, onto the recipes! Breakfasts Not actually a recipe: My family has a reunion at the Shore every summer and our foolproof feed-a-crowd breakfast is bagels plus fixings. Can’t be beat. BA Bake Club has a wonderful homemade bagel recipe, which you should save for later and not use for this occasion. Now is the time to buy and assemble: bagels (if they’re fresh, skip toasting; if not, broil on a sheet pan); a few flavors of whipped cream cheese; smoked salmon (skip if this breaks the budget); sliced tomatoes and onion; capers; pickles. Optional fruit alongside. The math: - 1¼ bagels per person = 75 bagels - 1½ oz. cream cheese per person = 90 oz. (12 eight-oz. containers) - 2 oz. lox per person = 7½ lb. (Costco is your friend) - ⅓ tomato per person = 20 tomatoes - ⅙ onion per person = 10 onions - 1 tsp. capers per person = 1 giant jar - Who can say how many cornichons per person = 4 jars Ham-and-Cheese Croissant Bake. A charming, crowd-pleasing dish that you can assemble in advance, then bake the next day. Serve with some store-bought prewashed mixed greens splashed with Three-Minute Vinaigrette. Simple and chic. Mix the custard in two batches, each in a humongous bowl. (I have one of these and, honestly, can’t recommend it enough. Sure, it only comes in handy two-ish times a year, and my family makes fun of me for it, but when you need it, nothing else will do.) Bake in disposable aluminum pans. The math (recipe times eight for 64 servings): - 80 croissants (cheap supermarket ones! Lidl is known for them) - 3 lb. Gruyère (could do cheddar for a cheaper alt) - 3 lb. ham - 40 eggs - 8 pints heavy cream - 1 cup Dijon mustard - 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt* - 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. freshly ground black pepper - 2 tsp. freshly grated nutmeg - 2 handfuls thinly sliced chives *Please get Diamond Crystal for this measurement or adjust the quantity for another brand. The type of salt always matters, but especially so in large batches. Lunches Olive Bar Pasta Salad. As my colleague Rebecca Firkser writes, “The beauty of this pasta salad is its flexibility.” In your case, I would actually avoid the supermarket olive bar; it can get pricey in large quantities. Instead, find a Trader Joe’s or Costco and make the most of their shelf-stable antipasti offerings: marinated artichokes, roasted peppers, pitted olives, white beans, etc. More cost effective and just as yum. If you have an ambitious pal who wants to grill or sear chicken for a crowd, that would be a nice addition, estimating ½ breast per serving, or 30 breasts total. But not needed by any means! The math (recipe times 10 for 60 servings): - 20 garlic cloves - 5 cups finely chopped oil-packed sun-dried tomatoes - 2½ cups sun-dried tomato oil (cut with olive oil if you don’t have enough) - 3 cups plus 2 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, plus more to taste - 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (optional) - 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. freshly ground black pepper - 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt - 10 (1-lb.) boxes short pasta - 5 lb. small mozzarella balls or torn mozzarella - 10 quarts (40 cups) mixed antipasti (see above) Marinated Mixed Beans. I can hear someone scoffing in the distance at the audacity of the suggestion that you serve your beloved guests canned beans. But hear me out. They are delicious and cheap, can be assembled days in advance, and can confidently anchor an unfussy menu. Serve the beans in the same bowl linked above (see? Already coming in handy again), along with: crusty sliced bread; one to three cheeses (burrata, Brie, whatever strikes your fancy); soft-boiled eggs; olives and pickles; maybe some charcuterie. Nosh-y and fun. The math (recipe times 15—gasp—for 1 cup per person): - 15 shallots, finely chopped (use a food processor if you have one) - 2¾ cups plus 1 Tbsp. white wine vinegar, plus more to taste - 7½ cups finely chopped tender herbs (again with the food processor) - 5 cups olive oil - 30 (15.5-oz.) cans beans (bride’s pick!) - 5 Tbsp. Aleppo-style pepper or gochugaru - Kosher salt, to taste Drinks For breakfast, get some travel boxes of joe from a nearby coffee shop and call it a day. For either lunch: If one of your friends (read: not you) wants to go the extra mile, set up a vermouth-spritz bar with: bottles of rogue and blanc vermouth; cans of seltzer; lots of ice; lemon and lime wedges. Celebratory but won’t have everyone sloshed in the middle of the day. Readers, what’s the best wedding food you’ve ever had? (Yes, sure, it can be from your own wedding. But only if you’re telling the truth!) Share in the comments. Warmly, Emma Questions may be lightly edited for clarity, length, and style.

item.title: 5 Easy Ways Our Editors Turn Store-Bought Gnocchi Into Dinner
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.80
Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. That’s when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can quickly morph into delicious meals. This month it’s all about shelf-stable gnocchi. You would never expect an unassuming pouch of store-bought gnocchi, tucked tautly in plastic, to be good. But it is! The little potato dumplings have a pleasantly chew and just enough earthy savoriness to make them feel like more than a pantry fallback. The trick is how it’s made. Most shelf-stable gnocchi starts with dehydrated potato flakes, which give each dumpling a consistent texture and make the product stable enough to be stashed away in your pantry. A clever little bit of food engineering. And there’s no shortage of ways to put this ingredient to work. Stir-fry gnocchi in a hot skillet until they crisp up. Plop them into creamy sauces, where they bob along like buoys. Roast them alongside veg for a one-and-done dinner. There’s a whole lot this humble little pouch can do. Read on for how our editors cook with store-bought gnocchi at home. This Crispy Gnocchi Caprese is a staple in my household. Oddly enough, the last time I made it, I could only find the mini shelf-stable gnocchi in my grocery store. Who knew that even existed? Not me. Because of their small size, the little dots of pasta cooked up quicker than the standard ones, which means dinner was ready in no time. I used a haul of Sun Golds and cherry tomatoes, plus balls of mozzarella and torn basil dressed in bracing vinegar and fruity olive oil. Shoveling into my mouth with a spoon was the only correct way to eat. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking I love busting out shelf-stable gnocchi anytime I need to round out a meal with a carb and don’t want to make rice or pasta. While boiling them and tossing them in sauce is great, I also like to roast them on a sheet-pan so the outside gets crisp while the centers stay pillowy. You don’t have to schlep out a pot, don’t have to wait for water to boil, and you can snuggle them up next to proteins and veggies so everything cooks at once. My current favorite combo is sausage and broccoli rabe; the fat from the sausage sizzles the pasta while the broccoli rabe adds a peppery bite. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor I bought my first package of shelf-stable gnocchi to make a sheet-pan recipe that everyone in the office couldn’t stop talking about. And wow did it upend everything I’d assumed about the premade pasta. It now ends up in my shopping cart more often than not. But what a revelation trying former staffer Kendra Vaculin’s Gnocchi-Leek Soup With Greens still was. So enchanted by the crispy texture the oven provided, I’d entirely missed out on the plushy goodness of these little dumplings in soup. They’re the perfect addition to this weeknight-friendly dinner, adding heft and chew to an otherwise bright meal. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor Many, if not most, of my meals during the week are sheet-pan dinners. I love being able to toss something in the oven, then forget about it. Store-bought gnocchi is perfect for this treatment, and you don’t even need a recipe. Just preheat the oven to 400° or 425°. Dump a bag of gnocchi onto a sheet pan along with your vegetable of choice; say, broccoli florets, chopped bell peppers and onions, or halved brussels sprouts. Toss with a drizzle of olive oil and sprinkle of salt and pepper. Roast until the gnocchi are browned and the vegetables are tender. Add some melty cheese on top—funky raclette is my vote here. Keep baking (or even broil) until the cheese melts into gooey puddles. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director The first time I consumed vacuum-packed gnocchi was in 2022 when deputy food editor Hana Asbrink developed her recipe for Sheet-Pan Gnocchi With Soy-Dressed Mushrooms. I was taken aback. These little nondescript nubbins were…good?! A few months later, it was again Hana who introduced another new-to-me food, rosé tteokbokki. Completely smitten by this stew, I started to think about what I could use in place of the tteok, an ingredient my colleagues and I love very much, but can’t always find in every grocery store. The answer, it turns out, is a pouch of gnocchi. They’re doughy and dense, but in this recipe, that’s a good thing. As the gnocchi cook, their starch gently thickens the auburn sauce, and they soften into a comforting bite. —Shilpa Uskokovic, senior Test Kitchen editor

item.title: The 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Soup You'll Fall For
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.46
It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Each fall the first crimson-hued leaf drops to the ground, declaring the start of Pumpkin Season. And suddenly the perennial darling is everywhere. Pumpkin bread, pumpkin spice lattes, babies in pumpkin costumes, the list goes on. This year we’re declaring our favorite: a comforting curry pumpkin soup that comes together with just three ingredients. A three-ingredient soup may sound like a hack job, but think again. Each element—pumpkin purée, curry paste, and coconut milk—brings its own strength, creating a flavor that’s as cozy as a vintage sweater. Start by heating oil in a pot. Any type works, but I like to use unrefined coconut oil for a tropical fruitiness. From there, add a dollop of red curry paste. For a gentle warmth, turn to a jar of Thai Kitchen. To level up the spice, grab a can of Maesri, our Test Kitchen’s go-to brand. Cook the paste until it deepens to a sun-baked terra-cotta hue and is fragrant enough to tickle your nose. This step unleashes the nuances so you can taste every ingredient, like chiles, shallots, and lemongrass—none of which you had to prep yourself. Next, dump in cans of pumpkin purée and coconut milk, add some water, and let it all simmer. Taste and add salt if needed. That’s it. You’ve just made soup in 15 minutes. And a really good one at that! Feel free to gussy it up. I like to reserve a few spoonfuls of coconut milk from the can to swirl on top. (Once a food stylist, always a food stylist.) You could stir in baby spinach or top with cilantro or mint. For a hit of protein, poach a handful of shrimp in the simmering pot. However you serve it, this soup is bound to be an annual favorite, a nourishing bowl you can pull off even on the busiest fall night.

item.title: The Best Time to Visit Greece For Island-Hopping, Fewer Crowds, and Ideal Temperatures
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 6.94
Many people travel to Greece to spend time along its coast or on one of its myriad islands—a holiday destination that leaves salt on your skin. And there's good reason to come for that alone, although it gives little sense of a country that is roughly 80 percent mountainous. Beyond the beach there are farming villages where a scenic adventure can segue into local wine and seasonal, farm-to-table food. Some places are worth visiting for a particular occasion: the grape harvest, or an Orthodox feast that brings a village’s scattered families home. Naturally, the best time to visit Greece depends on which of those pleasures you want to build a trip around. An Easter visit calls for early hotel reservations, while an island holiday late in the year needs a close look at ferry schedules and hotel closing dates. For help with those choices, we draw on recommendations from Curated Greece co-founders Vasilis Sarmantas and Seetha Ramanathan, along with Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist Ronnie Liadis of Liadis Travel. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date. When is the best month to travel to Greece? September is the best month for a first visit to Greece that combines Athens with an island. The sea has had all summer to warm up, and ferries still serve the main routes frequently. Sarmantas and Ramanathan recommend it for beach holidays with fewer crowds than midsummer: In the Cyclades, the Aegean island group that includes Mykonos and Santorini, the most sought-after hotels remain busy well into the month of September, and sometimes even October. Late May to early June is these experts' other preferred window, near the start of a beach season —which generally lasts until early October. Liadis favors May for wildflowers and comfortable weather, though the sea can feel cool this time of year. The water is warmest from July to September, Sarmantas and Ramanathan told us. April and May are good months to visit Greece for sightseeing. Cooler weather lets you linger at exposed sites such as the Acropolis, the ancient hilltop citadel of Athens, and the open-air theater at Epidaurus on the Peloponnese peninsula southwest of Athens. For a trip in late October, look to Athens or larger southern islands such as Crete and Rhodes, where more hotels stay open year-round. On smaller resort islands, check hotel closing dates alongside ferry schedules before settling on a destination. What is the temperature in Greece by month? July and August are the hottest months, but keep in mind that an Athens forecast tells you little about a village high in the Pindus mountains of the northern mainland. The table below gives a broad seasonal guide using historical monthly averages for five destinations: Athens, the northern city of Thessaloniki, Corfu Town, Heraklion (on Crete), and Rhodes Town. Each range spans the lowest and highest city average in that group. These are benchmarks, so individual days, especially during heat waves, can be considerably hotter. | Month | Typical daytime high | Typical overnight low | |---|---|---| | January | 49–60°F | 34–48°F | | February | 52–60°F | 36–48°F | | March | 58–62°F | 40–50°F | | April | 66–68°F | 46–55°F | | May | 74–79°F | 54–60°F | | June | 81–88°F | 61–68°F | | July | 84–92°F | 65–72°F | | August | 83–92°F | 65–73°F | | September | 80–85°F | 59–69°F | | October | 70–76°F | 51–62°F | | November | 60–68°F | 44–56°F | | December | 52–63°F | 37–51°F | In summer, plan archaeological visits for the earliest entry time available, and check the site’s hours that morning since extreme heat can bring abrupt closures. The EU’s Copernicus climate service recorded extreme heat stress in parts of Greece during summer 2025. Hot, dry, and windy conditions also raise wildfire risk: consult Civil Protection’s daily risk map before a rural excursion and follow local restrictions and any 112 evacuation alerts. Keep in mind that a clear sky does not guarantee a smooth ferry crossing. The meltemi, a northerly wind over the Aegean, can take the edge off a hot beach afternoon while roughening the sea enough to disrupt ferries. When strong winds are forecast, confirm your sailing with the operator before heading to the port. What is the cheapest time to go to Greece? November through March is generally the cheapest time to go to Greece (apart from Christmas and New Year’s). Sarmantas and Ramanathan put the potential savings on international flights at 30 to 50 percent of high season's prices. In Athens and Thessaloniki, that lower hotel bill still comes with plenty to do: Museums stay open and neighborhood restaurants have local regulars to feed through winter. On the islands, check what will be open around your hotel, since many resorts close from roughly November to April. For an island holiday, compare May with late September and early October, when rates can ease before seasonal businesses close. Check the connections while you compare hotels. An extra flight or an overnight stay between ferries can easily absorb what you saved on the room. Orthodox Easter fills rooms in places known for their Holy Week traditions, and its date may differ from Western Easter. Keep an eye on those dates, and if they align with your travel plans, book early and plan to arrive before the weekend. On Good Friday, worshippers follow an epitaphios, a flower-covered bier representing Christ’s tomb, through the streets. The mood changes at midnight on Holy Saturday, when candles are lit to cries of Christos Anesti, “Christ is risen.” By Sunday, families are gathering around tables of roast lamb. In Corfu, the island’s philharmonics, or local brass bands, accompany the Good Friday processions. At 11 a.m. on Holy Saturday, residents drop botides, large clay pots, from balconies. An Easter Sunday arrival would miss both. Patmos, in the eastern Aegean, draws pilgrims to the cave where tradition places St. John’s writing of Revelation. During Holy Week, the abbot of the Monastery of St. John washes the feet of 12 monks in the square of Chora, the island’s capital, reenacting Christ’s gesture to his disciples. In the Peloponnese town of Leonidio, the midnight Resurrection service is the moment to be there, as illuminated paper balloons rise from parishes across town. When is peak season in Greece? July and August are the busiest and most expensive months, although the folks from Curated Greece say the broader high season now extends from early June into mid- or late September. This is when island travelers have the fullest choice of hotels and ferry departures. Book ahead for a particular room or sailing, especially if your dates leave little room to adjust. Around August 15, Greece’s own summer holidays add to the international rush. The Feast of the Dormition, known as Dekapentavgoustos and often called “summer Easter,” commemorates the Virgin Mary’s death. Many families return to their home villages, while pilgrims sail to the Cycladic island of Tinos to visit the revered icon at the Church of Panagia Evangelistria. Some make the ascent from the port on their knees. At village panigiria, the communal feasts held for religious holidays, music, and dancing continue long after church. These homecomings help explain why a ferry can be full even when its destination is absent from the usual resort itineraries. If you want to visit such destinations, book your ferry tickets as soon as the relevant schedule is available, particularly if you need space for a car. How many days are enough for a trip to Greece? If you’re visiting Greece for the first time, try to go for about seven nights for a mix of city and island experiences. “With a week, you can comfortably explore Athens in two or three days, spend a couple of days on one or two islands like Santorini for iconic views or Mykonos for beach time and night life, and possibly include a day trip to a key mainland cultural site like Delphi or Meteora,” as suggested by Sarmantas and Ramanathan. If you have extra time, an additional stop on the mainland or another island, such as Crete or the Peloponnese, can provide further depth, from archaeological wonders to beautiful natural landscapes. Liadis offers a helpful reminder about factoring in travel time: “I don’t recommend less than three nights on any island because a good part of the time is spent transferring from island to island. There are flights that connect to the islands via Athens, but the ferry system is reliable and convenient.” What is the nicest part of Greece to visit? For a first visit, Crete can fill a week without another ferry crossing. Of its two main cities, Heraklion puts you near Knossos, the Bronze Age Minoan palace, while Chania gives easier access to the western beaches and White Mountains. Either lets you combine the coast with lunches in mountain villages, though trying to cover both ends of Greece’s largest island leaves too much of the week to driving. In the village of Elos near Chania, chestnut celebrations in late October or early November put roasted nuts and sweets preserved in syrup on the table. In the Cyclades, decide how much of the holiday you want to spend looking at the sea and how much in it. Santorini’s caldera hotels overlook a sea-filled volcanic basin with steep shores, so the famous view does not come with a long sandy beach below. For that, consider Naxos, where inland farming villages also give you reasons to venture away from the coast. On nearby Paros, look around the fishing village of Naoussa for restaurants and hotels within reach of the beach. May and early fall allow more comfortable exploring, with warmer water at the later end of the season. Corfu, in the Ionian Sea, is a good option if you don't want to rely solely on the beach because there is a substantial town to explore. Centuries of Venetian rule shaped its old streets and its cooking. Order pastitsada, meat in a spiced tomato sauce served with pasta, for a sense of how that history survives at lunch. On Kefalonia, another Ionian island, more of the holiday involves driving through mountain country to reach the next cove, so it is a better choice when beach weather is the priority. Spring and fall are good times for a road trip through the Peloponnese. Stay in the harbor town of Nafplio for visits to Mycenae, a Bronze Age citadel, and the theater at Epidaurus. From there, head south toward the Mani peninsula’s stone tower houses or inland to mountainous Arcadia. Here, the roughly 47-mile Menalon Trail connects villages in eight sections of varying difficulty—the stage between Stemnitsa and Dimitsana, for example, follows old mule tracks past cliffside monasteries above the Lousios River and is demanding. Choose your section based on local advice rather than assuming that any village-to-village walk will be gentle. In central Greece, Athenians spend ski weekends in Arachova, a mountain town below Parnassos Ski Centre. Its tavernas serve grilled formaela, the peppery local cheese made from sheep’s or goat’s milk. Farther south in Arcadia, the village of Vytina puts the eight slopes of Mainalo Ski Centre within reach of a village stay. The nearby MANNA hotel occupies a restored 1929 sanatorium, surrounded by fir trees at about 3,900 feet. The forest also merits a visit after the spring or autumn rains, when local guides lead mushroom hunts. Snow has become less dependable in Greece’s mountains, so check lift conditions close to departure and choose bookings you can change. Zagori, in the mountainous Epirus region of northwestern Greece, deserves several days on foot. Its UNESCO-listed landscape includes stone villages connected by old paths and arched bridges, with forests around the Vikos Gorge that turn color in autumn. The stone staircase into Vradeto was the village’s only approach until 1973. Walking it makes the region’s former isolation easier to grasp, and the route can continue to the Beloi viewpoint above the gorge. The village of Aristi is a convenient base near the Voidomatis River, while Papigo gives access to hikes in the Tymfi mountains. Save high routes for snow-free conditions and ask locally about trails after rain. For a fall trip built around wine, start in Thessaloniki and explore the vineyards of Macedonia in northern Greece. The Naoussa here is a wine town, distinct from its namesake on Paros, and the surrounding vineyards grow the red grape Xinomavro. The Kir-Yianni wine estate offers tastings and vineyard tours year-round by reservation. For a harvest visit, ask the estate when it expects to pick before booking your dates. The timing can differ by several weeks between vineyards, even in the same year. Do Americans need a visa for Greece? US tourists can visit Greece without a visa for up to 90 days in any 180-day period, counting time spent elsewhere in the Schengen Area toward the same limit. According to the Department of State, the passport must be valid for at least three months beyond departure, with a blank page available for each stamp. ETIAS, the European Union’s planned travel authorization for visa-exempt visitors, is not yet operating and is not accepting applications. Its timetable has changed, so check the official EU site before departure for the launch date and any new requirements. Plan your stay • Where to Eat, Stay, and Play in Athens: From modern art galleries and tsipouro bars to traditional live-music rebetadikos for dancing the night away, • The Best Airbnbs in Santorini: Where to rent for a private slice of the Greek Island this summer. • A ‘Mamma Mia’–Inspired Packing List for Greece: Flowy white dresses, linen skirts, and overalls included. • 11 Best Hotels in Mykonos: Smart, stylish, and supremely laidback places to stay.

item.title: Disneyland Discount Tickets: September 2026 Guide
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 6.05
You just can’t argue with that Disney magic. Whether you’re a Disney adult or a begrudging occasional visitor, at some point throughout the day, a little bit of Disney dust will hit you. Maybe it’s the fireworks, or the rides, or the many, many Disney-shaped food items. If not that, it might be seeing the excitement on kids’ faces when they run into a princess, Avenger, or cartoon character IRL. I’m no Disney evangelist, but I would say that if you can’t have fun at a theme park, consider looking inward. (And okay, as a former resident of both California and Florida, I have spent more than my fair share of time at the parks on both coasts.) All that aside, trips to the parks are expensive, so if you’re here to find ways to save, I get it—below, find all the current discounts and promotions to be aware of before planning your next trip to Disneyland. Disneyland discounts for Magic Key holders For the uninitiated, annual passholders are called Magic Key holders, and they can pop in and out of Disneyland as they please (with some terms and conditions in there). Through September 7, these theme park enthusiasts can save up to 20% on select Standard and Premium room types at premium Disneyland Resort hotels. The offer is tailored to Sunday through Thursday night stays at Disney’s Grand Californian Hotel & Spa, Disneyland Hotel, The Villas at Disneyland Hotel, and Pixar Place Hotel. Of note, you must present a valid active Magic Key pass at check-in to secure the discounted rate. Disneyland discounts for military members Savings are available on an ongoing basis for active-duty and retired US military personnel, including the National Guard, Reservists, the US Coast Guard, the US Space Force, the Commissioned Corps of the Public Health Service (PHS), and the Commissioned Corps of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Tickets start at $98 for kids of these travelers and $104 for adults purchasing a one-day, one-park ticket. These tickets may not be combined with other ticket discounts or promotions, and cannot be sold or transferred. Locals get discounted Disney tickets for as little as $71 Through October 8, 2026, Anaheim, California, residents can purchase one-day passes for as little as $71. This is valid for any day visit taken by October 8. Proof of eligible residency, including a valid government-issued photo ID, is required for both purchase and admission. Save on multi-day Disneyland tickets While going to the parks for just one day is the most cost-effective option, your per-day cost does go down when you opt for multi-day tickets instead. For example, a one-day ticket will run you between $104 and $224 based on the date you select. If you go for two days, your price per day starts at $168; for three days, it drops to $142 and up per day; for four days, from $120 per day; and for five days, from $104 per day. A few things to note: Disneyland is much smaller than Disney World, with just two parks, so it is possible to cover a good amount of ground in a single day. However, especially if you’re coming from out of town, you may want a few days there so there’s less pressure to squeeze every ride and meal into a single day. There’s also the question of purchasing one-park-per-day tickets or upgrading to a Park Hopper ticket (an extra $100 per day). If you’re visiting for just one day, I’d suggest the Park Hopper ticket so you get to experience both parks. For multi-day trips, it really comes down to preference; you’ll want to decide between chunking out your park visits or having the freedom to roam back and forth between parks throughout the day (which, size-wise, is definitely doable). Save on food, merchandise, and add-ons with Disneyland discounts beyond tickets Tickets are one thing, but once you’re inside the park, it’s easy to rack up charges on dining, souvenirs, and add-on experiences. If you’re concerned about sticking to a budget, there are a few surefire ways to cut costs. For one, take a look at the gift card section next time you're at Target, Costco, or Sam’s Club, as they sometimes sell discounted Disney Gift Cards. If you’re interested in an additional credit card, new Disney Inspire Visa Card holders can earn up to $500 in the form of a $300 eGift to spend at the park and a $200 statement credit after you spend $1,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. You’ll also earn Disney Rewards Dollars on all card purchases, including: - 10% on card purchases made directly with Disney+, Hulu, and Stream.ESPN.com - 3% on card purchases at gas stations and most Disney US locations - 2% on card purchases at grocery stores and restaurants - 1% on all other card purchases When it comes to food, placing mobile orders via the Disneyland App can help you track food spending more easily and find quick options in place of more expensive sit-down meals. Lastly, consider dining off-property or at Downtown Disney to curb costs. On my last visit to Disneyland, I stayed right across the street from the entrance at Park Vue Inn—the proximity was amazing, and it had a pool and hot tub. Rates start at $229 a night, and rooms with kitchenettes are available, which make coming back midday to prep meals a breeze. Find more verified promo codes for theme parks and family-friendly vacations:

item.title: Newport, Rhode Island, Is New England’s Gilded Jewel—Here’s Where to Eat, Stay, and Play
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.24
Newport, Rhode Island, has certainly been having a moment as of late. You can attribute it to the Gilded Age dramas taking over small screens, the old-money aesthetic taking over TikTok, the Real Housewives of Rhode Island taking over Bravo, or just the fact that it’s beyond beautiful all year long. Either way, it’s undeniable that this compact coastal city has become a mecca of sorts for travelers eager to live out their East Coast fantasies—seafood, seersucker, sailboats, and all. But truth be told, Newport has never been a bad idea. The charming city has been a popular summer destination since the early 19th century, first as a playground for America’s elite, with families like the Vanderbilts and Astors building massive mansions along the water to serve as vacation homes (more on those later). Today, it’s a little less exclusive and a hot spot year-round, with New Englanders and international visitors alike spending sunny days becoming one with the sand at Easton’s Beach, breezy afternoons hiking the Cliff Walk, and chilly nights imbibing their way through Bowen’s Wharf before retreating to shingled cottages and luxurious hotels across town. If all that sounds like your kind of bliss, keep reading for a guide to seeing Newport in all its glory, as compiled by two New Yorkers who have been returning over and over again for the past decade. Here’s where to eat, stay, and play in the City by the Sea. Where to eat We’d argue the food and drink scene in Newport is reason enough to come to town, boasting old favorites and newer hubs that have given the city’s dining scene some fresh energy. Early birds, hit up Cru Cafe for a cozy bistro vibe and elevated comfort dishes like smoked salmon avocado toast. If you’re willing to wait in line, The Nitro Bar is a newer favorite (especially among influencers) with coffee and pastries that just might be worth the hype. Or, head to locally loved Franklin Spa, a legendary diner that hasn't changed its retro greasy-spoon energy in decades, and still serves one of the best lunches in town. Speaking of lunch, if the weather calls for it, take yours alfresco. Use Bowen’s Wharf as your hub: Belly up at 22 Bowen’s outdoor bar-restaurant area, have a casual seafood lunch at The Mooring, or get your clam chowder fix at The Black Pearl, with its lively dockside setting. You'll also find Clarke Cooke House, one of Newport's most popular restaurants, at the wharf. Its ship-like setting is one for the books, and the bistro offers a big menu spanning summer sushi to burgers, native cod, and even steak frites. For something less serious, Wally’s Weiners is another classic, and the kind of place you'll want to work into a day of wandering around Thames Street, known for being the center of the city. For harbor views and a Mediterranean-inspired menu, head to Flora, one of the newer names in town housed within the Gardiner House hotel. White Horse Tavern, on the other hand, offers classic Americana, with upscale farm-to-table dining (and stellar rum drinks) inside a building dating back to 1673. Crossing the bridge into Jamestown? Head to Beech if you want dinner to be the main event, with tasty, seasonal American fare headed up by locals. Where to stay Newport has no shortage of gorgeous hotels scattered from busy Thames Street to breezy Castle Hill Cove. Most guest rooms fall on the smaller side—this is a compact city, after all—but the best properties go big on glamour, offering gobsmacking views, old-world interiors, and exceptional in-house eateries and wellness facilities. Those looking for a taste of the Gilded Age should opt for spots like The Vanderbilt, an Auberge property built by a member of the Vanderbilt family in 1908, or Francis Malbone House, a Georgian-style mansion that dates back to 1760. If you’re all about location, location, location, book The Chanler at Cliff Walk for easy access to the popular waterfront hiking trail, Hammetts Hotel if you want to be steps from some of the city’s best bars and restaurants, or Forty 1º North Hotel Marina Resort to be so close to the water you’re basically swimming. Whether you’re staying there or not, you don't skip a stop inside Castle Hill Inn, a landmark Victorian mansion and one of the most iconic hotels in town. With an incredible location atop rocky bluffs that overlook the sailboat-studded ocean, the property’s Lawn Terrace is where you’ll want to grab a glass of Sauv Blanc and pretend you’re an Astor. Of course, hotels in Newport can be pricey, so if you’re on a budget or traveling with a group, an Airbnb might be a better bet—especially if the sound of a kitchen or common hangout space tickles your fancy. You can find smaller homes and apartments in Newport proper, like this four-bedroom with harbor views right downtown or this minimalist waterfront condo in the Historic District, but many visitors look to Middletown, Rhode Island—a town right outside Newport—for bigger, more affordable rentals. This adorable three-bedroom cottage with a shingled façade, for example, is technically in Middletown, but just five minutes from downtown Newport. Where to play The soul of Newport is rooted in the very concept of play. It’s a family-friendly destination and a romantic coastal escape; a place where sweet boutiques meet cool bars and Gilded Age history meets a working harbor. In the warmer months, chase the sea: Easton’s Beach is the most convenient option near town, Gooseberry Beach is tucked along Ocean Drive, and Second (or Sachuest) Beach offers a long stretch of sand and Atlantic surf. Post up at Second for a lobster roll and fries (sold from a beachside concession stand, the best), then grab an icy, refreshing Del’s Lemonade served from its iconic truck before heading home. Oh, and before you go, buy your next beach read at Commonwealth Books of Newport in the Historic Hill neighborhood. If you time it right, you can hit Newport's renowned Jazz Festival and the Newport Folk Festival, both hosted annually at the end of July (and sometimes running through early August). Plan in advance to secure tickets, as they can go quickly. For a more last-minute excursion that's completely free to the public, walk the Cliff Walk on the southeastern shoreline. The scenic coastal path threads between the Atlantic and the Newport Mansions, which, of course, you'll want to go inside and tour. If you’d rather be on the water than beside it, Sail Newport offers a Try Sailing experience, as well as afternoon-to-sunset sails. For something further from the coast, the International Tennis Hall of Fame is a great rainy day pit stop for exploring the history of the beloved sport and sniffing your way through the gardens surrounding the iconic grass courts. The Preserve in Blackstone Valley offers guided horseback tours, carriage rides, and sunset strolls, while Shephard’s Run Winery is a dreamy estate that gives you an excuse to head inland in South Kingstown for a tasting. As for a great Irish pub, The Fastnet has frosty beers on tap, while O’Brien’s is ever-abuzz and makes a mean house mudslide. If you want to make a night of it, have a drink and bites at Hotel Viking’s French-inspired Pescadou restaurant, then dance to the live DJ at its rooftop bar, Cap Club. Midtown Oyster Bar is perfect for a nightcap.

item.title: The 12 Best Places to Go Apple Picking Near New York City
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.76
As the leaves start to don their sienna coats and the mercury drops into the comfortable-sweater- weather range, autumn's many joys come to the fore. Whether it's the morning PSLs or decorating everything head-to-toe for Halloween, it's no secret why the year's third season is oft-cited as a favorite. And one of the best ways to celebrate fall is by going apple picking, as crowd-pleasers like Galas and Honeycrisps begin blushing into their reddish-gold skins. If you're based in the Big Apple (pun definitely intended), you'll be happy to know that several pastoral orchards and farms lie but a stone's throw away from New York City. Think New Jersey boltholes and easy upstate pit stops where you can fill your wicker basket to your heart's content and then some. And apples aren't the only fruit on offer—prepare to pick out pears for your next holiday dinner, or a pumpkin brimming with the potential to become a fearsome jack-o'-lantern. You can also extend your farm life fantasies by grabbing a seat on a family-friendly hayride, visiting a petting zoo, or being the hero of Thanksgiving by taking home a bottle or two of home-brew cider. Without further ado and in no particular order, here's where to find some of the best apple picking near New York City. Location: 1 Alstede Farms Ln, Chester, NJ Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 15 minutes by car If your palate asks for more than just the crisp bite of an heirloom apple, how about a satisfying bowl of homemade ice cream, smears of fresh-churned Amish butter, or steaming pans of ratatouille packed with farm-fresh produce? At Alstede, you're in luck—the farm has an online store that can deliver right to your door or local farmers market. Beyond apples, your whole grocery run practically lives here, whether you’re looking for eggplant, potatoes, or blueberries. But if it’s the ambience of the grounds that you find yourself obsessed with, they also host regular tours, seasonal harvest moon nights, and weddings for those who are truly in love with the venue. Where to stay nearby: Situated an eight-minute drive away from Chester in Peapack, New Jersey, Pendry Natirar charms with its historic brick mansion façade, incredible spa, and over 500 acres of parkland. Location: 9 Fishkill Farm Rd, Hopewell Junction, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 45 minutes by car Sample the Champagne of ciders when you have a sip of this farm's tree-to-bottle Treasury Cider. A family-run operation, as some of the best apple-picking orchards are, Fishkill Farms presses its own special breeds of dessert and bittersweet apples on-site to achieve the label's signature taste. And that's just one example of the level of effort you can expect here. Not only does the farm grow organic Crimson Crisp and Spartan apples, but it also farms most produce according to eco-certified and ecologically grown standards, which both have rigorous requirements for what the fruit is exposed to from seed to sale. But the fun’s not just in the fruit—dine at the Fishkill Farms Grill with all the Catskills surrounding you, or catch an evening performance of live music from a visiting band. Where to stay nearby: If you're apple picking here, you're practically steps away from Beacon and Cold Spring, two of upstate's most accessible gems (just hop on the Metro-North commuter line). We recommend staying at The Roundhouse in Beacon, a property that is a destination in and of itself for food, art, and shopping. Location: 306 NY-304, Congers, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour by car Welcome to your classic apple and pumpkin picking experience, where the beauty of the tried-and-true shines through. Having been around since 1891, the farm, now run by the practiced hands of fourth- and fifth-generation Davies family members, runs like a well-oiled machine. Admission is $17 in cash per person, and if you don’t know where to start with the over 5,000 trees and 27 different apple varieties on the farm, the website has a “Meet Our Apples” page where each is identified with a well-lit picture, ripening timeline, and flavor profile. If you’d like to enjoy even more fruits from the farm but not your own labor, the brewery arm, Red Barn Cidery, produces a host of its own ciders, local beers, and nonalcoholic options. Where to stay nearby: Stay right on the Hudson at a warm Airbnb that sets the mood with a crackling fireplace and wooden rafters across from Congers, in Ossining, New York. With four beds and two-and-a-half baths, this Hudson Valley escape is plenty capable of hosting the whole family. Location: 45 Ball Rd, Warwick, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 45 minutes by car; 3 hours by train Sprawling orchard grounds have never been more accessible than at Masker—open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. every day of the week rather than being condition- or season-dependent. The orchard is also designed for driving through, so you can take your car right up to the trees you want to pick from or picnic under.
