Beforehand, consult the website banner that clearly states which varieties are ready for picking, and download the map of the orchard so you’ll know ahead of time that Red Delicious apples can be found on the corner of “Strudel” and “Pie” lanes. Where to stay nearby: Sometimes, the greatest gift our travels can bestow upon us is a true sense of quiet. There's no better place to seek it in Warwick than at this cozy cabin Airbnb you'll want to claim as your own neck of the woods. Location: 250 Hurds Rd, Clintondale, NY Distance from NYC: About 2 hours by car The name might’ve already clued you in, but this farm goes all out for the kids—there’s a busy bee train, chances to leave their mark on the Chalk Bus, a tire climbing wall, a giant bounce pillow, and that’s not even to mention the petting zoo or 2.5-acre corn maze. While there’s more than enough to keep the whole family engaged with those activities alone, the best time to visit is throughout October, when the lion’s share of the farm’s apples are ripe, and the pumpkins are ready to pick too. Where to stay nearby: Check in a 15-minute drive across the river at The Heartwood at Vassar in Poughkeepsie, a gorgeous college town. Soak in the autumnal, academic atmosphere from one of the 50 rooms and suites at this recently opened property. Location: 244 Werimus Rd, Hillsdale, NJ Distance from NYC: About 1 hour by car; 1 hour and 30 minutes by train This farm puts its vast-spanning orchards to use as a canvas for one of the best light shows in the tristate area. In the daytime throughout the summer and fall months, peaches and apples are the main attraction, but when the sun sets during the Halloween season, new life is breathed into the orchards as they host a ghoulish light extravaganza peppered with skeletons, jack-o'-lanterns, and a gallery of classic monsters. During the winter months, the Orchard of Lights features giant snowflakes, reindeer, and even Dr. Seuss’s Grinch. Where to stay nearby: If fall doesn't feel complete to you without a little side of spookiness, get right in the middle of the action at the Sleepy Hollow Hotel. The property features weeknight fall specials, reduced rates for locals interested in a staycation, and a restaurant that's open all day. Location: 91 Wemrock Rd, Freehold, NJ Distance from NYC: About 2 hours by car Owned and operated by the Applegate family for the past 118 years, Battleview is the oldest pick-your-own farm in New Jersey. This year, the orchard is offering 19 varieties of apples throughout the fall, and it also has year-round opportunities to pick sour cherries, strawberries, peaches, and pumpkins. As kids explore some of the 130-acre grounds on the seasonal hayride, parents can walk the aisles of the on-site country store stocked with favorites like house-made cider and fresh-baked pies, and speciality items such as the customizable fruit baskets. Its website has Applegate family recipes for every variety of fruit the orchard cultivates. Where to stay nearby: Did someone call for a Hallmark movie set? Look no further than this quiet and cozy Airbnb in Monroe Township that boasts plenty of space, perfect for a multigenerational outing. The wraparound porch was practically made for fall evenings spent watching the wind rustle through the tree line. Location: 139 Hardscrabble Rd, North Salem, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 30 minutes by car These orchards don't just offer some of the best apple picking near New York City—they're a celebration of all things autumnal. The best time to visit is throughout September and October, when Outhouse puts on its Fall Festival. Every corner of the grounds offers something built to entertain, whether it's racing rubber ducks or blowing bubbles for the little ones, hayrides for the whole family, or snacking on wood-fired pizza and washing it down with homemade hard cider for food lovers. With 12 apple varieties that ripen during the pick-your-own season, there’s enough diversity to satisfy fans of tangy McIntoshes and honey-sweet Jonamacs alike. Where to stay nearby: When it comes to a weekend escape near North Salem, you don't have to choose between woodsy or luxurious. Instead, ask yourself, “por qué no los dos?” with stays like the Martha Stewart–approved Bedford Post Inn waiting to welcome you in. Location: 82 Four Corners Rd, Warwick, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 45 minutes by car If you’ve ever wanted to live inside a Bob Ross painting, this is the orchard for you. At Apple Dave’s, the farm’s own lake is a backdrop for sweeping views of the northern Appalachian Mountains. Meandering walking trails through the trees plus an on-site store filled with fresh produce and charming Halloween decor provide casual yet engaging activities for a fun day out with the family. But for the 21+ crowd, the distillery offers Apple Jacks, Shawangunk wines, and cocktails enhanced by the farm’s produce amongst the usual suspects of local beers and ciders. Where to stay nearby: Cozy and tiny are two words that fit hand-in-hand, and you'll find both qualities in spades at this minimalist cottage that subtly signals “designer” with its muted tones and plush Scandi-coded furnishings. Location: 62 Granite Springs Rd, Granite Springs, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 30 minutes by car Beyond its orchards, Stuart’s is also home to a Christmas tree farm and bakery that churns out irresistible cider donuts and fresh-baked pies. The farm also does not charge entrance or parking fees, meaning visitors are only charged for what they pick and purchase at the store. But this is definitely one of those trips where the journey getting there is just as worth it as the destination—driving through Granite Springs, visitors get to experience Westchester at its autumnal best, as the mountains pass by in a montage of gold and orange. Where to stay nearby: Extend your itinerary beyond the main event of apple picking by staying the weekend at Hotel MTK Mount Kisco, which sits at the junction of the Caramoor Center for Music and the Arts and Rockefeller State Park Preserve. Location: 155 N Ohioville Rd, New Paltz, NY Distance from NYC: About 2 hours by car This is an orchard for the epicurean. After you spend an afternoon at the orchard plucking Fujis, Galas, Honeycrisps, and Cortlandts, take the load off at Twin Star’s on-site restaurant. Wood-fired pizzas are sumptuous and savory, with options such as sweet sausage and broccoli rabe and Dragon’s Breath for the daring. Inclusive items like the vegan pizza and black bean burger also feature on the menu to accommodate dietary preferences. And for those truly looking to indulge, be sure to visit on Saturdays and Sundays for the low-and-slow barbecue and to stack your plate with fall-apart ribs and brisket. Where to stay nearby: Experience living history at Mohonk Mountain House, where you will be immersed in the wholesome pastimes and stunning natural beauty of an American icon. This historic backdrop stays revitalized with a slate of fresh offerings—don't skip the spa. Location: 2 S Mountain Rd, Pomona, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour by car; 2 hours by train These orchards in the quaint town of Pomona are the ideal weekend day trip out of the city. In addition to sampling some of the newest and coolest apple varieties on the market (who wouldn’t want to take a bite out of a Ludacrisp?), the bakery offers everything from timeless apple pies to peanut butter custard pies that are begging to be your next holiday dinner centerpiece. While there’s enough to occupy your Saturday and Sunday afternoons, the farm also has a strong presence at local farmers markets such as Bronxville, Riverdale, and White Plains. Where to stay nearby: Don't just stop at the leaf-peeping. Take in everything fall has to offer by the water at AMC Corman Harriman Outdoor Center hotel, where guests can take out free kayaks and paddleboats for a new flavor of fall adventure.

item.title: At Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy, Exploring Eastern Indonesia by Boat and Board
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.52
There are not many places left in the world like the tip of Rote. It’s a fragment of coastline on an island off West Timor, which itself is a far-flung extremity of the eastern Indonesian archipelago, closer to Darwin than Jakarta. Aussie surfers started coming here 40-odd years ago, arriving for Rote’s long, clean waves, magicked up by a rare blend of wind, swell, and bathymetry. There are other elements that give Rote its dream-come-true energy: tropical weather, white sand beaches, dense fringes of coconut palms, lingering sunsets, a steady trade wind in the dry season that keeps the mosquitoes down. Rote is, alluringly, always on island time. Crucially, it’s not easy to reach—good for surfers who don’t much like sharing a wave. The long journey to get here is why Rote has stayed Rote, one of the most wonderfully inconvenient places out there. Amid all this remoteness, the first top-end resort has just opened, Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy, sister property to Nihi Sumba, west of here. Both these hotels—a few hundred miles apart—front one of the most coveted waves in the world. When I visit, the hotel is still taking shape. At the eastern end of the bay is a clutch of thoughtfully designed, thatched, low-rise villas, each with a swimming pool; the interiors in mine use local materials such as lontar palm and ikat textiles. The gathering place is beach club Nammo, with its poolside restaurant and watersports instructors, smack in front of Bo’a break. Here I wait for the tide to turn before paddling out. When Nihi Rote launches fully in October, there will be 21 villas, three pools, a spa, a pump track, and a golf simulator. It is also planning to build and sell multimillion-dollar residences alongside the property. One night, I’m invited to Rote Hospitality Academy, where Timorese trainees have prepared an endearing evening of traditional song and dance; storytelling; and a feast of coconut rice with lemongrass, rendang beef stew, and grilled fish with sambal. Sitting around the fire pit, toes in the sand, the students share stories with me about the cuisine; traditional string instrument sasando, made of bamboo; and their struggles with learning to swim. For many, it is their first job, or their first job in hospitality, and it’s been a fast-track whirlwind. Before the hotel opened, they had already hosted a big-splash 50th birthday party for its owner, Michael Schwab, son of investment firm founder Charles Schwab. “We’ve never seen anything like this on Rote,” says one student. Change is not always easy, especially in a place that, until recently, relied on seaweed farming and fishing. I feel a pang as I drive past Rote’s cinder-block and tin-roof huts, women on the porch pausing to wave as they plait each other’s hair, sepia-tinged frangipani blossoms strewn on the ground. Rote has long been open to outsiders—and that is increasingly rare in this world of ours. “Do you live here?” is a regular refrain from locals as I freewheel around town. It is always uttered with a smile—on the harbor, at a café, down on the beach. When I reply that I am passing through, they say: Come and live here, you are welcome, bring your family. Many have taken up such invitations, seduced by the island’s stress-free, go-slow rhythm. “We were also passing through,” a South African surfer tells me, echoing my line. “But that was two years ago.” He and his partner have had a baby, bought some land, and are now building a cottage. I borrow a bike to explore the main coastal road, sealed but potholed and set back from the seafront, with sandy lanes trailing down to the beaches. Village merges into village, and the only demarcations are bollards painted “selamat datang" (meaning welcome) or a trio of life-sized crucifixes, prettily decorated despite being a symbol of execution. One is painted lavender, another strewn with flowers. The churches here are enormous and numerous, towering vaulted monuments, one resembling a gigantic Noah’s Ark. Catholic, a man tells me, then to be contradicted by his wife: no, Presbyterian. Another says Methodist. The pastor tells me Calvinist. Tropical Christianity, let’s agree on, and fervent. At Easter, I’m told, crowds enact the Stations of the Cross, parading through the streets in the garb of Roman soldiers. The rest of the year, there’s not much more than a scrap of traffic. One day I drive 40 minutes and count two motorbikes and one water bowser. I reach the end of a road that peters out into scrub, nothing beyond and nowhere for me to go. Although there are few vehicles, there are scads of roadside vendors selling gasoline in fancy glass bottles that look more like love potions. Lines of laundry flap. Animals are everywhere: languorous cows, silky-haired goats atop bathroom-tiled gravestones, and broods of chickens crossing the road, I could only assume, to get to the other side. This easy-going scene belies the region’s bloody colonial history. Timor was fought over by the Dutch and Portuguese—a battle rooted in the sandalwood and spice trade—resulting in its split into East and West. The British muscled in, but only for a few years, and the Japanese occupied the area during the Second World War. Remnants of history and cultural heritage are not obvious at first glance; some can be seen in the weaving of tessellated tenun ikat textiles and the ti’i langga, resembling a ten-gallon cowboy hat made of lontar palm, worn by men, with a phallic spike on the brim. The best way to explore Rote, with its offshore islands, reefs, and consistent breaks, is by boat. At one rocky outcrop I find a vast cave of screeching fruit bats. I drop into the water with a mask and snorkel and fast-float in the choppy current to spy on triggerfish and parrotfish. I was told oceanic manta ray and whale sharks congregate here, so I focus my eyes towards the deep, which falls away fast; the next strike of land is Australia. I check out surf sites, ending up on the far side of Ndana Island, Indonesia’s most southerly point. Nobody is around. I spend most of my time crashing and splashing, but nothing can beat the occasional moment standing aloft, feeling the push of a wave, the water so clear I can see fish dashing about the coral. A couple of haggard, sun-smashed Aussie surfers arrive close to the end of the day, so I bow out of the wave, instead bobbing about straddling my board to watch the colors of the sky shift. Back on land I meet locals and newcomers with surf shacks, market stalls, and motorbike hire shops. Hotelier Mick Fogarty is just opening on Rote, after more than 30 years in Bali running the fabled Mick’s Place on Bingin Beach. When I ask him if he feels an ache about leaving Bali, he says “no” before I’ve finished the question. He and his Danish wife, Sascha Hansen, have three pretty self-catering bungalows, and, sensibly, used the best land to build a house for themselves. “We were going to build a restaurant but then thought, why don’t we build a home,” says Fogarty. That sums up the spirit of those who come to Rote. “Everyone moves here for the lifestyle,” he continues, “not to turn a profit, just to sustain a life.” After sunset, when everyone lopes back from the beach, there are a few couples hitching their gear onto motor scooters and a few families carrying babies, bags, and boards, toddlers in tow. Everyone’s sandy with wet, tangled hair. It’s a strong, fit, healthy scene. “No drugs, no nightclubs," as I keep hearing on repeat. One hotel owner points out, “many of the people here already had their 20 crazy years, so now we can all chill.” Another labels Rote a “retirement village for surfers, who come for peace and quiet." Carla Lázaro Ferro from the Canary Islands calls it differently. She lived here, then moved to Berlin, where she found herself “crying for Rote." “Here you feel you can give back. Life is more meaningful, more chaotic, more free,” she tells me. On my last night, I sleep out on the deck of my villa at Ferro’s Bo’a Vida resort, overlooking the Bo’a wave and the Timor Sea. Here on the southern edge of Indonesia, the stars glow like light bulbs, even on the horizon. Only the dazzle of the rising moon dims them. I feel as far away as I could be. Where to stay Following the success of its sister resort in Sumba (to the west of Rote), the 21-villa Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy on Bo’a Beach opens the renowned surf sites to top-end travelers. Villas are a mix of one-bedroom, duplex, and family-style set-ups, and larger residences are planned. The westerly rooms have the best views of the Bo’a break. Bo'a Vida owner Carla Lázaro Ferro opened a thatched shack 15 years ago atop a rocky outcrop at the end of Bo’a Beach, overlooking the legendary wave of the same name and the sunset beyond. Now she has six climate-conscious villas, five of which were designed by her husband, award-winning architect Álvaro Carrillo Eguilaz, with stone paths meandering down to slips of sand and the yoga sala. Ferro also runs the café Indika in town, which serves fruit bowls until 5:30 p.m., when everyone heads out to catch a wave. Nat and Matt Thistlewaite of Rote Island Huts came here from Australia in 2011 after finding the island of Rote on Google Earth. They arrived with the aim of creating a nonprofit holiday retreat that channeled income into local education and the community. There are five simple huts: three are family-style with bunks, all have beachfront access. It’s a heartening enterprise, and they are now preparing to hand over management to local Rotenese, as they always intended. Pika and Pascal Chevillot, a Slovenian and a Frenchman, used to own Sardine, one of Bali’s top restaurants. At Sardine Beach Rote, they’ve created a spectacular three-villa property in five acres of gardens on one of the island’s best beaches. The rooms use lontar palm and coconut leaf to create traditional roofing, paneled walls, and sconces. Pascal’s breakfast is a real event, with Parmesan omelettes and smoked Spanish mackerel. I notice a copy of Tao Te Ching on a side table, which just about sums up the place. Aussie Mick Fogarty and Sascha Hansen from Denmark are the creators of Mick’s Place Rote, three delightful beachfront bungalows with private courtyards in a glade of coconut trees. The couple are strong on sustainability, harnessing solar power, reusing grey water for the gardens, and lending bicycles for guests to get around on. There's a one-week stay minimum, and the lap pool is set to be the gathering place. Close to the T-Land break at Nemberala Beach, Spaniards Julia Davila Solana and Jose Miguel Murgui have built 81 Palms and its six A-frame cabins on the soft sand, plus they’ve recently opened four smaller bungalows at their new Next Door property. The Spanish restaurant is the best place for dinner in Rote, with former Michelin-starred Murgui in the kitchen cooking up gazpacho, tapas, and seafood paella. Natural World Safaris can arrange an 11-day trip combining a B&B stay at COMO Uma Ubud on Bali and a seven-night full-board stay at NIHI Rote & Hospitality Academy on Rote, from £5,800 per person. The price is based on two people sharing and includes all transfers and domestic flights. International airfare is excluded. This story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Sennheiser Coupon Codes & Discounts | September 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.28
German audio brand Sennheiser has made its mark on all types of travel experiences, from providing the ideal in-flight headphones for the Concorde, to developing microphones favored by artists on stages across the globe, to launching immersive, speakerless audio for vehicles. To put it simply, you can’t travel well without good sound, and if you’re in the market for noise-canceling headphones that’ll get you through that next long-haul flight, this audio brand’s got you covered. Established in 1945, Sennheiser has long been a household name among audiophiles, but has also won the ears of casual listeners. It all began when Dr. Ing. Fritz Sennheiser founded Laboratorium Wennebostel outside of Hanover, which later became Sennheiser Electronic. The first product was the DM 1 microphone, made for Siemens. The company has been credited with creating the world’s first open-back headphones in 1968, and in 1991, it launched the legendary Orpheus electrostatic headphone (whose successor would be the HE 1 in 2015), followed by the Evolution Microphone Series in 1999. The very best in sound technology doesn’t come cheap; if you’d like to shop the Sennheiser brand, read on for the coupon codes, discounts, and free shipping offers to use before making a purchase. Use a Sennheiser coupon code for 10% off your first order If you’re new to the brand, you’re in luck: First-time customers can sign up for the official Sennheiser newsletter to receive an exclusive 10% off coupon for their initial purchase, up to $100. And once you’re subscribed, you can stay informed about new product launches, flash sales, and subscriber-only promotions—all delivered directly to your inbox. Subscribers can also benefit from free shipping on all orders sitewide with no minimum spend, ensuring extra savings on every purchase. Once you sign up, the discount and free shipping will expire by December 31, 2026, so make sure you put it to use before then. Keep an eye out for limited-time offers at Sennheiser Sennheiser is currently offering limited-time discounts on industry-standard gear, including headphones and soundbars—often available without a specific code. Right now, for instance, the AMBEO Soundbar Max Refurbished has been marked down from $2,999 to $1,299.5, rounding out to a total saving of $1,700. This home theater tool will level up how you watch movies, with a 3D audio experience. Students, military members, and first responders can enjoy a 15% discount Sennheiser is committed to honoring those who serve our communities, from students learning how to make music to nurses who commute to work with a pair of headphones. As a gesture of gratitude, the company offers a 15% discount code to military personnel, veterans, government employees, medical professionals, first responders, seniors, students, and teachers. All you have to do is verify your status through ID.me. Once you’ve completed your verification, you’ll be given a unique promo code, which you can enter into the “Discount Code” field when purchasing an item on the Sennheiser site. Unfortunately, this code can’t be combined with other offers. Shop refurbished Sennheiser products at a discount without a code If you don’t mind giving up on that shiny new toy feeling, Sennheiser offers discounts on "like-new" products that have undergone professional inspection, testing, and restoration to meet original performance standards. You can find previous-generation models, open-box items, or cosmetic-blemish products—like the HD 560S or HD 599 headphones—at a fraction of their price. All refurbished products typically come with a warranty, ensuring peace of mind with your purchase, similar to new items. What to do if your Sennheiser coupon code isn’t working If your Sennheiser coupon code isn't working, be sure to check for typos, extra spaces, or incorrect capitalization, as well as any terms and conditions. The 10% newsletter sign-up promo code, for instance, is capped at a $100 discount and limited to first-time users only. You can also try clearing your browser’s cache and cookies, or switching devices or browsers. When all else fails, Sennheiser's Consumer Experience team is there to help.

item.title: 9 Standout Galapagos Cruises for Sailing the Bucket-List Wildlife Destination
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.64
An extraordinary archipelago 600 miles off the coast of Ecuador, the Galapagos promise a once-in-a-lifetime travel experience—and many agree there's no better way to visit, than by ship. Unlike the typical island-hopping cruise itinerary you'll find elsewhere, Galapagos Island cruises invite travelers to experience some of the most unspoiled environments on earth. The vessels here are small, too—sometimes accommodating as few as 16 passengers. There are no water parks, Broadway-style shows, or casinos on board. Instead, pristine surroundings, uninhabited islands, and rare wildlife are the featured attractions. These cruise itineraries offer the chance to get up close to giant tortoises and playful sea lions, to snorkel among coral and stingrays, and look for rare birds like the blue-footed booby, a species only found in parts of the Pacific Ocean. Leave the logistics to your captain, and let yourself enjoy an incredible adventure of hiking through untouched natural environments or kayaking, paddleboarding, or snorkeling through one of the most interesting parts of the Pacific Ocean. After all, in the Galapagos, animals outnumber people and some of the most interesting scenes are found on the water. Cruises to this remote region usually span about a week and visit multiple islands. And while it is generally an expensive destination, given the hard-to-reach nature of the islands, there are some more affordable ways to cross off this bucket-list trip. Below, we cover nine of the best Galapagos cruises—with options for every type of traveler. The best Galapagos cruise for luxury travelers Ecoventura offers one of the most luxurious—and family-friendly—cruises in the Galapagos. The company operates three expedition yachts, Origin, Theory, and Evolve, each of which can accommodate 20 guests across 10 staterooms. Children six and up are welcome on board, and some staterooms can be connected to create spacious family suites. The crew is the shining star of these yachts, ensuring personalized service, pleasant surprises—like a pirate-themed send-off party to end the trip—and a menu to suit every palate. There’s a breakfast buffet every morning featuring Ecuadorian specialties and international favorites, and a multicourse dinner every night, with plenty of options for vegetarians. Onboard Ecoventura’s yachts, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, snorkeling gear, and zodiacs are on offer. There’s also a hot tub, fitness center, and plenty of outdoor nooks for taking in the unforgettable views. Off the ship, experienced naturalists lead daily excursions to lava fields, scenic viewpoints, idyllic snorkeling spots, and secluded beaches. Even if you're new to watersports like snorkeling, the ship’s patient guides will teach you how to get comfortable in the water so you can enjoy swimming among turtles, fish, and stingrays. The best Galapagos cruise for solo travelers Join a small group of future friends on the Reina Silvia Voyager, G Adventures’ newest catamaran that’s custom-built for sailing the Galapagos. Two of its 10 cabins feature single beds and are reserved for solo travelers. All come with a private bathroom, desk, and a large picture window to frame the pristine Galapagos views beyond. A 10-day itinerary starts and ends in Quito, taking guests on a journey through the Central and East Islands to look for sea lions, iguanas, and a seemingly endless variety of birds. Go kayaking, snorkeling, scuba diving, or paddleboarding—or kick back and relax on the spacious sundeck while enjoying some of the most unspoiled views in the world. There’s a chef on board to ensure you never go hungry, a hot tub to soothe any sore muscles, lots of spaces for socializing when you want to, and a bar that’s perfect for sunset cocktails—with or without your shipmates. The best Galapagos cruise for travelers craving personal space The Celebrity Flora is one of the largest ships sailing the Galapagos Islands, but don’t expect it to be packed with crowds. While it's about twice the size of the Celebrity Xploration, which also sails to the Galapagos, the Flora carries the same number of people—about 100. The size difference gives the ship a more spacious feel and roomier suites that start at around 224 square feet. Some cabins have floor-to-ceiling windows that open up to make your suite feel like it has a balcony. Others have actual balconies, some as large as 321 square feet. These eco-conscious ships are designed to navigate the most remote parts of the Galapagos Islands. There’s also a retractable marina onboard to make it easier for travelers with mobility issues to get in and out of the vessels ferrying them from ship to shore. The best Galapagos catamaran cruise Avalon Waterways may be better known for its European river cruises, but it also sails the Galapagos Islands, with a chartered luxury catamaran, the Treasure of the Galapagos. The boat can accommodate a maximum of 16 guests and offers a rare amenity in the Galapagos: private balconies. The largest suite comes in at 430 square feet and features not one but two private outdoor spaces. Guests feast on dishes from creative, locally inspired menus featuring seasonal ingredients. There’s also a hot tub and a naturalist on board, and fares include wine with dinner as well as coffee, tea, and water. The best Galapagos cruise for foodies There may be few better places to eat in the Galapagos than The Grill, one of two restaurants on board the Silver Origin, a 100-passenger ship operated by the luxury cruise line Silversea. The Grill serves up premium cuts of meat cooked tableside atop fiery lava stones. Indulge in locally sourced lobster, Andean quinoa, and fresh Galapagos-caught fish. Meals at The Grill are served alfresco, and it’s hard to find a better view for dinner than these natural landscapes. Elsewhere onboard, guests can learn the art of ceviche-making from the ship’s chef and sample Ecuadorian cheese that has been aged in lava tubes. The smallest suites on board are 325 square feet, and many come with balconies. Even the showers offer ocean views, and there’s butler service onboard for anything you might need. While the Silver Origin is another one of the largest ships sailing the Galapagos Islands, these voyages tend to sell out—book early. The best Galapagos cruise for adventure seekers Sailings on board the La Pinta, operated by Uncruise, are designed for adventurous spirits who also appreciate time to unwind. This isn’t the newest or most luxurious ship sailing the Galapagos, but it’s comfortable, unpretentious, and recently refurbished. Onboard this 48-passenger yacht, you’ll find plenty of gear: kayaks, paddleboards, snorkeling equipment, scuba equipment, and a glass-bottom boat included. The itinerary includes visits to seven islands and islets as well as a visit to the Charles Darwin Research Station. Hike Dragon Hill on Isla Santa Cruz while looking for iguanas and flamingos, paddleboard alongside sea lions at Isla Floreana, or enjoy a stroll along a secluded white-sand beach. If you think cruising isn’t your thing, Uncruise might just change your mind. The best Galapagos cruise for science lovers If ever you’ve wondered what life would be like as a scientist, HX Expeditions has the Galapagos cruise for you. The company operates a Citizen Science Program on board the MS Santa Cruz II, enlisting guests to help with completing research projects. Guests can join onboard researchers in collecting samples, learn to make field observations, and visit the onboard science lab to analyze materials and work with experts to process data. Between following in the footsteps of Charles Darwin, visiting his namesake research station, and working with onboard researchers, this is a vacation where learning is accessible—and prioritized. The best affordable Galapagos cruise For travelers craving the wild majesty of the Galapagos at a more affordable price, Nature Galapagos & Ecuador delivers an authentic, expertly curated experience that doesn’t compromise on adventure nor break the budget. Specializing in small-ship and land-based tours, their budget-class cruises—aboard intimate, 8 to 10-person yachts like the New Flamingo and Merak—offer access to remote islands, expert bilingual naturalist guides, and daily excursions that bring you face-to-face with marine iguanas and Galapagos tortoises. Accommodations are simple but comfortable, with snorkeling gear, meals, and interisland logistics seamlessly included. Expect to spend around $3,000 for a four‑ to five‑night cruise, compared to about $7,600 for a seven-night sailing on G Adventures. The best Galapagos cruise for kids Inspire your kids to learn about science and exploration by hopping on board the National Geographic Gemini, a ship that sails the Galapagos as part of a partnership between Lindblad Expeditions and National Geographic. These journeys, led by National Geographic experts, give kids the chance to become National Geographic Explorers-In-Training. The exclusive, hands-on program is designed to teach kids about geographical exploration and scientific research. The National Geographic Gemini can accommodate up to 48 passengers in 27 suites. More than a dozen suites come with private balconies, and one of those balconies is large enough to accommodate a private hot tub. But don’t fret if that suite is already booked; there’s a whirlpool hot tub on the sundeck that’s open to all guests. There’s also a library, well-stocked bar, and meals made with locally sourced ingredients on board. FAQ: How early should I book a Galapagos cruise? For the widest selection of vessels and sailing dates, aim to book your cruise four to nine months ahead of your intended sailing. More spontaneous travelers may find last-minute deals booking two to eight weeks ahead of their intended departure, though some itineraries will be sold out by then. Where do I embark on a Galapagos cruise? Getting to the Galapagos requires some logistical planning. After flying into Quito or Guayaquil, passengers typically spend a night in one of these mainland destinations before flying to the islands to board their ships. Your cruise line will tell you where to be on the islands for your departure, and in some cases, flights from the mainland will be included (or booked for an additional fee). When is the best time to cruise the Galapagos Islands? With a consistently mild climate year-round, the Galapagos can be visited at any time, although certain seasons offer exceptional wildlife viewing. December is when the giant tortoises hatch, and July marks the mating season for blue-footed boobies and short-eared owls. In April and May, marine iguanas typically hatch, while sea turtles begin laying their eggs at the start of the year. Given the diverse wildlife and year-round natural phenomena, there's never a "wrong" time to visit the islands. Are Galapagos cruises expensive? The Galapagos Islands aren’t a bargain destination. Expect to pay somewhere between $5,000 and $12,000 per traveler, depending on the ship, itinerary, and length of the voyage, though there are options starting in the $3,000s. What kind of wildlife can I expect to see on a Galapagos cruise? The Galapagos Islands are renowned for their unique wildlife, including giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies, and sea lions. The islands’ ecosystems are so diverse that you can see a variety of species in different environments, from volcanic shores to lush highlands. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Paris Wilson.

item.title: The Best Things to Do in Monaco—the Crown Jewel of the French Riviera
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.58
Monaco’s ritzy reputation began more than 150 years ago with the debut of the James Bond-famous Belle Époque-style Casino de Monte-Carlo. Throw in a fresco-adorned clifftop palace, the super yacht–lined harbor, and one of the most anticipated events in the luxury sports industry’s social calendar (the Monaco Grand Prix), and it’s no wonder the principality has emerged as a summertime playground for jetsetters and royalty alike. Flanked by the Mediterranean Sea and the French Alps, the petite principality may be the world’s second-smallest state, but with freshly revamped grande dame hotels, a sleek new seaside promenade, and two billion dollar land expansion project Mareterra—which rapidly earned the nickname “world’s most expensive neighborhood”—Monaco is proving it’s more than royals and race cars. There’s also the prestigious Rolex Monte-Carlo Masters tennis tournament—and some seats even come with panoramic Mediterranean Sea views, too. While the principality may claim a few superlatives—with the annual Monaco Yacht Show, the unofficial closer to high season, often touting the world’s priciest super yacht—it’s much more accessible than most travelers realize. And thanks to an uptick in direct seasonal flights, it’s even easier to reach. Here’s where to go and what to do when you get there. Getting there and around The Nice airport is the gateway to the French Riviera, and now you can fly direct year-round from New York (JFK) or Newark with business-class-only La Compagnie; seasonally from Atlanta, Philadelphia, and Washington, DC; or from most major cities in Europe. If you’re taking a train from another part of France or Italy, you’ll have to connect in Nice or the Italian border town of Ventimiglia. From Nice, it’s a 25-minute drive or seven-minute helicopter ride to the principality via Blade. Once you arrive in Monaco, the easiest way to get around is by foot or bus (you can tap a credit card or pay for a ticket onboard). Carshare services like Uber and Bolt will drop you in the principality, but you can’t request a car to take you from Monaco to another destination. You can, however, order a taxi or request one through your hotel and charge it to your room, if you’re staying at one of the Monte-Carlo Société des Bains de Mer properties. The best things to do in Monaco Monaco’s rocky shoreline doesn’t sport the same swaths of sandy beaches as some of its neighbors, which is why so much real estate is dedicated to pools (there’s even an open-air, Olympic-sized saltwater pool on the port). Sunbathe along the waterfront solarium that's the Côte d'Azur version of Scandinavia's floating saunas, or set off on a half-day whale-watching safari around the coast to spot migrating fin and sperm whales. While Cannes is defined by La Croisette and Nice’s pebble-strewn shores are bordered by the Promenade des Anglais, Monaco’s main beachside stretch, the crescent-shaped sliver Larvotto, recently received a modern makeover helmed by Renzo Piano. A handful of beach clubs and restaurants spill out along the palm-fringed promenade. For a more subdued scene than Saint-Tropez that’s every bit as glamorous, sprawl on a floral-patterned sunbed (a nod to the 1960s-era motif designed for Princess Grace) at La Rose des Vents’s seasonal, Gucci-themed beach club. If you don’t want to peel yourself away from the plage for lunch (and who could blame you?), you can dine on caviar and king crab tacos (a definite must-order) at your lounger. Across the bay, cliffside La Vigie Zanoni, chef Simone Zanoni’s al fresco Italian eatery, resembles an intimate, unfussy version of Capri. The sweeping views of the principality alone are worth it—and if you’re taking part in a boat day, you can even pull up to the restaurant’s private dock. Rooftop Nikki Beach Monte Carlo’s cabana-clad pool embraces the Riviera’s party-heavy beach club vibes, but for something more understated, cruise over to La Môme Riviera’s rose-striped parasols and Italian restaurant, which hover along the rocks in nearby Roquebrune-Cap-Martin. When you arrive at the private pontoon via boat (Star Boat Luxury offers shuttles departing from Port Hercule), the tucked-away enclave feels like you’ve stumbled upon a private island. Nearby Loulou Pirate is a spruced-up take on a fisherman’s hut and embraces the same barefoot-chic vibe today as when the original locale was a hotspot for the likes of Brigitte Bardot in the 1960s and ‘70s. At Monaco’s newish fashion district, One Monte-Carlo, near the casino, splurge or window shop at designer boutiques like Cartier and Saint Laurent, or sip a glass of champagne under the Art Nouveau-style pavilions at Le Jardin Belle Epoque by Perrier Jouët’s pop-up outside Hôtel Hermitage Monte-Carlo. For vintage and second-hand luxury finds, browse Le Dressing’s two boutiques in the portside La Condamine district. If your trip falls over a Friday, hop on a direct, 30-minute train to Ventimiglia for the open-air weekly market—among the largest in Italy—and pause for lunch at waterfront stalwart Marco Polo 1960. In the evening, catch a performance by the likes of Norah Jones, James Blunt, and John Legend during the Monte-Carlo Summer Festival; take a seat for a classical concert or opera like Carmen at Opéra de Monte-Carlo; or watch a film under the stars at the open-air cinema beneath the Oceanographic Museum. Where to eat and drink The French Riviera is dotted with Michelin-starred restaurants running from the coast up to perched medieval villages like Èze and the neighboring town of Menton, where for the past 20 years Mauro Colagreco’s three-star Mirazur has been as revolutionary for France’s culinary scene as Noma for Denmark’s. Inside Monaco’s covered Condamine market hall in the Place d’Armes square, Colagreco’s Mitron Bakery features a selection of sourdough loaves that are milled and baked daily in Menton. (While the indoor market is closed for construction, vendors are serving from kiosks in the square.) If the weather is nice, head to the smaller port in Fontvieille to Les Perles de Monte-Carlo for platters of freshly shucked oysters and perfectly seasoned sea bass (this place fills up fast, so reserve in advance). Nearby, the original Beefbar—which has expanded to include a swish collection of restaurants everywhere from Saint-Tropez to luxury cruise ships and private flights—draws a local crowd for lunch (the smash cheeseburger is one of the house favorites). The terrace of Liguria-born Zeffirino is another go-to for its Genovese pesto coating fresh, square-shaped mandilli pasta (even Frank Sinatra was a fan of the namesake chef Zeffirino’s pesto). At new eco-district Mareterra—where homes and buildings were designed by Renzo Piano, Tadao Ando, and Sir Norman Foster and residents include billionaires and Formula 1 local legend Charles Leclerc—a handful of shops and restaurants have also opened their doors, including London transplant zēphyr, anchored by its own sultry cocktail bar Naked & Famous. Throughout the principality, young chefs are shaking up stuffy fine-dining concepts, replacing decadent, drenched-in-sauce dishes with lighter fare that lets the Riviera’s seasonal ingredients shine. One of the best examples is Blue Bay Marcel Ravin, where subtle flavors of the Caribbean and its distinct spices are infused into the Martinique-born chef’s cuisine. Picture artisanal plates dressed with vanilla sugar cane vinegar and cassava crumble. The open kitchen unfolds into the airy dining room accented by natural materials like sleek wood paneling and coral-inspired screens disguising tables, so they feel more like private booths—but the true showstopper is the seaside terrace, especially at sunset. There’s no shortage of places to see-and-be-seen in the principality, from Roaring Twenties-inspired rooftop restaurant La Môme Monte-Carlo, where a singer serenades tables that peer over the port and Prince’s Palace, to Amazónico, another rooftop setting that overlooks the glistening casino and where entertainment ranges from Bossa Nova and Cuban music to DJs spinning “electro-tropical” beats. Across the square, book dinner at Greek-Mediterranean GAIA, which draws a fashionable crowd of locals and famous faces year-round (discretion is key, so avoid trying to snap shots of F1 drivers). Take a seat in the foliage-filled terrace, which feels plucked out of the Athens Riviera, and sip a selection of expertly curated Greek Assyrtiko wines. Share classic spreads like taramosalata before ordering from the restaurant’s own fish market, where options include carpaccio or ceviche, as well as grilled whole fish with a drizzle of lemon oil. Then, as the evening progresses, join the well-heeled crowd filing into speakeasy-style, members-only lounge NYX. Monaco’s nightlife ranges from bottle service at late-night lounges like velvet-lined SASS CAFE to DJs spinning tribal house beats at nearby COYA Monte-Carlo, a waterfront, Peruvian-fusion eatery with a pisco bar and lounge. (If you’re after a cavernous, late-night club, you’ll find a few of those, too, including Twiga and Jimmy’z Monte-Carlo). For something more lowkey, start or end your evening with apéro (pre-dinner drinks and light bites) or a nightcap under the Eiffel-designed glass dome at Gustave at Hôtel Hermitage or at Hôtel de Paris’s legendary Le Bar Américain, a 1920s-era haunt popular with everyone from Joséphine Baker and Cary Grant to Lady Gaga. Open year-round, jazz, swing, blues, and soul performers entertain every evening and bar snacks include some of the best barbajuans (Swiss chard-filled fritters) in town. Where to stay Monaco’s sprinkling of five-star Belle Époque hotels are huddled around the Carré d’Or (Golden Square), crowned by the historic centerpiece Casino de Monte-Carlo. The independently owned, Jacques Garcia-designed Hôtel Métropole Monte-Carlo boasts designer names like the Spa Métropole by Guerlain and the Karl Lagerfeld-designed Odyssey, an urban rooftop oasis with a heated saltwater pool and Italian poolside restaurant Zia. Reviving Joël Robuchon's longstanding institution, the late chef’s former right hand is at the helm of the namesake, two Michelin-starred Les Ambassadeurs by Christophe Cussac. Jacques Garcia was brought back on board to spearhead the two-year renovation of the restaurant, which features an open-kitchen concept, chef’s table with 360-degree views of the team at work, and cigar lounge in the extended lobby bar, where a trio of museum-worthy pieces by Pablo Picasso, Francis Bacon, and Andy Warhol anchor the space. One other aspect popular with fans of the former Robuchon eatery has also been brought back: the legendary bread and dessert trolleys. Facing the casino, the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo is perhaps the most emblematic of Monaco, and after a multi-year, multimillion-dollar renovation, it’s among the most modern as well. You’ll still see timeless glamour in the gilded dining room of three-star Le Louis XV – Alain Ducasse, with its gold leaf-painted frescoes and columns (and Bordeaux-modeled wine cellar lined with more than 350,000 bottles). But with revamped Art Deco rotunda rooms overlooking the super yacht-filled harbor, and the expansive Prince Rainier III Suite, outfitted with a two-level outdoor lounge and infinity pool perched over the casino, rooms not only offer some of the best views, they’re some of the most luxurious in the South of France. The family-friendly Monte-Carlo Bay Hotel & Resort feels like more of a Mediterranean island retreat, with seaside sun beds and beach fare from two Michelin-starred chef Marcel Ravin; Balinese-style beds by the sand-bottom lagoon; and water sports like parasailing and tubing available off the hotel’s pontoon. At the opposite end of the principality, in what’s technically considered France, the terra cotta-colored Monte Carlo Beach exudes retro, 1930s charm with Art Deco, California villa-inspired rooms hugging the coastline, and an Olympic-sized saltwater pool that served as a backdrop for Helmut Newton’s Vogue and Vanity Fair shoots. A perk for guests staying at Monte-Carlo Beach, Hôtel de Paris, and Hôtel Hermitage: access to the pool and private plage at Monte-Carlo Beach Club, which sports a Jacquemus-themed pontoon with matching striped beach beds. For a stay that comes with sky-high rooms showing off sweeping views of the principality, modernist The Maybourne Riviera is perched along the rocky peninsula of Roquebrune-Cap-Martin and features chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s New York transplant, abc kitchens riviera, plus a striking infinity pool suspended nearly a thousand feet above the sea.

item.title: 11 Scenic Train Rides in the US Worth Booking for the Views Alone
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.27
Every year, instead of flying home to southeastern Virginia, I always opt to take the train. My journey typically starts in New York, winding down the Northeast Corridor before stopping in Washington, DC. While this busy stretch of track is far from the most scenic train ride in the US, there were still moments when I found my face pressed against the window—like near Havre de Grace, Maryland where the Susquehanna River widens—unable to look away. It was a reminder of how the joys of slow travel can sneak up on you, even in familiar places you may have traveled through countless times before. That said, there are certain train routes in the US with scenery so mesmerizing that they are worth taking for the sights alone. Amtrak, of course, has more than 30 different train routes crisscrossing every US region, from the vast deserts of the Southwest to the sparkling coast of California, and majestic mountain ranges in between. But even more private rail operators in states like Alaska and Hawaii offer their own scenic train rides that shouldn't be overlooked. The challenge, then, becomes picking which train trip to take—and when. Below, we’ve selected 13 of the most scenic train rides in the US that are worth booking for the views alone. This story has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: How I Travel: Shania Twain Brings Spinach To Her Hotel Rooms
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.94
Most people’s carry-on bags hold items like a sweater, book, tablet, chargers, snacks, maybe hand sanitizer, and an eye mask. Pop music icon Shania Twain is bringing a mini recording studio everywhere she goes. “In my carry-on for many, many years is my Pro Tools set-up for recording,” says Twain. “I do a lot of writing and recording in my hotel rooms, so I bring an Apollo [audio-processing hardware], my microphone, the laptop, all of that.” Her latest album, Little Miss Twain, features songs that she wrote and produced years ago, with themes stretching back to her teen romances. The best-selling country-pop artist of all time, Twain got nostalgic with Condé Nast Traveler about her first business-class flight, which she took after signing her record deal, as well as more recent travel—like her 12-night stint performing with Harry Styles in London at Wembley Stadium this past summer—and shared future trips, like the one she’s plotting to India this winter. Plus, other quirky items on her packing list. Her favorite mode of transportation: If we're speaking about touring, bus is my favorite way to travel. I just love moving into it and then not having to unpack every day. I don't love living out of a suitcase. I like to settle in; that's my thing. I like sleeping in small spaces. Her first flight in business class: It was from Toronto to Nashville, after I signed to my record label. They bought me a business-class ticket. People were still smoking on planes then, and I’m so sensitive to cigarette smoke. I thought ‘gee, if you’re moving up in the world, do you have the right to say, Do you mind?’ I was so perplexed that people could smoke in business class, but that was the way it was. And I remember the food was better. Her packing approach: I'm a good packer, a really good packer. I would say I'm a thoughtful packer, in the sense that I've got a good routine down. I pack in categories: I’ll do the shoes, then jewelry, then pajamas, then underwear and socks. Quite organized. How she passed the time in London between shows this summer: I love London. I love to walk, and London has a lot of really quaint, walkable areas with pubs and cafes and shopping. I love Hyde Park. I've ridden horses and gone to concerts there, and it's all walkable from the hotels. And there's the theaters! This summer, I took advantage of seeing Paddington, which was extraordinary. It was just adorable. The cast is really exceptional. I mean, the story is great—we all know the story—but I just thought the theater was ideal for the intimacy of it. Her favorite places to stop through on tour: Quebec City is a great place for a day off on tour. It’s very Paris-like, this little time capsule—like a little bit of Paris was brought over to Canada. It's so quaint and beautiful, and on the water. Very walkable as well. The part of Canada she wants more tourists to see: I would recommend people visiting Canada see more of where I'm from [in northeastern Ontario], because nature is the most extraordinary. We've got areas where you can go moose watching, for example. You're not in a zoo. You see all these wild animals and it's really beautiful. Her priorities when planning a vacation: Food definitely motivates me when I'm traveling. I need to make sure that I'm going to enjoy the food because, as a vegetarian especially, it can be quite limiting. One of my favorite places to visit and eat as a vacation trip is Egypt, because it gives me everything I need. I like to walk everywhere and see the architecture. That's a big thing for me—to see history on every block. I love ancient history particularly, and the cities and villages that are museums in themselves. And then, like I said, the food. The Lebanese food [in Egypt] is extraordinary for vegetarians. So that's a part of the world that I really love. Why she chose to have a home in Switzerland: I had a language base of French growing up in a bilingual town in Ontario and I wanted to maintain that, which I get to do in Switzerland, living on the French side. Plus, the benefit of being in Switzerland is you have the valley and the lakes below, but then you can just drive up for 20 minutes and be on a glacier. I'll never give up my four seasons—and being Canadian, I love winter. The items she needs in her hotel room: One thing I miss the most when I'm traveling in hotels is not being able to cook. I love to cook so I always make sure that there is a really good blender, and that I have things like raw spinach, avocados, tomatoes, and bread—things that I can put olive oil and salt and pepper on and make my own snack without calling room service. The place she’s never been that she’d like to see next: Even though I’ve been very lucky to travel in my career, there's a lot of places I haven't been. I've never been to India. I've got a trip planned this January to Hyderabad, because I have friends from there. I've heard so much about [the country], and I know so many people that have gone, but this will be my first experience. And don't forget, India has the best vegetarian food!

item.title: 13 Best Hotels in Key West, From Historic Inns to Private Islands
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.92
Long known for its free-spirited vibe and its identity as the iconoclastic “Conch Republic,” Key West welcomes you to come as you are, whether that means strolling past street-roaming roosters in your finest cowboy hat and Daisy Dukes, joining the revelers on Duval Street à la Mardi Gras, enjoying family time on the beach, or just staying put around your hotel pool “wasting away again in Margaritaville.” (Jimmy Buffett actually wrote the final verses of the song circa 1977 while stuck in traffic on the Seven Mile Bridge heading back to the Florida Keys, then debuted it on Duval Street shortly thereafter.) It’s definitely a place that caters to hedonistic tendencies at land’s end, especially during Fantasy Fest and other wild celebrations throughout the year, but it’s equally suited to soaking up the sun and embracing an IDGAF attitude. Beneath the more recent commercialization of Key West lies a deeper charm, reflected in its eclectic mix of resorts. The most sought-after stays are in Old Town, which occupies the island’s western edge, touching both the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean. Old Town is remarkably walkable, with fabulous restaurants, historic sites, and kitschy dive bars never more than a short stroll away. True, there are plenty of places to stay in New Town, often at lower rates. But why rely on an hourly shuttle to Old Town or stare at a chain mall parking lot from your room when so much of the fun of Key West is crawling back to your hotel through picturesque neighborhoods and lush gardens after a night of debauchery? There’s also something to be said for actually sleeping in one of the historic cottages and buildings that speak to Key West's earlier days, recalling the words of Hemingway and lyrics of Buffett. Whether you’re after a romantic retreat, a fun weekend with your besties, a gay nudist escape, or a laid-back family vacation, you’ll find it among our picks for the best hotels in Key West. Explore our complete Key West travel guide, which includes: - The Best Things to Do in Key West - The Best Restaurants in Key West - The Best Beaches in the Florida Keys How we choose the best hotels in Key West Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.
