item.title: This Dual-Voltage Hair Dryer Is Actually Lightweight and Compact Enough to Pack
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.83
I envy my friends who arrive at the airport with nothing but a slim carry-on in tow. I, on the other hand, check a bag every time. And yes, I do overpack, but I really try not to; by the time I lay all my hair tools on one side of my suitcase, it's halfway full. So, I accepted the fact that I'll never be a carry-on-only traveler a long time ago. But recently, I got my hands on Dyson's new Supersonic travel hair dryer—and for the first time, I might actually be able to save some space in my suitcase. Dyson's latest hair tool is specifically designed with travelers in mind—it's 32% smaller and 25% lighter than the brand's OG best-selling Supersonic hair dryer, meaning it can be tucked away in the corner of a suitcase or pocket of a weekender bag with ease. I've had the Dyson Airwrap for years, and don't get me wrong, it's great—but between the long barrel, the multiple attachments, and the thick cord, it's usually way too bulky for me to pack. When I'm traveling, I want something easy, fuss-free, and overpacker-friendly. On a recent bachelorette trip to Rosemary Beach, Florida, I easily packed my Dyson Supersonic travel hair dryer in my suitcase. And because my friends and I were staying in an Airbnb, a hair dryer wasn't provided, so it was even more important that I bring one. If you, like me, are tired of filling up the majority of your suitcase by packing a bulky hair dryer or styling system, Dyson's new travel tool is worth checking out. I had two main concerns when the hair tool arrived. First, is it actually smaller and lighter than your average hair dryer? And yes, it absolutely is. It's really not much bigger than my iPhone, and takes up a fraction of the space in my bag that my Airwrap does. Second, I wanted to know if it actually worked as well as other Dyson hair tools—or if this smaller version would mean I sacrificed power. Within seconds of turning it on, I could tell this mini hair dryer packed a serious punch. It heats up in seconds and has just as much strength as my full-size Dyson Airwrap. The major pro for this travel hair dryer is that it's dual voltage, meaning you can safely use it in outlets abroad too—unlike the Dyson Airwrap and original Supersonic hair dryer. I love knowing I can take this tool anywhere, whether I'm at home in New Jersey or traveling to Europe. I also love the look of it sitting on a hotel bathroom counter. It's so simple and sleek—and the slim barrel is easy to grip and hold while drying. Its design is simple: There's a button to turn it on and off, a button to control the three heat settings, and another for its two speeds. I have long hair, and the Dyson can fully dry it in about 10 minutes—even when it's sopping wet right out of the shower. It also leaves my hair with a glossy, shiny finish—unlike the hair dryer usually found at hotels that can sometimes leave my hair feeling dry and brittle. I like that the cable length is shorter than most tools (it's only 6.5 feet, compared to the original model that is 8.6 feet). It also comes with a Styling Concentrator, a small attachment that helps prevent frizz and leaves your hair a little smoother. Another cool perk is that it's compatible with attachments for the original Supersonic hair dryer, so you don't have to buy additional parts if you want to mix and match. My only gripe with this hair tool is the price. $300 for a hair dryer is expensive—a lot pricier than others I've used in the past. But it does work way better than any hair dryer I've tried before and is much lighter and smaller. Given its compact size, impressive power, and dual-voltage capabilities, I say it's worth it. I originally got this hair dryer with only travel in mind. But for the past two months, it's been my go-to hair tool, even when I'm home. Call me lazy, but it's so much easier to pull this thing out than my bulkier Airwrap to dry my hair. I recommend Dyson's new hair dryer for any frequent travelers looking for something compact, lightweight, and dual voltage. Or anyone wanting a go-to hair dryer that's less bulky but works just as well as larger hair tools on the market (perfect for those with limited storage space in their bathroom). Whether I'm packing for a two-week trip overseas or a quick weekend escape, you'll definitely find this small-but-mighty hair tool in my bag.

item.title: 29 Best Hotels in Miami (2026), From Key Biscayne to Wynwood
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.79
Once dominated by pastel Art Deco and late-night bass, the best hotels in Miami have evolved into an eclectic, high-design, sprawling ecosystem. Beyond the legendary oceanfront icons of South Beach lie moody art-filled sanctuaries, discreet European-style retreats, and soaring glass towers anchored in the cosmopolitan energy of Brickell. Luckily, when it comes to picking the right one, towering Downtown Miami and iconic Miami Beach alike have a wide variety of top-tier accommodations for every need (and bank account). City-loving travelers will be pleasantly surprised by the sophisticated hotels in Miami’s dense urban core. Beach-goers can look forward to thousands of square feet of pristine beach to enjoy at a number of oceanfront resorts. Whether you are chasing Damien Hirst gold, rooftop bars, or pristine (and velvet-rope-free) beaches, here are the absolute best places to check in right now. Our top picks: - Best overall: 1 Hotel South Beach - Best for beach access: Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club - Most romantic: Faena Hotel Miami Beach - Best for families: Loews Miami Beach Hotel - Best for first-timers: Andaz Miami Beach by Hyatt - Read Full ReviewAfter a six-year closure and a $100 million restoration, the Delano Miami Beach returns knowing exactly what made it legendary in the first place: design, drama, and glamor with a sense of place. Elastic Architects resisted turning the hotel into a museum of its former selves, instead weaving together restored favorites like the Rose Bar with guestrooms that feel warmer and more inviting than before, especially the two-story Poolside Bungalows just steps from the hotel's iconic pool. In the Delano’s third incarnation, one of Miami Beach's best beach-and-pool scenes returns (both cocktail- and kid-friendly this go’round), paired with high profile restaurants by Paris Society, namely Gigi Rigolatto and Mimi Kakushi, where locals often outnumber overnight guests. Add Café Delano's irresistible pistachio croissants, heartfelt service, an immaculate art collection, and members programming open to hotel guests, and the Delano once again is all the hype on South Beach. - Read Full ReviewA crisp, minimalist European import that seamlessly blends modern corporate cool with Miami's vibrant rooftop culture all while being tucked away on a quiet leafy street in Brickell’s bustling neighborhood. The 275 rooms here are a calm and cool retreat from Miami’s loud and frenetic downtown. Spacious and flooded with natural light, thanks to floor-to-ceiling windows, the rooms lean into a soothing palette of cool grays, warm wood accents, and pops of yellow. Brickell’s glittering skyline envelopes this high-rise and, depending on where your room is situated, you can catch a glimpse of Biscayne Bay or the lush Simpson Park that cuts through a swath of downtown. Bathrooms are streamlined and modern with expansive glass walk-in showers and all rooms include Lavazza coffee makers and mini-fridges. - Read Full ReviewArriving at the Surfcomber feels a bit like hopscotching through Miami Beach history. The hotel's Collins Avenue neighbors—The Sagamore, National, SLS, among others—line the street in linen white. Not one to break dress code, the Surfcomber's façade is also marked by sharp lines; a dramatic, semicircle driveway to coast into; and smooth, matte-white walls—a fitting canvas for the party lights that paint the South Beach streets neon. With 186 rooms, there is a box-of-chocolates variety of accommodations to choose from, whether you're a solo traveler just looking for a place to settle at night, or you're looking to really treat yourself by booking an oceanfront suite with your own private balcony. All rooms come with luxury Atelier Bloem bath products, and keep to a generally neutral palette to keep the attention on the view from your room. A visit to the pool and backyard space is just about necessary when it comes to staying at the Surfcomber. Be amazed by the difference the distance of the lobby can make between the bass-boosted streets and the secluded beach bar and stunning pool—go ahead, rent that cabana. - Read Full ReviewUnframed, Autograph Collection signals a fun, cutting-edge design chapter for Miami Beach—with bold, curvy architecture and easygoing spaces that invite you to stay a while. Behind its sculptural façade, you’ll find plush rooms, a rooftop pool for lingering, and a French Riviera–inspired dining scene that gives the hotel its own personality. It’s a stylish home base for exploring South Beach—close enough to the action, but with plenty of reasons to come back before the night is over. The 149 rooms feel like a cool retreat from the buzz of Miami Beach. Rich velvet headboards, warm wood finishes, and pops of blush and rust make the spaces feel inviting and chic, while details like marble vanities and sleek microcement showers add just the right amount of drama. - Read Full ReviewBlink and you might think you mistakenly hopped a plane to Savannah instead of South Beach: At the northernmost end of Ocean Drive, this hotel’s Florida-Georgia style of architecture sticks out like a colonial masterpiece in a sea of pastel-colored Art Deco gems. While some people head to the neighborhood with only late nights out on their mind, The Betsy attracts a different, more erudite crowd. Yes, they love being in the thick of all that touristy mayhem, but prefer that it not happen right outside their window. And it’s not just the hotel’s quaint façade that seems to attract a different type of South Beach reveler; inside, the public spaces act as a sort of art gallery, with photo exhibitions rotating throughout the year. Rooms are spacious and have mini libraries, writing desks, and oversized marble bathrooms; the hotel also counts two pools and a rooftop ocean deck among its attractions. - Read Full ReviewThe first new hotel to grace South Beach’s storied Española Way in a decade, the enchanting Esme Miami Beach is all about the boutique hotel charms. Rather than replicate the easy, breezy, sand-in-your-toes style of South Beach’s grand dames, this restored enclave (which comprises eight buildings connected by charming paseos) offers a well-placed base from which to explore South Beach. You know you’re in for a unique experience as soon as you walk in the door; the lobby is outfitted with thick crimson carpeting, Moroccan-style benches, and accents of brass and dark green, setting the tone for the Moorish influence on decor throughout the property. The rooftop pool is small but striking (and not really made for anything other than dipping), but it’s a perfect spot for catching sun under the connected peach and white striped daybeds that line the deck. - Read Full ReviewLocated in the trendy Brickell neighborhood, this Four Seasons lets you discover Miami beyond just the beach—without sacrificing those turquoise water views. With a two-acre, palm tree-lined rooftop pool overlooking Biscayne Bay, you can access the best of the city’s vibrant downtown area while still enjoying the tropical relaxation one deserves when vacationing in South Florida. Most of the guests here are well-heeled business travelers, but there were also a fair amount of (well-behaved) young families and friend groups on vacation mode at the property’s sprawling pool facilities. Among Miamians, the hotel is best known for its extravagant Sunday Brunch; all tables become immediately filled with a combination of local residents and hotel guests, a natural overlap felt throughout the property, which is also home to the Four Seasons Residences. - Read Full ReviewJust as he did back in the 1990s with the Delano, Ian Schrager is reinventing the Miami Beach experience with The Edition. Here, every amenity a person could want (or even know was possible) is there for the taking—ice skating rink included—and the hotel has five fabulous drinking and dining options, including Matador Room, Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s innovative Latin fusion restaurant. There’s no detail in the rooms that hasn't been scrutinized in an attempt to exceed guests’ every expectation, and the heavenly, low-slung bed—which sits atop a light oak frame that blends in with the walls, and is topped with a down comforter and pillows—is no exception. - Read Full ReviewThere are two entry points to the Gale: through the high-ceilinged, grand valet on one side, and rose-hued in-house restaurant Casa Gianna on the other. Either route makes for quite the entrance to this sparkling 51-story tower, where glamorous people with things to do come and go at a steady clip. This is an affordable, reliable stay smack dab in the thick of Downtown Miami that feels impenetrably tranquil despite the noise all around. The rooms here mirror the residences in the same building, so you can book a studio, one-bedroom, or two-bedroom ranging from 410 to 910 square feet. Most of these have full kitchens and washer-dryers, so you can really set up shop. Decor is minimal and modern, with black-and-white photography on the walls and furniture in neutral colors. The windows are floor-to-ceiling for the most part, meaning massive Miami views. Take out a bike to Miami Beach—you’ll fly past traffic and will not regret it. - Read Full ReviewThe Ritz-Carlton South Beach, one of a string of hotels on Miami’s destination waterfront, is a refined respite from the area’s pool parties and 'til-the-sun-rises nightlife, while still providing easy access to the city’s best restaurants, a great lobby bar scene, and ocean views. The rooms are crisp and modern, with white walls and linens punctuated by deep cerulean blue furniture—a velvet bed frame, plush chaise—and midcentury-style accents like bronze reading lamps and caned armchairs. In the ocean-view rooms and suites, which make up a majority of the room categories, the brilliant Atlantic out of the window is the real star of the show, just as it should be. Like most Ritz-Carltons, the experience is reliably five-star: service is fantastic, the decor is elevated and modern while nodding to the destination, amenities leave little to be desired, and the location is ideal. - Read Full ReviewThe first hotel to officially open in Wynwood, Miami’s graffiti-clad neighborhood that’s now home to dozens of galleries, shops, and restaurants—the Arlo is an art-filled oasis that seeks to strike a balance between being a splashy getaway and a vibrant urban hotel. The hotel’s aesthetic draws on the neighborhood’s high concentration of street art, with the property's exterior walls featuring works by Miami-based artist Hoxxoh, and 250 pieces of contemporary art positioned throughout the public spaces and guest rooms. There’s an inviting ninth-floor rooftop pool with a cocktail bar and views of the Miami skyline. The hotel also strives to be a hub of activity for its guests with weekly programming like comedy nights, fitness classes, and space devoted to loungey coworking environments with a pool table and a yoga deck. While the hotel is lacking in certain frills (like room service), there are also thoughtful touches like complimentary fortune cookies in the rooms with unique fortunes and bicycles for guests to explore the neighborhood. - Read Full ReviewMiami Beach’s midcentury Art Deco scene may have cemented its place in design history, but today a new, grown-up iteration can be found in the form of The Shelborne By Proper. Guest rooms are reflective of the entire property’s mood: elevated yet easy. My room on the sixth floor featured a partial ocean view, just enough of a glimpse of that turquoise blue water to whet my palate. The room’s design feels calm and grounded, which I owe to the soft, earthy tones and warm, natural textiles. It’s a nice counterbalance to the energetic vibe that Miami Beach naturally offers, a true retreat that feels intentionally devoid of flashy artwork and instead focuses on curved, architectural furnishings that are low-profile and slim. Also noteworthy is that the design is nowhere near that stereotypical Florida coastal-chic image with wooden floors and shiplapped walls. Instead, the rooms are elevated with marble flooring that is warmed up with a textured off-white rug. - Read Full ReviewEven amid the architectural exhibitionism of Miami Beach, the gleaming curved main tower of the 1,500-room Fontainebleau Miami Beach is a knockout. The design of this essentially launched the so-called Miami-Modern style, and the resort dominates its stretch of Miami Beach. It’s a clean and classic escape where contemporary vibes meet retro in a flash of glamour. Although the Fontainebleau has been upgraded at no small expense, guests still feel like they’re part of its storied past. - Read Full ReviewOpened in 2024, this 13-room hotel is nestled inside the four-story landmark Moore building, which also houses a posh coworking space, private club, art gallery, and restaurant on the ground floor. Upon walking inside, you’re immediately struck by the Zaha Hadid site-specific installation Elastika that spans the light-filled atrium connecting the different levels with stretches of web-like material. It’s both cheeky and iconic. The main spot here is Torno Subito, located on the ground floor of the atrium and headed up by famed Italian chef Massimo Bottura and his team. The menu focuses on modern Italian cuisine and includes dishes like Mediterranean Sea Bass stuffed with pork, tiny, handmade tortellini served in a rich Parmigiano broth, and “Oops, I burned the Key lime pie”—a South Florida-inspired reimagining of Bottura's iconic "Oops, I dropped the lemon tart" dessert. Guests of the hotel can also dine on the second-floor balcony restaurant that is part of the members’ club. My lunch there included a delicious hen-of-the-woods mushroom pizza and spicy tuna crispy rice from the sushi bar. During city-wide events like Art Basel and Formula 1, the place is a hive of activity. FAQ: How we choose the best hotels in Miami Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind More Miami recommendations Read our complete Miami travel guide here, which includes: This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 23 Best Airbnbs in Vancouver for Proximity to Nature, Culture, and Delicious Cuisine
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.53
A born-and-raised Vancouverite, I’ve spent a lifetime exploring my city’s distinct neighborhoods, and many of my favorite places are found well beyond the downtown core where most of Vancouver’s top hotels are located. Settling into one of the city’s distinct neighborhoods puts the area’s best attractions right outside your door, offering a chance to connect with the surrounding nature, exceptional food scene, and immersive cultural experiences you might otherwise miss. To truly get a taste of all this city has to offer (and experience it like a local), consider booking an Airbnb. A short-term rental gives you options, whether you want to be steps from sandy Kits Beach, close to the eclectic shops and cafés of Commercial Drive, or tucked away on a leafy residential street in Shaughnessy. For those exploring without a car, many of Vancouver’s neighborhoods are well connected by public transit, too. From a cozy houseboat in the harbor to a light-filled log home on the beach, these are the spots I’d choose for a truly unforgettable stay in the city. Read on for the best Airbnbs in Vancouver to bookmark for your next trip. We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. Our top picks: - Best for families: Trendy townhouse near Mount Pleasant - Best for couples: Beachfront living in West Point Grey - Best for a unique stay: Floating home in Lonsdale Quay - Best for large groups: Voguish villa for 10 FAQ: What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Vancouver? While there are plenty of neighborhoods in Vancouver to choose from, each suits different interests and budgets—there are no wrong choices. Downtown Vancouver is bustling, dynamic, and offers easy access to iconic landmarks like sprawling Stanley Park and vibrant Granville Island. Meanwhile, Yaletown, located within the city's core, is chic and replete with upscale restaurants, trendy boutiques, and vibrant nightlife. Giving a glimpse into Vancouver's storied past, Gastown welcomes visitors with cobblestone streets, gas lamps, and the iconic Steam Clock. What’s the best way to get around Vancouver? If you’re staying in the heart of the city, it’s easy to explore Vancouver’s best sites by foot, bike, bus, or boat. Rideshare options are also available and easily accessible. If you plan to stay downtown, the Vancouver Skytrain serves areas between downtown and Metro Vancouver's larger suburbs. To experience the greater Vancouver area, especially if you plan to venture to Vancouver Island, driving is the way to go—just be sure to book your car rental in advance. How long should you visit Vancouver for? You'll want to spend at least three days in Vancouver to experience the best of both nature and city. Enjoy a day exploring the stylish boutiques, world-class museums and galleries, and diverse cuisine. Then spend time outdoors, cycling the Stanley Park Seawall, sunbathing on the sandy beaches, paddling the coastline, or hiking the forested trails. If you have extra time, venture beyond the city proper. Head to the North Shore for an action-packed day of hiking, skiing, or wildlife spotting at Grouse Mountain, or teeter across the Capilano Suspension Bridge—a must-try for first-time visitors to Vancouver. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Megan Honan.

item.title: 11 National Parks That Are Even More Beautiful in the Fall
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.42
I’ve traveled far and wide through America’s national parks, and if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that some landscapes are simply better with a little fall color. Come September and October, sweeping valleys turn gold, forests flare in riots of red and pops of orange, and high country trails welcome that crisp, exhilarating drop in temperature that makes you want to keep trekking a little farther. Even parks we know and love in summer feel completely transformed: the sunsets shine differently, wildlife activity changes, and the seasonal crowds begin to give way to a quieter, more immersive experience. Thanks to the breadth of terrain across the US national parks, there’s no single version of how to experience fall. You might be leaf-peeping beneath the peaks of the Tetons, winding through Acadia’s brilliant coastal forests, hiking Yosemite in the cooler weather, or watching the aspens flicker across the Rockies. And when the sun goes down, the day doesn’t have to end: there are campfires to linger around, stars to seek out, and hot springs to slip into. Below, I’ve rounded up 11 national parks that are particularly spectacular in autumn. Take note: Fall may be shoulder season, but don’t assume that means easy availability—lodges, campgrounds, permits, and popular activities can still book up, so check current park conditions and reservation requirements before you go. —Jessica Chapel This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Calling All Women Who Travel Solo—Add These US Destinations to Your Bucket List
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.18
There’s something wonderfully freeing about traveling alone as a woman. You get to make every decision—where to stay, what to order, whether to spend the afternoon in a museum or outside, and when to call it a night—and there’s a particular pleasure in discovering a place at your own pace. The best destinations for solo women travelers make that freedom feel easy, too: welcoming enough to settle in, interesting enough to keep you curious, and full of reasons to leave the hotel and see what happens. Across the US, that might mean wandering Savannah’s moss-draped squares, pedaling along Nantucket’s bike lanes, lingering over Palm Springs’s colorful midcentury architecture, or heading to mountain towns in Wyoming or Montana. It could be a long weekend of galleries and good food in Kingston, a guided hike through Joshua Tree, or a cocktail at the bar in Carlsbad. The appeal is really as varied as us girls. If you're looking for a little inspiration to get out and go, our Condé Nast Traveler editors and trusted contributors have shared destinations below that deliver on both the fun and the practicalities of hitting the road solo, adding ideas for where to stay, eat, and explore along the way. Consider this your excuse to book the room for one, order exactly what you want, and go somewhere simply because you want to see it. Read on for the places we recommend most for women to travel solo in the US, in alphabetical order. Big Sky, Montana I became a little infatuated with solo travel after heading to Big Sky, Montana, on my own for Cowgirl Up Week, an annual gathering at the iconic Lone Mountain Ranch. The celebration takes place each September at the tail end of the summer season and draws women from around the world itching for a taste of the quintessential American West. Our days were filled with horseback rides led by head wranglers, a guided trip to Yellowstone, an end-of-season rodeo, and lessons in everything from trotting to communicating with your horse. What stuck with me most was how many women had come alone—some finally making a bucket-list trip happen, others simply giving the dude ranch life a shot. You could ride off on your own or join a group, so making friends with the other gals was remarkably easy. My group even has a group chat called “Cowgirls Forever,” filled with new mothers, local ranch-owning women, and travelers from Florida to Connecticut. More and more dude ranches are creating women-focused weeks and general programming, so it's easier than ever to saddle up solo in this New Age, women-led, John Wayne world. —J.C. Where to stay in Big Sky: - Best for a stay right on the ranch for Cowgirl Up Week: Lone Mountain Ranch - Best for a convenient base for treating yourself: Montage Big Sky - Best for a more affordable base right in town: The Lodge at Big Sky Boston, Massachusetts I went to Boston two falls ago to visit a friend, and it was one of the most comfortable solo travel experiences I’ve had. I loved that I could reach most areas of interest in Cambridge and Charlestown on foot, and it’s sure hard to beat a crisp autumn in New England, especially in a city with such deep-set roots. I stayed at a houseboat Airbnb docked in the Charlestown marina, which was as serene as it was unique. It was fantastic being able to spend long nights on the deck, looking out to Boston city proper after spending the days romping through town. While this isn’t the part of the country that usually takes the cake for hospitality, I found that everyone local was incredibly friendly, helpful, and eager to share recommendations on where to head next. If you think you’re tired of hearing AI-this, new buzzy techword-that, still pay a visit to the MIT Museum, where the cutting edge feels hands-on, interactive, and actually exciting. —Kat Chen Where to stay in Boston: - Best for an iconic houseboat rental: A spacious yacht Airbnb - Best for a music-inspired hotel: The Verb Hotel - Best for a five-star waterfront hotel: Boston Harbor Hotel Carlsbad, California Often overshadowed by its flashier southern neighbor San Diego, Carlsbad has a more laid-back, surfy charm perfect for solo female travelers. I stayed at Beach Terrace, a family-owned hotel built directly on the sand about 50 feet from the water, when I visited. Sunday morning started with oceanfront yoga, where I connected with fellow travelers before exploring on foot (no car needed). Carlsbad Village is incredibly walkable and safe, even at night, with everything from antique shops to boutique clothing stores and Michelin-starred dining within reach. I joined a Carlsbad Food Tour to sample the town’s best eateries—such as the Strawberry Shack and Señor Grubby's—with a small, friendly group. For a solo dinner that doesn’t feel lonely, grab a seat at the bar at Campfire, where wood-fired dishes and communal energy make it easy to strike up a conversation with locals. —Kaila Yu, contributor Where to stay in Carlsbad: - Best for surf charm: Beach Terrace - Best for proximity to Carlsbad State Beach: The Green Room - Best for affordability but great service: Cape Rey Carlsbad Beach, a Hilton Resort and Spa Cody, Wyoming One of my favorite trips was a solo journey deep into Wyoming for a week on a ranch. Having traveled all the way from London, I took a couple of days to relax beforehand in Cody—the town I flew into—before continuing onward. Founded by none other than Buffalo Bill, this small town proved to be the sweetest spot for a few days of travel all alone. Everything worth visiting is within comfortable walking distance, with most restaurants, shops, and attractions no more than a 10-minute stroll away—a welcome relief if you feel hesitant about relying on rideshares in unfamiliar places. There is a fantastic range of museums—head to the Buffalo Bill Center of the West, which is so vast that entry tickets are valid for two consecutive days. I loved the historical Old Town Trail, which was altogether too absorbing for me to ever feel lonely. I frequently struck up conversations with locals in restaurants, so dining solo also never felt awkward. In truth? I hardly felt alone at all. Another highlight is Cody’s proximity to Yellowstone: I booked an excursion with CoveredGround Adventures, who picked me up directly from my hotel and had us deep among the pines within a 40-minute drive. By the time we returned that evening, my guide, a Cody local, and I had gotten on so well that she offered to drive me around the next day if I needed a ride anywhere. With welcoming faces, stunning landscapes, cowboys, and some of the finest cinnamon buns I have ever tasted (courtesy of Cody Coffee Bar), I would repeat the experience on my own in a heartbeat. —Charley Ward Where to stay in Cody: - Best for a historical hotel: Buffalo Bill's Irma Hotel - Best for a charming small town experience near Yellowstone: Chamberlin Inn - Best for a park-friendly, amenity-forward base: The Cody Johns Island, South Carolina On rugged Johns Island, 40 minutes outside of Charleston, Auberge’s debut of The Dunlin deftly centers the coastal charm of the South Carolina sea islands—the second most bioactive habitat in the world, after only the Amazon Rainforest. Aptly named for a ploving shore bird, the 72 cottage-style guest rooms and suites offer transformative wildlife immersion over the 2,000 acres, from dolphin and seabird safaris amid the towering piles of massive oysters that make up the meandering coastline (and will be fresh on your plate come dinner time), to an on-site farm and 20 miles of waterfront hiking trails to work up a sweat on before sinking into a bedroom soaking tub overlooking the marsh. Guests are chic Southerners (expect plenty of chatty Texans who will strike up a conversation at the stylish bar) and transplants here for the relaxing natural setting, spa treatments, and wine-paired food in between hikes and river cruises. The setting is intimate and the visitors friendly, from babymooning couples at the pool to girls trip groups in Lily Pulitzer shift dresses by the birdcage-themed bar. —Shannon McMahon Where to stay on Johns Island: - Best for a lush nature escape in solitude: The Dunlin, Auberge Collection - Best for a waterfront rental in the trees: Private elevated tree house Airbnb - Best for a riverfront porch with coastal views: The Oystercatcher bungalow Airbnb Key West, Florida Key West is no stranger to group travel—walk down Duval St. at night, and you’ll encounter crowds of bachelorette parties, cruise-goers, and rowdy spring breakers. But the quirky Conch Republic is also home to a thriving artistic community that opens its arms to solo travelers without hesitation. Stop by Andy’s Cabana on open mic nights, the Key West Yoga Sanctuary for community classes or creative writing workshops, and Fort Zachary Beach to camp out under the palms. By doing just this, I have befriended fishing guides, van-lifers, painters, musicians, and writers who welcomed me into their creative circle. My favorite part about traveling solo is that it forces you to meet new people and try new things, and the Keys have long embodied the essence of this independence and freedom. Just don’t be surprised if you get invited out on a sailboat (or two) on your first day. —Hannah Towey Where to stay in Key West: - Best for an oasis of calm: Pier House Resort and Spa - Best for sunsets: Ocean Key Resort and Spa - Best for those drawn to the historic side of Key West: Ella's Cottages Kingston, New York I recently took a solo trip to Kingston, New York, and it was exactly what I needed. Just a quick jet up north via Amtrak, the town is easy to explore on foot and has a calm, welcoming vibe. I started my day with breakfast at Hotel Kinsley—home to good coffee, a quiet atmosphere, and vintage records by each window. Then I spent time reading with a cappuccino at Rough Draft Bar and Books. From there, I wandered through Italian provisions at Salamone’s, picked up playful stickers at quirky bookstore Everywhere Shop, and browsed the home goods at Kingston Social. What stood out most was how safe and queer-friendly it felt. The rainbow crosswalk near the main street felt like a warm welcome, and every shop I visited felt easy to be in. —Laura Delarato, contributor Where to stay in Kingston: - Best for vintage vibes and fresh air: Hotel Kinsley - Best for a tucked-away cabin retreat: Hutton Brickyards - Best for woodsy wellness nearby: Woodstock Way Hotel Litchfield, Connecticut Anytime I mention Litchfield to my colleagues, there’s invariably one person giggling or rolling their eyes. Not because they don’t think it’s a deserving mention, but because of how much love I have for this tiny region in Connecticut’s northwest corner. First, a short geography lesson: While Litchfield is a town, it is also a county—but think of it as a daisy chain of little towns and villages. Base yourself in the main town for a long weekend and drive around for easy access, passing through bucolic landscapes along the way. This is the kind of place that feels especially rewarding solo: You can spend your days following your own curiosity—from architecture and antiques to nature walks—while still finding a sense of community along the way. I usually stay at Belden House and Mews (from the owners of the Hudson Valley estate hotel Troutbeck); go for drinks and dinner at The Abner, refashioned from the town’s old courthouse; get coffee and crumb cake at Krafted Brew Lab; shop at chic home-goods store Milton Market; take a pottery lesson with Charlie at Dumais Made; and browse Jeffrey Tillou’s inventory of 18th- and 19th-century furniture and fine arts.—Arati Menon Where to stay in Litchfield: - Best for good style and tasty bites: The Abner - Best for splendid wellness and design: Belden House and Mews - Best for some peace and quiet: The Litchfield Inn Miami, Florida A little over a year ago, I flew from Denver to Miami for my January birthday, as I wanted to be somewhere warm, near the water, and full of vibrant food. I chose to stay at The Standard—it’s a solid hotel with easy-to-access water, plus it's removed enough from the hubbub of South Beach (but also just close enough, if that's what you're looking for). There are a handful of restaurants within a short walking distance, and even more restaurants a quick rideshare away, making it easy to move around at night alone as well. Pop over to Little Havana for exceptional Cuban food via a food tour (an opportunity to make new friends) or just by exploring on your own. The Brickell area has a cozy little wine bar called Niu Wine, and I can't recommend SuViche enough for casual, fresh Peruvian ceviche after a sunny walk or lazy beach day. —Amanda Villarosa, photographer Where to stay in Miami: - Best for a conveniently located and reliable hotel: The Standard Spa - Best for splurging on a maximalist-designed oasis: Faena Hotel Miami Beach - Best for an affordable stay in South Beach: Hotel Greystone Nantucket, Massachusetts Last October, I took a trip to Nantucket in the off-season to enjoy a “readaway”—that is, a vacation where the main objective was to get some fresh air and read my book. I stayed in this gorgeous loft above a bookstore, and felt so safe in the heart of town. I had a marvelous time visiting the Whaling Museum and counting how many lightship baskets I could find at antique shops—with not one single person rushing me along. Perhaps the highlight of my trip was the sunset hike I took along the Bluff Walk, where I peeked into quiet, gray-shingled cottages, spotted some seals, and marveled at the towering Sankaty Lighthouse. The scariest part of the trip was the plane ride over the Atlantic on a nine-passenger Cape Air propeller, but even then, I've never experienced a softer landing than with my two female pilots. —Jessica Sulima Where to stay on Nantucket: - Best for a true literary oasis: Traveler-recommended readaway rental - Best for one of the few year-round stays: The Nantucket Hotel and Resort - Best for a central 20-room boutique: Greydon House Nashville, Tennessee The Tennessee capital is a quintessential bachelorette town in every sense of the phrase, but works just as well for a solo trip. There’s no need to get glammed up unless you absolutely wish to: If you’re feeling lonely, your next best friends might be just a honky tonk dance floor away. And while the world’s your oyster here, that also includes kicking back and enjoying the city’s slower offerings, like a day filled with art at the Frist Art Museum, or balmy outdoor reading at Centennial Park. You can’t go wrong with a show at the Opry, which turned 100 last year, and where—famously—there is no such thing as a bad seat. Nashville is kitsch, it’s booming, and between the hot chicken and barbecue, you won’t miss out on heartwarming food. I grew up visiting every year when I was a kid, and I still feel a childlike sense of adventure when I visit now. Dare I say it may be even more fun all grown up. —K.C. Where to stay in Nashville: - Best for a colorful and lively stay: The Graduate Nashville - Best for wow-factor: The Russell - Best for easy access to the hubbub: Drift Hotel Nashville North Fork, New York There's something about a solo getaway that isn't far away, or wildly different from where you live, that purely exists to give you permission to carve out a type of me time you can't get at home. One of those places, for me, is the North Fork at the very end of Long Island. It's a waterfront getaway—within three hours of my apartment in Brooklyn—where the pace is slow, the towns are small, the beaches are quiet, my main mode of transportation is a bicycle (available at most hotels), and I can spend my days eating farm-to-table (or sea-to-table) with no sense of urgency. There are lovely places to stay, like the Silver Sands Motel or Hotel Moraine, and cheffy restaurants, like Nookie's and the North Fork Table and Inn, but you can also rent an Airbnb and grab your own seafood at Little Creek Oyster Farm and the Southold Fish Market. Every morning, I go for a run, end it with a swim in the sound, then plan my days around reading between meal times—all to rinse and repeat. I suggest taking two or three days off mid-week (my hack for a solo trip without the FOMO), and keeping a small cooler and oyster knife in your car for whenever you pass honor-system fresh seafood stalls on the side of the road (like Peconic Gold). —Megan Spurrell Where to stay on the North Fork: - Best for a foodie-forward stay: Silver Sands Motel - Best for a chic farm stay in Southold: North Fork Table and Inn - Best for a splashy, seaside resort in Greenport: Hotel Moraine Palm Springs, California On a solo trip to Palm Springs for a group design tour with Palm Springs Mod Squad, I experienced a showcase of several pristinely preserved architectural gems built in the prevailing Desert Modern style. I spent an afternoon indulging in the city’s incredible vintage shops along the strip before popping into Superbloom, an innovative paint studio, where a childlike sense of play emerged as I splattered paint on a new passport holder and luggage tag. For pampering, do as I did and make your way to the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians's Spa at Séc-he and indulge in a hot stone massage with cold lavender-scented towels. Then sip on a phenomenal prickly pear lemonade before relaxing in the hot spring–fed thermal pool. Don't skip the designated Dark Sky Park that is Joshua Tree—knowing I’d eventually lose cell phone reception, I downloaded an offline map to navigate the park alone in the dark—an anxiety-inducing experience that felt like driving into an endless void, yet one I’d recommend to women looking to step out of their comfort zones and build confidence in an unforgiving desert landscape. My disappointment about not having enough time to see the Mojave Desert’s famous succulent in the daylight quickly dissipated during my stargazing tour with Joshua Tree Astronomy Adventures. Sharing a canopy of stars with just a few strangers, I contemplated the magnitude of the universe and felt humbled by my own existence. —Katherine Gallardo, contributor Where to stay in Palm Springs: - Best for a tucked-away boutique hotel: Villa Royale - Best for a full-service hotel in the middle of town: Kimpton Rowan Palm Springs Hotel - Best for a design-forward, restorative oasis: Korakia Pensione Savannah, Georgia I took a February trip to Savannah two winters ago—a long weekend based at Hotel Bardo—during which I planned to walk lazily through sunny parks, indulge in great food, and soak up the small city’s history. I traveled with my partner, but when a work thing came up on his end, I had a day to myself and found the city to be perfect for a party of one. At Mrs. Wilkes Dining Room, an institution of a soul-food kitchen (they still have the chair Obama sat in when he visited on display), you’re seated around a big, family-style table with whoever else walks in when you do—ideal for a solo traveler looking for company. The gorgeous Common Thread, where fluke crudos and roasted sunchokes sit side by side, also has seats at the bar if you don’t have a reservation (bar seats are most often the perfect choice as a solo traveler). Because this was a city where I actually wanted to do a tour, I easily slid into a mixed group being guided through the Owens-Thomas House and Slave Quarters. It was a highlight of the trip: Home tours of opulent 1800s-built properties are popular in the city, and the team at Owens-Thomas does a particularly great job of acknowledging everyone who lived in the home, including the enslaved people who kept it running. It was yet another reminder of how much there is to learn in this city—and how it is evolving constantly. —M.S. Where to stay in Savannah: - Best for the seasoned and curious traveler: Hotel Bardo - Best for a sweet and aesthetic stay: The Drayton Hotel - Best for a central boutique hotel: The Douglas This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: I Spent Four Days Touring Scotland’s Whisky Island—and It Was Better Than I Expected
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.03
My dad’s 60th birthday was coming up, and as an avid whisky drinker with a particularly sharp nose, his dream trip has always been to explore the coastline of Islay, a Scottish island famed worldwide for its smoky, peated single malt whiskies. I often travel solo and am fond of organized tours, so when I came across Rabbie’s four-day Islay and whisky tour—with pickup from Edinburgh, a selection of historic stops, a maximum group size of 16 people, and plenty of opportunities for drams—it sounded ideal for us both. Islay is the southernmost island of the Inner Hebrides, with a landscape of rugged beaches and peat bogs, and traveling through it usually involves many small logistics. I was thrilled to see that this tour handles all of the planning for you—including transportation, accommodations, attractions, and providing a local guide for the four-day trip. It starts at just $609 per adult without accommodations or distillery tours, or around $1,464 all-in, which seemed like a great deal. I was convinced, so I booked it! Our trip began with an evening in Edinburgh to recover from jet lag. The next morning, we made our way to the Edinburgh bus station to meet our driver and group. A 16-seat Mercedes mini coach pulled up, and we all piled in as our guide’s Celtic music played and we said goodbye to the city. Our first stop was the historic town of Falkirk, just 25 miles from Edinburgh, where we saw the iconic towering Kelpies sculptures and grabbed a coffee. I knew I was going to like our Glaswegian guide, Peter McShane, from the excitement in his voice as he told us about Scottish folklore. We then rode through the Lowlands and mountainous regions surrounding Loch Lomond and Trossachs National Park en route to the town of Oban, known as the “Gateway to the Isles.” There, we browsed local shops and grabbed some fresh seafood. Bellies full and a dram or two later at Oban Distillery, we hopped back on the coach and drove to Kennacraig to make our evening ferry to Islay. For two hours, we sailed along the glass-like Sound of Jura before the Paps of Jura mountains came into view, signaling that the island was just ahead. Arriving in Islay was like nothing I’d experienced before. At just 240 square miles, the island felt entirely remote yet surprisingly homey. We settled in for the evening in the town of Bowmore. We didn’t know what to expect when our itinerary said accommodations would be shared, but we were pleasantly surprised by the setup we were met with at Bowmore Distillery Cottages. There were four bedrooms, and my dad and I each had our own room, while two others from our group took over the other two rooms and shared the communal kitchen and living spaces with us. Our first full day on whisky island started with a short two-minute walk to the distillery that would kick off our tour: Bowmore Distillery. We learned about the distillery’s 240-year history on the island, which was a great starting point for the days ahead. Then came a tasting (straight from the cask!) in the cellar, and another tasting upstairs to end the tour, this time with whisky, chocolate, and views of the sea. Since Islay is a very small island with a population of a little over 3,000 people, it’s important to be flexible on these types of trips and just roll with the punches. Depending on the days of your tour, some distilleries may be closed or not open to full tours. Our itinerary said we’d be visiting Kilchoman on day one, but instead, we diverted to Ardnahoe for a lively tour and quick tasting before driving through the countryside to Bunnahabhain. With sweeping views of the clear blue waters, we explored the facilities and sampled four drams at Islay’s most remote distillery. While it's always great to meet new people and travel around with them, I appreciated that lunches and evenings were free for us to explore at leisure. After full days of sampling whiskies, it was a nice respite to just enjoy some quality time with my dad. That said, by day two, our group was buzzing as we became more comfortable with each other—and this second day was the big one for most of us as we took on the villages of Ardbeg, Lagavulin, and Laphroaig, each with their own distilleries. Though the island is small, the differences between the West Coast and Southern Coast became evident as we left Bowmore toward Ardbeg. Because it was a Saturday, our itinerary mentioned our visit to Ardbeg would not include a tour—but, as I said, roll with the punches. We did, in fact, get to see some of the facilities and end with a five-dram tasting. This experience was probably one of the most memorable moments of the trip for me—sitting around a table in the sunshine with people I’d just met, laughing, and sampling some of the finest whiskies in the world. We made a quick stop at Kildalton Church, home to an eighth-century cross and one of Scotland’s finest early Christian monuments, before continuing toward Port Ellen, a tiny town built around Loch Leòdamais, for a lunch break. Again, these parts of the tour are not organized, so if you have a restaurant or attraction in mind you want to visit, make an early reservation or chance your luck at walking in. At Lagavulin Distillery, our visit didn’t include a tour or tasting, but we chatted around the bar with our new friends and strolled down to the coast. In under five minutes, we made it to Laphroaig—our last whisky tasting of the trip. Here, we enjoyed an immersive tour of the peat kilns, stills, and warehouses before sampling a few more of their whiskies, our Glencairn glasses conveniently attached to lanyards around our necks. On day four, we had an early start and set sail again for a two-hour journey from Islay to Kennacraig. We treated ourselves to a full Scottish breakfast and explored the ferry, this time passing strangers-turned-friends. After an hour’s drive, we stopped in the castle town of Inveraray for lunch before making our way through the rugged Arrochar Alps to the “Rest and Be Thankful” mountain pass viewpoint. Our final stop was the quintessential village of Luss, where we, of course, found yet another distillery to visit. There was something heavy yet appreciative in the air during our last stop—we were sad it was our last day, but incredibly thankful for the new connections, laughs, and memories we’d made along the way. I’ve done Rabbie’s day tours in the past, but this one was particularly immersive because we were with the same people for the entirety of the trip—and we lucked out with our guide. All in all, this experience came at just the right time for my dad and me, and it was amazing learning more about his passions. According to him, a man with a collection of over 200 whiskies, “it was well worth the money.” How to book Rabbie’s Islay & the Whisky Coast tour Founded in Edinburgh in 1993, Rabbie’s specializes in small-group tours throughout Scotland, the UK, Ireland, and Europe. The four-day Islay & the Whisky Coast tour departs from Edinburgh and includes transportation, ferry crossings, entrance fees, and three nights in Bowmore (some distillery tours and tastings are available for an additional fee). You can book the tour on Rabbie's website, Viator, or GetYourGuide.

item.title: 12 best islands in Thailand to visit 2026 for honeymooners, families and solo travellers
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 6.34
The best islands in Thailand evoke images of pristine white sands, rustic-chic beach shacks, and gently swaying hammocks offering views of the turquoise sea and famed rock formations. But with a total of 1,430 islands spread across the Gulf of Thailand and Andaman Sea, not all are born equal. The largest, Phuket, is one of the busiest in terms of travellers, with its own international airport and some of the best hotels in Thailand. Then there are the tiny, off-the-beaten-track gems like Koh Lipe, small enough to explore by foot and only accessible by speedboat or ferry from the Thai mainland. With so many to choose from, one of the best approaches is to base your itinerary on the time of year. Islands off the West Coast such as Phuket, Koh Lanta and Koh Lipe are at their best in December to April, while Koh Samui and Koh Tao off the east coast are ideal for visiting from February to September. There's no need to choose just one island either, with day trips by boat readily available to take you from plush resort to remote islet and back again. Lauren Burvill For inspiration, we round up the best islands in Thai including what they offer and where to stay. Editor's picks of the best islands in Thailand - For families: Koh Samui - For couples: Koh Lipe - For solo travel: Koh Pha Ngan and Koh Phi Phi - For divers and snorkelers: Koh Phi Phi How to travel between islands in Thailand? It depends on what islands you'll be travelling to during your holiday. It is best to take the ferry between islands in Southern Thailands. For example, Phuket (a great starting point) has a daily ferry to Ko Phi Phi that takes anywhere between 45 minutes to an hour plus. There are also some islands like Phuket, Krabi and Koh Samui that can easily be accessed via airplanes too.

item.title: Where was 'The Dog Stars' filmed? The surprising mountainous hideout that stood in for Canada's peaks
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.91
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Dog Stars filmed? The year is 2035. Along a mountain range on the south side of Denver, survivors are navigating an unprecedented, post-pandemic world. A deadly flu outbreak has wiped out a vast majority of the human population, and many who have survived remain with a debilitating blood disease. This is the premise of Ridley Scott’s latest blockbuster, starring Jacob Elordi as young pilot Hig, Margaret Qualley as Cima and Josh Brolin as Bangley. While Bangley has no intentions of leaving the efficient homestead he and Hig have settled into, Hig is determined to track down other survivors, frequently embarking on tracking missions alongside his trusty dog, Jasper. As these stories unfold in a post-apocalyptic world far from crumbling metropolises, the natural world plays a major role in Scott’s latest movie. While set in Canada, filming took place in Italy between April and June 2025. “The size and scale of the production footprint in Italy was ideal for what we needed,” says The Dog Stars production designer Chris Seager. “We found a combination of quality locations that could convincingly represent Colorado, while also being relatively close together. This allowed us to work much more efficiently from a production point of view.” “We also considered Canada,” says Chris. “But ultimately Italy offered the best combination of location quality, scale and practical logistics. Being able to concentrate so many of the locations within a manageable area was a huge advantage for the production, helping us maximise our time and resources.” So where exactly did the team set up camp during the epic-scale production? Here, we uncover some of the key locations to keep an eye out for. Cinecittà Studios, Rome While much of The Dog Stars’ cinematography took place beside forests and mountain peaks, Rome’s Cinecittà Studios played a crucial role in the scenes set at Grand Junction Airport. “Cinecittà was amazing,” says Chris. “It quickly became evident that, to achieve the scale and complexity of the effects that Ridley wanted, we needed to work on a soundstage where we could have complete control over the environment.” Chris recalls how the set within Europe’s largest film studio was built in just four weeks. On the studio filming, cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt said, “[Cinecittà Studios] houses Italy’s most modern sound stages. It’s the centre of studio production and is familiar to all local crew. It was the best and most obvious option.” Abruzzo Much filming also took place in Italy’s Abruzzo region. One such apocalyptic scene honed in on the city of Avezzano. Chris says: “One of the biggest and most challenging locations was the petrol station [in Avezzano] where we filmed the city landing sequence – we actually landed the plane in the street! We transformed the location entirely: we trashed the petrol station and the surrounding area to create the sense of a world that had been abandoned and reclaimed by nature. The greens department and the layered set dressing played a huge role in this. “To represent the cycle of life, we created a swimming pool and diving board, which we filled with dead bodies and overgrown vegetation, crocuses growing through the remains. It was a very strong visual expression of the post-apocalyptic, graphic world, but it also presented considerable logistical challenges in terms of access and working within the location.” EUR, Rome The Roman business and residential district of EUR (Esposizione Universale Roma), known for its cultural happenings and Fascist-era architecture, saw the production team set up more post-apocalyptic scenes. “The Roman neighbourhood of EUR stood in for the Denver city hall triage centre where Hig goes to retrieve supplies. It was a challenging place to shoot, as it’s normally a busy city, but the Roman authorities were very helpful in making it happen for us, and it was ultimately one of the most successful sections of the film,” says Erik. Bordano Bordano was an empty field that is used for hang-gliding, so we had to transform the entire site from scratch,” says Chris. “We built nine airplane hangars, Bangley’s house and tower, as well as a number of smaller sheds and a trailer home. We also dressed large quantities of grass and other greenery to make the location feel abandoned and overgrown.” “The whole process took approximately five weeks, which was a very tight turnaround given the scale of the build. The major benefit of working on location was the sheer amount of space and the ability to create the environment at the scale required, rather than being constrained by a studio. It also allowed the buildings, runway and surrounding environment to exist together as one cohesive world, giving the finished locations a greater sense of authenticity and scale.” The Dog Stars is in UK cinemas now

item.title: The world's most connected airport has been revealed – and it's no longer London Heathrow
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.48
Each year, the OAG Megahubs Index reveals the best-connected airports around the world, revealing the sleek aviation hubs are best for getting us on our merry way – whether that’s on a fly-and-flop resort stay or somewhere altogether more niche and intrepid. Airport connectivity is assessed across various categories: Top 50 Most Connected Airports; Top 25 Most Connected Low-Cost Carrier (LCC) Airports; Top 25 Most Connected US Airports; Top 10 Most Connected Airports (International) by region. Ascertaining the world’s most connected airports is a mammoth task. To do so, flight data specialists at OAG analyse data from the 100 largest international airports over a 12-month period and calculate the number of possible connections between inbound and outbound flights within a six-hour window. In 2025, London Heathrow (LHR) retained its title as the world’s most connected airport for the third consecutive year, with more than 59,000 connections to 226 destinations on the busiest day of operations. Istanbul Airport (IST) saw one of the greatest increases from eighth position in 2024 to second in 2025, while Kuala Lumpur (KUL) was the best-connected Asian airport, in joint fourth place globally with Frankfurt (FRA). However, geopolitical tensions and airports’ determination to attract new travellers, among other factors, have led to significant movement in 2026’s rankings. London Heathrow has officially been overtaken by Istanbul, which has become the most connected airport in the world for the first time. As a result of connections to 337 global destinations – many serviced by Turkish Airlines, the world’s best-connected airline – the eighth-busiest airport globally acts as a gateway to much of the world. London Heathrow only slips by one place to second, with potential connections on the busiest day of operations between September 2025 and August 2026 falling by six per cent compared to the year before. Middle East schedules have undoubtedly affected Heathrow’s position, with Istanbul often serving as an alternative to hubs that experienced flight cancellations and delays as the conflict persisted. Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS) has seen both capacity and destinations grow, claiming third position, while Kuala Lumpur retains fourth position – despite potential connections falling slightly since last year, destinations served have increased from 151 to 154.

item.title: Where was 'Slow Horses' filmed? 5 London locations to look out for in the Apple TV+ series
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.16
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Slow Horses filmed? In 2022, Apple TV+ viewers were introduced to sinister forces and an underground world of espionage via London’s Slough House. Here, a dysfunctional team of British intelligence agents, all of whom have committed career-ending mistakes, work behind the scenes in an MI5 ‘dumping ground’. Across five seasons, chaos has followed the Slow Horses as they duck and dive their way through the city, uncovering plots and secrets along the way. Now, Emmy Award and BAFTA winner Sir Gary Oldman returns as Jackson Lamb for Slow Horses’ highly anticipated sixth season – with plenty of recognisable London locations to look out for. Here, we highlight some of the key filming locations across the city so you can turn them into a set-jetting walking route – free of menacing encounters, hopefully. Aldersgate Street The Slow Horses’ base, Slough House, has remained the same since the show first aired. You can find the dumping ground on Aldersgate Street, just around the corner from Barbican Underground Station. The office site sits next to Vecchio Parioli, a family-run Italian restaurant that’s been serving up hearty fare since 1950. Duke of York statue This London landmark, a column dedicated to Prince Frederick, the second son of King George III, is the backdrop of Lamb and Taverner’s final exchange in season one. Regent’s Park Eagle-eyed viewers will have spotted filming across parts of Regent’s Park in season three, as Taverner (played by Kristin Scott Thomas) and Lamb meet away from prying eyes. Scenes use the park’s North Gate entrance and one of the canalside benches. Granary Square Fountains River (played by Jack Lowden) and Frank’s season four showdown takes place in Granary Square Fountains. While this takes place on the banks of the River Thames in the novels, it proved a bit of a logistical nightmare on-screen – it turns out that having actors chucked into the Thames isn't the most health-and-safety-friendly stunt. Beppe's Cafe This is the real cafe that Jackson Lamb visits for his breakfasts. The hideout is a greasy spoon popular with those who live and work around Smithfield Market. Season 1 - 5 of Slow Horses is available to watch on Apple TV+ now. Season 6 airs weekly until 21 October 2026.

item.title: 10 best ultra-light suitcases that will save you from airline weight fees for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.83
Every traveller knows the sinking feeling of heaving their case onto an airport luggage scale, only to watch the numbers tick perilously close to the limit before you’ve even packed a souvenir. Whether you’re attempting to breeze through security with a single cabin bag or hauling a fortnight’s worth of gear across multiple long-haul legs, every extra gram built into your suitcase is one stolen from your overall packing allowance. Put simply: lightweight luggage is the way to go, especially if you’re a known over-packer. Fortunately, our favourite luggage brands prove that trimming total weight down does not mean sacrificing structural integrity or clever interior organisation. Our constantly-travelling editors have tested nearly 100 suitcases over the years, and the below solidly rank most highly on the weight front, leaving plenty of room for heavy winter knits, extra boots – or a selection of buys from your latest travels. We’ve selected only carry-on cases under 3kg, and checked suitcases under 5kg to earn an esteemed spot as one of our best lightweight suitcases. For the complete edit of the top luggage to know about in 2026, see our full guide, or our guide to the best suitcase sets. Below, the best lightweight suitcases for 2026, thoroughly tested by our editors on real-world trips to ensure they survive the rigours of the baggage carousel without dragging you down. The best lightweight luggage at-a-glance The best lightweight carry-on suitcases The best lightweight check-in suitcases How we test lightweight suitcases Every suitcase in this guide undergoes initial hands-on evaluation in our office by commerce writers Charley Ward and Lauren Burvill, before being trialled on real-world trips by our broader editorial team. Across dozens of flights and rail journeys, we rigorously test shell durability, 360-degree spinner wheel smoothness, lock security, internal organisation – including zip dividers and laptop sleeves – and general value for money. Key metrics like empty weight, exterior dimensions, ease of handling, and overall aesthetics are also weighed during our process. Airline hand luggage weight and size limits - British Airways: 1 personal item (40 x 30 x 15 cm, up to 23 kg) + 1 cabin bag (56 x 45 x 25 cm, up to 23 kg). - EasyJet: 1 under-seat bag (45 x 36 x 20 cm, up to 15 kg). Large cabin bag (56 x 45 x 25 cm) available for an additional fee. - Emirates: 1 personal item + 1 cabin bag (55 x 38 x 20 cm, up to 7 kg combined). - Etihad: 1 personal item + 1 cabin bag (56 x 36 x 23 cm, up to 7 kg combined). - Ryanair: 1 small personal bag (40 x 20 x 25 cm). Large cabin bag (55 x 40 x 20 cm, up to 10 kg) available with Priority booking. - Singapore Airlines: 1 personal item + 1 cabin bag (max combined dimensions of 115 cm, up to 7 kg). - Virgin Atlantic: 1 personal item + 1 cabin bag (56 x 36 x 23 cm, up to 10 kg). What dimensions should a cabin suitcase be? While exact carry-on restrictions vary by carrier, most standard cabin bags measure around 55 x 35 x 25 cm, which comfortably fits into the overhead bins of most major airlines. Most carriers also permit a secondary personal item to stash beneath the seat in front of you – ideal for quick-access items like passports, tech gadgets, and water bottles. If you pack efficiently, a well-structured personal item can even eliminate the need for an overhead trolley bag on quick weekend getaways. What is the maximum weight allowance for hand luggage? Carry-on weight allowances generally range between 7kg and 15kg depending on the airline, with the global average sitting around 8 kg. EasyJet remains one of the most generous carriers with a 15 kg allowance, whereas budget lines often enforce stricter 7kg or 10kg caps. To avoid unpleasant surprises or excess baggage charges at the gate, we recommend investing in a portable luggage scale and double-checking your specific airline's baggage policy prior to departure.

item.title: This sun-soaked destination has been named the best place for a last-minute autumn escape
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.44
As one record-breaking summer draws to a close and the guarantee of drizzle and plummeting temperatures hangs over us, the prospect of catching some last-minute autumn sunshine is extremely tempting. While there is no shortage of chic winter sun destinations on our radar, whether that’s Christmas in the Caribbean or banishing the January blues along Mexico’s Pacific coast, there’s still time to top up the vitamin D closer to home. But where should we be heading for sun-sure adventures this September and October? According to the number-crunchers at travel insurance site Quotezone.co.uk, Antalya is the best destination for an autumn sun getaway right now. The ancient Turkish city has long been a favourite destination among sun-seekers, with a plethora of sleek hotels and resorts catering to every type of escape along its glittering coast. With some of the best beaches in Turkey, plenty of history to uncover, a lively city centre and natural landscapes beloved by active travellers and adrenaline junkies, it’s the perfect place to don the swimwear one last time. To uncover the dreamiest autumn sun destinations, Quotezone selected ten of the most popular holiday spots in southern Europe and pitted them against each other across several factors. These include the average temperatures in September and October, sunshine hours, rainfall and sea temperature – plus the lowest price for a three-night stay. With an average temperature of 27.6°C, 9.5 sunshine hours and a particularly balmy sea temperature of 27.5°C, Antalya is a clear winner. In second place is the Canary Island of Tenerife, included in the survey as an autonomous community of Spain, with average temperatures of 26.3°C and some of the cheapest stays at £108 for three nights. The Cypriot city of Larnaca is third, also offering 9.5 hours of sunshine, while the largest and most southerly of the Greek islands, Crete, promises an escape from the northern hemisphere’s chill and 24.5°C waters for bathing.

item.title: The 10 best hotels in the Bahamas for a postcard-perfect stay in the Caribbean in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.18
When Nasa astronaut Scott Kelly spent a year in the inky, star-filled skies of the International Space Station in 2015, it was the vivid azure waters of the Bahamas that he called "the most beautiful place from space.” With 700 islands teeming with endlessly soft, empty beaches and towns filled with brightly coloured clapboard cottages, swaying palms and creeping bougainvillaea, it’s even better when you’re dipping your toes directly in it. The turquoise shallows of the Bahamas are an underwater sensation thanks to its barrier reef, making it one of the best countries in the Caribbean for snorkelling and diving. There’s a dizzying amount of hotels on offer, from postcard-pretty cottages on the A-list favourite Harbour Island to the all-singing, all-dancing family-friendly resorts in the capital of Nassau; here’s our pick of the best hotels in the Bahamas. Editor's picks - For luxury: Coral Sands Inn & Cottages - For couples: Eleven Bahama House - For families: The Royal Atlantis Bahamas When is the best time to visit the Bahamas? For low humidity and plenty of sunshine, the Bahamas is at its best between December and April. December is the peak season and while that will certainly keep the beaches busy, it also means perfect weather. Our tip: strike out for Harbour Island, a three-mile-long, mile-and-a-half-wide sliver of sensational, pink-sand stretches, where there are always enough sunbeds to go around. For less crowds and lower prices while still enjoying good weather, aim to visit between May to June or Mid-November. The island's peak hurricane season usually hits between June to November. How we choose the best hotels in the Bahamas Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We're always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

item.title: Why we're obsessing over the Balkans right now: 5 destinations to visit before the crowds arrive
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.87
A region of mountains, beaches, waterfalls and wonder, the Balkans feel like West shading into East. You can taste it in the food and hear it when different religions pray. The cognoscenti have been heading to these eccentric nations for years, lured by lower costs and visitor numbers compared with Western Europe – but travel insiders are only just cottoning on. I have been visiting the Balkans for a decade. I’ve enjoyed hanging out of the window of a smoky train carriage clattering through the hills from Mostar to Sarajevo, exploring the remains of the 1960s vision of a futuristic Skopje and taking a cable car up Mount Dajti outside Tirana. The game-changer this year, though, is the EES chaos, which has ruined so many previously simple EU hops. In non-Schengen Kosovo, Serbia, Bosnia, Montenegro, Albania and North Macedonia you don’t have to worry about missing your plane while you’re stuck in a passport queue, and the entry and exit process is a breeze. The topography of the Balkans is dramatic to say the least. There aren’t bulky hotels or giant developments, and the region feels smaller and more friendly than the rest of Europe. The mountains provide a glorious backdrop for climbing and walking galore – one of Europe's most stunning international hikes is the Peaks of the Balkans, which connects Kosovo, Albania and Montenegro in a 124-mile loop. As well as hiking, wellness retreats have been booming here in southeastern Europe, but they’re unlike their counterparts in other European countries, largely because they aren’t on the same scale. Here you can really unwind at spa resorts, spend time in nature, wild swim and paddleboard on deserted lakes, then clamber up paths not chock-a-block with tourists. Coastal hotels have more space, and jagged coastlines mean smaller beaches, remote coves and dreamy turquoise waters. The Balkans have pushed back against million-dollar hotels and large resorts, embracing ecotourism. Montenegro established the Eco Fund in 2020 and has committed, as far back as 1991, to becoming an environmentally sustainable country. Eco-resorts are blossoming, with the likes of Oblun offering an alternative vision to mass tourism: glamping, gardening and kayaking in the heart of the countryside, surrounded by orange, fig and pomegranate trees while you practise yoga. Visitors are also discovering the lesser-known cities of the Balkans. Pristina, Kosovo, is a fascinating and friendly spot, home to incredible socialist murals and gorgeous period architecture. The National Library of Kosovo, by Andrija Mutnjaković, from 1982, is a wild and wonderful journey into the soul of Kosovan heritage, inspired by mosque domes and books – it is the architectural highlight of Europe’s newest capital. Albania’s second city, Durrës, is also on the rise, with easy access to the country’s increasingly popular beaches. Skopje, meanwhile, attracts fans of 1960s Japanese genius Kenzō Tange, who redesigned the city and built the modern train station in a so-called metabolist style following the catastrophic 1963 earthquake. There's plenty to explore in the Balkan cities and the wilderness beyond – here we round up the best destinations to add to your travel wishlist. The best Balkan destinations to visit Montenegro This is the year to visit Montenegro – the country on everyone’s lips. Kotor Bay is flashy these days, and the super-rich who don’t want to die young flock to wellness retreats such as Siro Boka Place. Underrated capital Podgorica is where design-literate travellers are heading. Svetlana Kana Radević was a heroine of Montenegrin design who became the most famous female architect in the former Yugoslavia. Her Hotel Podgorica is remarkable – its exterior is clad in stone from the Morača river bed, and she designed the building as a series of steps blending into the side of the river valley. Montenegro also offers serene mountains, chances to sail along its coast and homely eateries such as family-run indie Scala Santa, open since 1996 and serving fish pâté and octopus salad in Kotor Old Town. Lake Ohrid, North Macedonia This year marks 25 years since the Ohrid Agreement was signed in this pretty North Macedonian town, bringing peace to the country then known as Macedonia. Today the lake and town both attract visitors seeking peace and quiet. The surrounding hills are ideal for walks, and Ohrid is famous for the ancient remains you can dive into the lake to see and the Monastery of St Naum on the lakeshore. The iconic money shot visitors want is of the 13th-century Church of St John at Kaneo, which overlooks the lake's cool waters. With 17 native fish species, angling is a way to unwind here, and fish feature heavily in the local cuisine – lake trout and clear fish soup are classic dishes. The coast of Albania With prices skyrocketing in Greece, Albania makes perfect sense as a coastal destination. Hike to Gjipe Beach and wild camp a stone’s throw from soft sand and dramatic cliffs. The peaceful, secluded Mirror Beach has the kind of turquoise water that'll have you plotting your return before you've left. Albania is heading towards a classy version of style-led, low-impact tourism. Zoe Hora in Dhërmi is telegraphing a different way forward – this design hotel is built around a series of houses. Aragosta overlooks the sea in Durrës, and serves fish pizza, qofte meatballs – Albania’s unofficial national dish – and trileçe, a milk cake with caramel. Check out the newly restored and reopened Pyramid cultural centre in the capital, Tirana, a city being radically renewed with pedestrianisation and outdoor art. Bosnia Spomen or Spomeniks are the defining feature of the Bosnian countryside, and can be found all across the former Yugoslavia. Most were erected by former president Tito, commemorating the partisan army who fought Nazism in the mountains. In Bosnia you can hike the Kozara National Park to the Kozara Spomenik – titled Monument to the Revolution. A two-and-a-half-hour trail leads you through forests and over streams to this historical site. Spomenik Database is the best resource if you’re on the hunt for Spomeniks. Mostar is full of ancient charm, and its famous bridge attracts the world’s best divers; Sarajevo has become a lively European city in the past decade, with bars, restaurants and rooftop venues. Bosnia also has a sliver of coast at the intriguing town of Neum. Serbia Belgrade is preparing for its year as an international host city, with Expo 2027 kicking off in May. The event, with the theme “Play for Humanity – Sport and Music for All”, will feature exhibitions, pavilions and talks encompassing architecture, technology and the arts. Although it won’t be ready for May, a new metro – a project that began decades ago – is finally set to be completed in 2027. More proof that Belgrade is ready for a new breed of in-the-know travellers is the opening of the newest outpost from the French design-hotel mini-chain Mama Shelter.
