Outside the capital, Novi Sad surprises with its Hungarian architecture and extensive riverside beaches, where the city goes to relax, and the mountains are ripe and ready for travellers looking for ski escapes that won’t break the bank.

item.title: 17 national parks so beautiful they look like another planet
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.52
Some places are beautiful for one specific reason: a beach at sunset, a mountain perfectly reflected in a lake, a rainforest humming with wildlife. But national parks offer something broader. By definition, they protect entire landscapes and ecosystems – drawing a line around expanses we’ve collectively decided are too precious to lose. For travellers, having a list of designated wonders is also an easy way to know exactly where (and how) to see some of the world’s most incredible natural wonders. That could mean rafting under waterfalls in Argentina, ballooning over fairy chimneys in Turkey, ice caving in Iceland, or hiking for three days to reach a wildflower-filled valley in India. There are many thousands of national parks around the world, so the trickiest part is narrowing down the list – but these 17, spanning six continents and encompassing an extraordinary range of scenery, are a good place to start. Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, Brazil At first glance, Lençóis Maranhenses looks like an enormous white desert – but this vast expanse contains multitudes. The park’s sand dunes are striped with turquoise and emerald lagoons (which accumulate during the rainy season), creating the effect of infinitely repeating oases. Book a five-hour bus ride from São Luís for a surreal swim break. Iguazú National Park, Argentina This park protects the Argentine side of the enormous Iguazú Falls (Iguaçu National Park is a hop over the border in Brazil), a system of some 275 roaring cascades deep in the rainforest. The bombastically – but fittingly – named Devil’s Throat is the standout waterfall here. Admire it from one of the walkways, or ride a speedboat right into the spray. Cabo Pulmo National Park, Mexico Who says national parks have to be in the mountains – or even on land at all? Located on the tip of Mexico’s Baja California Sur peninsula, Cabo Pulmo is a coastal wonderland of quiet beaches and rock formations – but its true appeal lies under the surface. Just offshore, the brilliant Pacific waters protect a vast coral reef system teeming with sea turtles and swirling schools of zooming jacks. Yellowstone National Park, United States Choosing just one US park is a near-impossible task, but Yellowstone takes the narrow lead. Not only was it the first designated national park in the country (and, by most accounts, the entire world), but its geological diversity can’t be beat – within its 2.2 million acres, you’ll find mountains, canyons, geysers, rainbow-gradient hot springs, and more. Banff National Park, Canada This one’s no surprise. Banff National Park is one of Canada’s shining stars, beloved for its staggering views of the Rockies and glacial, almost impossibly blue lakes. Lake Louise, Moraine Lake, and Lake Minnewanka are all standouts, equally lovely when reflecting sunshine in summer and frozen over in winter. Namib-Naukluft National Park, Namibia Namib-Naukluft is the Namibia you came for: burnt-orange sand dunes, blindingly white salt pans, and the eerie skeleton trees of Deadvlei. It’s a little bit Mars, a little bit Fury Road, but an absolute original that has no peer. Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park, Madagascar Madagascar is one of the world’s hardest-to-reach countries, which makes its landscapes feel even more immaculate. Case in point: the Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park. Famous for its forest of limestone needles jutting into the sky, the park is almost terrifying in its beauty – though lightened by the fact that the Malagasy word “tsingy” roughly translates to “where one cannot walk barefoot.” Noted! Serengeti National Park, Tanzania The Serengeti occupies an almost mythical space in our collective mind. The Great Migration, in which millions of wildebeest move across the plains, is one of Earth’s greatest natural shows. But even in stillness, the region is magnificent – golden grasslands rolling beneath the open sky, with acacia trees punctuating the otherwise endless horizon. Vatnajökull National Park, Iceland Iceland is known as the land of fire and ice, and no place better encapsulates that dramatic epithet than Vatnajökull National Park. Its eponymous glacier and accompanying ice caves dominate the scene, but active volcanoes simmer beneath the freeze, and rivers of meltwater cut through the terrain. It’s a true study in contrasts, both elemental and chromatic – brilliant blue ice, inky black rocks. Las Salinas de Torrevieja National Park, Spain Yes, it really is that pink. Torrevieja’s salt lagoon gets its hue from microorganisms that release red pigments in saline conditions – an imperceptible process that yields magnificent results. It’s an Instagram darling, sure, but it’s also a place to appreciate nature’s inner workings and see the world through bubblegum-coloured glasses. Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia Plitvice Lakes National Park may not be hidden, but it sure is a gem. Sixteen interconnected lakes cascade through the forest, linked by a series of waterfalls and natural travertine barriers, and ranging in hue from brilliant turquoise to deep blue and green. Make your way through the selfie-snapping crowds, find an empty spot on one of the wooden walkways, and just stand in awe. Valley of Flowers National Park, India The name pretty much says it all: During the summer blooming season, Uttarakhand’s Valley of Flowers transforms into a huge natural garden, with wildflowers blanketing the Alpine meadows in a riot of colour. Getting here requires a lengthy trek (we’re talking several days) through the Himalayas, but the effort just makes the visual payoff that much sweeter. Göreme National Park, Türkiye Göreme is defined by Cappadocia’s fairy chimneys, which are about as magical as they sound. The mushroom-shaped rock structures, carved over millennia by volcanic activity and erosion, are best viewed from above – namely in the basket of a hot-air balloon. Set your alarm and time your ride to sunrise, so you can be the first to watch the landscapes awaken for the day. Kelimutu National Park, Indonesia Three lakes, three wildly different colours. Kelimutu National Park’s bodies of water shift at the whims of the minerals and gases beneath the craters, so you never know exactly what shade you’ll see when you arrive – red, blue, green, or black. It’s as if Mother Nature is wearing a trio of mood rings. Zhangjiajie National Forest Park, China Located in China’s Wulingyuan Scenic Area, Zhangjiajie boasts thousands of jagged sandstone peaks that rise dramatically over lush treetops – and when mist shrouds the valley below, they almost seem to float above the clouds. (Look familiar? The park famously inspired the Hallelujah Mountains in Avatar.) Fiordland National Park, New Zealand Fiordland National Park showcases some of New Zealand’s most striking features, all in one space: mountains, rainforests, waterfalls, and deep glacial fjords. Many visitors zero in on Milford Sound, the undeniable star attraction; but there truly are no bad views here. Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park, Australia Few landmarks are as recognisable as Uluṟu, a sandstone monolith rising from an otherwise flat and open desert. The rockface changes colour depending on the sun’s position – ochre during the day, blazing orange and pink at sunset, and purple at twilight.

item.title: The best Airbnbs in Naples to book in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.52
Naples is finally having its moment, and the spike in foreign tourism has also helped revitalise the city’s hospitality scene. The best way to experience this relatively unsung spot for a few nights? By living like a local in one of the best Airbnbs in Naples. This gem of the Mediterranean has always been an inspiration and a second home for artists, so much so that prominent literary figures like Goethe, Shelley and Dumas spent years living in this eclectic and gorgeously complicated city. With visitors of that calibre, the hotel scene was already well developed, but Airbnbs are now catching up, with some so well-curated that they could easily compete with the best hotels in Naples. This southern urban destination has many faces, and choosing your base could really transform the way you experience it. From the buzzing chaos of the Rione Sanità and the chic shopping streets of Chiaia to the affluent Posillipo neighbourhood, we have selected some of the best Airbnbs in Naples to enjoy it all on your terms. Editor's picks: Best location: A luxury flat on the sea in Posillipo Best for culture: An artsy flat in the historic centre Best affordable stay: A history-filled stay in the city centre How we choose the best Airbnbs in Naples We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. All listings featured on Condé Nast Traveller are independently selected by our editors. If you book something through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This is our pick of the best Airbnbs in Naples.

item.title: 10 of the best pubs in Bath for West Country buzz, low-slung beams and crisp cider pints
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.32
There’s something about a cold pint in one of the best pubs in Bath that is instantly happy-making. “There ain’t nothin’ like good cider for to make your smile grow wider, and there’s still more cider way down west!” sing The Wurzels. And it’s true: the West Country buzz, the low-slung beams and the beer gardens spilling out alongside the River Avon – it all truly makes you smile. Then there’s the old-world lure of Bath’s drinking holes in a city so drenched in history that the oldest is the Saracens Head at the bottom of Broad Street, built in 1713 and visited by Charles Dickens. If you spend your teenage years sliding in and out of Bath’s pubs as I did, there’s a risk that cider is ruined forever. But time, it turns out, is a healer when it comes to scrumpy overconsumption. And returning to live in the West Country as an adult, there are cooler taphouses and a heady influx of craft beer to discover, as well as the nostalgic old haunts to sink into until last orders. On Saturdays during the summer, Dick Willows cider farm in the pretty village of Claverton Down, just outside of town, opens its doors for live music. And towards Bradford-on-Avon is the Iford Cider Taphouse with its megawatt sunset and sourdough pizzas. In a city where it’s tempting to ferociously frog-march yourself around the sights, here’s our pick of pubs to proudly skive off to, where a swift half happily turns into a whole afternoon at the bar. The Marlborough Tavern It’s hard to trump the location of this 200-year-old pub just minutes from John Wood the Younger’s show-stopping Royal Crescent: the perfect refuge once you’ve ticked off the sights. Wind up here for a run of inventive small plates (think Asian-style king prawn salad), before saddling up for a Marlborough Tavern burger, towering with pickles and smoked cheddar. The head chef’s Bloody Mary is the perfect warm-up for its Sunday roast, and when the sun shines there’s a shady walled garden to spill out into. Address: The Marlborough Tavern, 35 Marlborough Buildings, Bath BA1 2LY Website: marlborough-tavern.com Hop Pole Inn When this 16th-century inn, less than four miles outside of Bath, shut its doors in 2018 and property developers loomed, the villagers launched the Save the Hop Pole Inn campaign with fervour. Fast forward to the beginning of 2025 and the doors were open, interiors stripped back (muted greens and scrubbed wooden tables) and the menu cleverly curated by chef Charlie Rawlings, with meat sourced from his family farm less than a mile away. Locals can once again descend for a pint of ale and the hearty sandwiches (think Coronation chicken piled high in a milk bun from Pipit bakery in nearby Bradford-on-Avon) make it a non-negotiable pitstop for hungry cyclists navigating the towpath along the Kennet and Avon Canal. Address: Hop Pole Inn, Woods Hill, Limpley Stoke, Bath BA2 7FS Website: hoppoleinn.uk The Talbot Inn With a 15th-century church tucked behind it (complete with a statue by Sir Alfred Munnings), the Mells River meandering nearby and the best of Somerset’s rolling countryside as the backdrop, The Talbot Inn is farcically bucolic. This is one of the Beckford Group’s West Country pubs and another masterclass in what a pub should be: candles lit, regulars lining the bar, local ales and tired dogs at heel. Step under the carriage archway into a cobbled courtyard and settle in for a pint of Talbot ale on a wrought iron table or decamp inside for plates of chalk stream trout pate and salted fennel perhaps, or the hearty ploughman’s with Wiltshire ham, Vale of Camelot cheddar and pickles – all well worth the 20-minute trip from Bath. Address: The Talbot Inn, Mells, Somerset BA11 3PN Website: talbotinn.com Electric Bear Brewing Taproom In an industrial corner of town to the west of the city, a cool crowd descends on the taproom at the Electric Bear brewery each weekend. Queues snake for pints of craft beer and the long trestle tables fill with plates piled high from the street food vans (cheese toasties, Greek gyros, slow-cooked beef tacos…) with an eclectic line-up of live music as the soundtrack – plus the chance to recover from the night before with Sunday morning yoga sessions. Address: Electric Bear Brewing Taproom, Unit 12, The Maltings, Brassmill Lane, Bath BA1 3JL Website: electricbearbrewing.com The Bell Inn If arty Walcot Street is proudly rebellious in a city that can feel a little strait-laced with its Georgian grandeur, then the 300-year-old The Bell Inn might be its flag bearer. In 2013, Glastonbury’s Michael Eavis was among the 500-plus-strong customer buyout, which promised to keep this a place that showcased live music, celebrated real ale and cider, artisan produce and analogue sounds and championed Bath’s artistic community. Inside it is happily bohemian, with fairy lights, hops hanging over the bar and live music ringing out. Address: The Bell Inn, 103 Walcot Street, Bath BA1 5BW Website: thebellinnbath.co.uk The Grapes Once a townhouse for the affluent taking the waters in the city, by the late 18th century this pub had its name ‘The Grapes’, and over 200 years later it’s still a place to let off steam. Drinkers spill out onto Westgate Street armed with pints of cider from nearby Iford Manor, or gin from the Bath Distillery, all to the sound of jazz and traditional folk sessions as well as DJ sets. Upstairs in the Jacobean living room (which features an early 17th-century ornate lime plaster ceiling), the pace is altogether calmer, with a roster of events from life drawing classes to its ‘People, Planet, Pint’ meet-ups where locals gather to put sustainability in the spotlight. Address: The Grapes, 14 Westgate Street, Bath BA1 1EQ Website: thegrapesbath.co.uk The Raven Tucked on the cobbled Queen Street in the centre of town, here is a Bath boozer to settle into until last orders. On Bath rugby match days West Country patriotism is alive, but on any weekend it’s as noisy as a good pub should be (it has form as a watering hole: during the Second World War it was a favourite with pilots stationed at a nearby airfield and in the 1980s it was said to be a go-to for the city’s goths and bikers.) You can bag a hearty pie to fill up on (try the ‘deer stalker’ with venison, bacon, lentils and red wine), but it’s the ale that you’re here for. Pull up a stool for its exclusive brews, the Raven Ale and Raven’s Gold, as well as a pick of craft beers including its own hazy IPA brewed by Arbor in Bristol. Address: The Raven, 6-7 Queen Street, Bath, BA1 1HE Website: theravenofbath.co.uk The Chequers In the smartest corner of town, tucked on Rivers Street between The Circus and the Royal Crescent is The Chequers, where head chef Sam Stone has masterminded a menu at odds with any notion of simple pub grub. There’s burrata with crispy garlic chilli oil while you wait, then coppa from nearby Somer Valley Farms perhaps, rarebit made with Westcombe cheddar from Bruton and rib of beef (also local) with brown butter jus. But that doesn’t mean it’s a pub that’s morphed into a hushed restaurant: the bar is reassuringly noisy with locals armed with an ale and after-work drinkers spilling onto the pavement benches outside. Address: 50 Rivers St, Bath, BA1 2QA Website: chequersbath.net The Welly A buzzing taproom rather than a cosy pub, The Welly on pretty Green Street was opened last year by the team behind Somer Valley Farms and Somer Valley Brewing. Here, the best of the West Country’s bounty is up in lights: there’s gin from the Bath Distillery, bread from Landrace Bakery, cider from Iford and beef from its own farm. A perfectly placed pitstop in the middle of town to refuel with nose-to-tail, zero-waste small plates (don’t leave without trying the Somer Valley scotch egg) and a pint of pilsner. Address: The Welly, 9 Green Street, Bath, BA1 2JY Website: somervalleyfarms.com The Wheatsheaf Combe Hay Drive less than 15 minutes south out of town and you’ll end up in rolling Somerset countryside and the village of Combe Hay with its Bath stone cottages. The beer garden in the 16th century The Wheatsheaf, run by the Barton family for over 20 years, is the best kind of post-walk sanctuary. After navigating the impossibly steep footpaths up towards South Stoke or the tiny hamlet of Twinhoe, settle in for a pint of ale or a scoop of Purbeck ice cream. Or succumb to a well-earned long lunch: whole Brixham plaice with samphire, garden beans and café de Paris butter perhaps, with a steaming sticky toffee pudding to refuel you. Address: The Wheatsheaf, Combe Hay Ln, Combe Hay, Bath BA2 7EG Website: wheatsheafcombehay.com

item.title: D.C.’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Started as a Pop-Up
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 2.22
This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings. When chefs Justin Ahn and Alex McCoy opened Alfie’s as a pop-up restaurant in 2016, they didn’t expect the road to a brick-and-mortar location to last nearly a decade. The temporary D.C. location where the duo served northern Thai cuisine to the city’s tight-knit service industry and other regulars was open for just a few months. After that, Ahn and McCoy began operating it as a roving concept all around the world, but now they’re finally returning to D.C. with a permanent venue in Georgetown. Now the team is settled into a new 25-seat venue tucked in an alley off of Georgetown’s M Street serving Thai dishes made with Mid-Atlantic ingredients and natural wine produced just over the river in Virginia. Still, elements of the pop-up — like its run-and-gun service and chalkboard menu that shifts based on what local purveyors have in season — remain. We caught up with McCoy to learn more about how the team has shifted this scrappy pop-up model into a brick-and-mortar concept while keeping that dynamic energy intact. Liz Provencher: Why did you decide to launch Alfie’s in a pop-up format? Alex McCoy: We [already] had a permanent space in Petworth that we were building out [for our brick-and-mortar restaurant]. There was another restaurant space down the street that was slated to be demolished, so we talked to the landlords and they were like, “It’s yours until your space is ready or our project starts.” We thought it was a great opportunity to train our staff, test the food, and work through the menus while our spot was in construction. It was in a quiet part of town, and we just really wanted to have fun with it, but it ended up becoming this cult sensation. We were packed for months in advance. We had Vogue writing about us. Bon Appetit called it one of the top new restaurants in America. But it was really only about six months total that we had the place open, which is kind of wild. We closed the pop-up in 2017. That Petworth space didn’t end up working out for us, so we had to look for a new space. In the meantime, we were doing pop-ups in New York, D.C., London. We spent a lot of time overseas and some of the bigger pop-ups were in London with our buddies at Carousel. In that time, we were always looking for a new venue, and it was the time in Europe that really evolved the brand into what it is now. How did that time on the road shape the concept and operation plan? After COVID… everyone was struggling to try to figure out how to make restaurants work. With operating and staff costs going up, people were coming up with these creative service styles with [fewer] servers and less table service and more QR codes. The math isn’t mathing, you know? It seemed to me that the model should be similar to the way things operate in Europe with these little hole-in-the-wall places in Paris and London. Chefs don’t own six or seven restaurants; they’re in there [in one place] with one or two people. Not only was that the heart and soul of what Alfie’s always was, but it felt to me to be the way forward with the brand. After we did our last pop-up in London, we found this funky little spot in Georgetown, which is a neighborhood that feels the most European of anywhere in D.C. to me. It’s this incredible 25-seat space in an alleyway behind the hustle and bustle of M Street. It’s a little gritty. You step down into the alleyway and you have to dodge cars. It’s a really cool, funky space with a lot of character. So immediately it was like, this is the spot. This encapsulates the vibe and the ambiance and the feeling and the energy of what we’re trying to do. Have things changed since running the restaurant as a pop-up? It’s very much still a pop-up mindset. Justin, myself, and Ian, who is our sous chef, we’re 90 percent of the staff at this restaurant. From a cooking perspective, twenty-five seats is perfect because it gives us this opportunity to really [pore] over small batches of food. If we’re making a curry for the day, we’re [only] making 30 orders. We’re able to look at the menu on a daily basis and assess based on what ingredients come in. If our local fishmonger has five beautiful seabreams that he’s bringing in, we’ll just throw them on the menu because we have that ability to be scrappy and change things up and make adjustments and not have to retrain the staff and everything. That also plays into Thailand’s market culture, which is the ethos of our brand. We want to challenge ourselves to make dishes utilizing what’s available around here: rockfish, soft shell crab, foraged asparagus from the Eastern Shore, morel mushrooms, things like that. Does your drink menu also play off of local ingredients? When you go to France or Italy or another wine-producing region, you go to a bar or restaurant and you’re drinking what was made in the town or right around it. You don’t often see that in D.C., even when Virginia wineries are making spectacular stuff, literally 15 to 20 minutes away by car. The majority of our wines by the glass are from Virginia and we have more than 2,000 local producers by the bottle too. Our bottles, for the most part, are between $35 and $75. We only have a couple that top that. I think a lot of people go out to eat dreading the check. But I want people to come in and just get lost in the experience and not have to worry that they can’t take a chance on something that they haven’t tried before because it’s too expensive. They don’t have to be thinking about the price of everything they’re eating and drinking while they’re here. Alfie’s also has a wine club. How does that work? Alfie’s has always [drawn] a lot of regulars, and we’ve always tried to facilitate this vibe of being your other living room. If you love wine, we want this to be a place that you want to spend a lot of your time and cater that a little bit more. Our wine club has 19 spots, and for a monthly fee of $150, you basically get a rack of your own [in the restaurant]. If you have a great collection at home, you can bring it in. Or if you have specific tastes and things that you enjoy when you come here, we can curate the wine locker for you so you can actually purchase wine at a steep discount that we don’t have on the list. If there are special selections that are too expensive for us to put on the menu, we can get those for you, and you’ll pay 50% less than standard restaurant prices. After releasing the first few days of reservations, you immediately had 700 bookings. Were you expecting that kind of reception? I wouldn’t say I expected anything. [But] I was hoping for it, and I kind of felt it. Sometimes in this industry, you can feel when something is gonna hit. Leading up to [opening] and seeing some of the interest on social media, it seemed like it was gonna go that route so we were trying to plan for it. Alfie’s scratches an itch that [D.C. diners] haven’t been able to scratch at least since 2020. The city is getting burnt out [by] small businesses being replaced by big corporate restaurant group spots, and we’re very much the antithesis of that. You walk in, and Justin and I are in the kitchen, so we can say hi to you and run food to the table. I think it’s a vibe that D.C. hasn’t had in years.

item.title: Oxbridge’s formal dinners have had a reboot
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 3.33
Oxbridge’s formal dinners have had a reboot Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Recently I was invited to a formal hall dinner at Worcester College, Oxford. The Provost Lord David Isaac wanted to show me what food at a modern, progressive college looks like. In 2019, in an attempt to be more inclusive, the governing body voted to abolish some of the college’s formal hall traditions. Candlelit, multi-course dinners are a fixture of older universities such as Oxford, Cambridge, Durham and Trinity College Dublin; attendees wear gowns and lounge suits (black tie on Sundays, except for informal dinners), students are required to stand as fellows approach the high table and grace is said. Surprisingly, the undergraduates at Worcester voted overwhelmingly to retain these customs, prompting one Oxford academic to observe that “some of the governing body are more woke than the student community”. Nevertheless, Isaac has been anxious to make the dinners feel more inclusive. A former chair of Stonewall and the Equality and Human Rights Commission, Isaac attended grammar school in Abergavenny before reading law at Trinity Hall, Cambridge. He vividly remembers being served grapefruit on a plate at a formal dinner and having no idea how to eat it. “Given my own background, I’m committed to ensuring that, as an elite institution, we’re not elitist in the type of students we educate. Our undergraduate body is 86 per cent state school students. I also want our food to be high-quality and to reflect everyone’s tastes.” Hence the introduction of meat-free Mondays and 60 per cent of the food being vegan, vegetarian or suitable for other special diets such as halal. As a Cambridge graduate, I am familiar with the formal hall traditions. I can’t say, however, that the meals I consumed as an undergraduate contributed to my love of gastronomy. “The food was execrable,” recalls former Labour party activist and Worcester graduate Lord Richard Faulkner of his experiences in the ’60s. A common complaint with a few notable exceptions: “In my day, Merton College had the best food, which may have contributed to why the Emperor of Japan went there [in the ’80s],” says former head of MI6, Sir Richard Moore. At Worcester, it seems, the British institutional tradition of serving up slop is through. When I dined there, the menu included leek, pea and watercress soup with poached halibut followed by roast guinea fowl ballotine with artichoke purée, wild mushrooms and Madeira sauce and a white chocolate and raspberry tart. The three-course meal cost students £15 (and £18.60 for their guests). Worcester’s formal hall honours the Benedictine traditions on which the college was founded – “studying, living and eating together and being in dialogue”, says Isaac. At a time when just one in three British families eat together each day, there’s surely value in this. Other formal hall traditions such as “sconcing” (a drinking game where students must down a large tankard of ale for breaking certain rules, such as talking about religion or politics) have long been retired. Latin grace, however, still remains. Robin Geddes, an alumnus of St John’s College, Oxford, from the 2010s considers the custom archaic: “I’m sure my classics tutor would be horrified to hear me say that.” Fergus Murison, a Worcester maths graduate from the 1970s, values it as a way of giving thanks and “acknowledging the lucky position we’re in. [For younger generations] who have less pomp and circumstance in their lives, these rituals have even more significance,” he says. Most importantly, the meal times are designed to prompt conversation and help students interact with more social ease. Prior to coming to Worcester, Ruby Steele, an undergraduate in classics and modern languages, “had never had the experience of sitting next to someone I didn’t know and making small talk before. Nor had I ever sat at a meal with more than one pair of cutlery.” It’s one of the many formalities the provost makes a point of “demystifying” for the fresh intake each year. “You learn how to speak with people who are considerably more senior,” adds Worcester MCR president and current postgraduate Georgia Neilson. “How to ask good questions and listen; how to bring others into conversation. [The specialness of the occasion] prepares you to be open-minded.” You might also get to meet some of the world’s great thinkers and doers. Moore remembers being introduced to English civil servant Oliver Franks, “who was a complete hero – to have access to such interesting people was a thrill”. The lure of the dining halls means visiting guests can be eclectic. “Recently Mick Jagger was at a formal hall at Oriel College,” says Steele. “That was very cool.” “I’m always surprised at how – despite coming from a wide range of backgrounds – our students enjoy Oxford traditions and dressing up for dinner,” Isaac says. “They reject the Waugh image of Brideshead privilege, but perhaps because they grew up on Harry Potter, they wholeheartedly embrace formal hall by making it their own.” Comments

item.title: The joy of messy eating
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 2.84
The joy of messy eating Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. I’m a messy eater. The tablecloth in front of me is always more stained and crumb-laden than anyone else’s. But perhaps I should take pride in my artlessness. Swiss artist Daniel Spoerri turned his messy tablescapes into wall hangings: mounting his empty bottles, dirty plates and soiled tablecloths to the wall. In polite society, messy eating is discouraged. “The peril of pasta is sauce,” says Bocca di Lupo chef-patron Jacob Kenedy, whose upcoming book, Pasta Tricolore, celebrates recipes made with green, white and red sauce. “Tomato sauce is dangerous because it’s red and splotchy and people don’t often wear red,” he says. “Butter and sage or anything greasy have the potential to mark clothes for a long time. Long pasta is especially troublesome as it has the propensity to flick.” Tucking a serviette under one’s chin offers one solution. But that’s hardly chic. At Simpson’s in the Strand, guests are offered a napkin with a buttonhole that attaches to their shirt: an elevated take on the bib inspired by old gentlemen’s clubs. One of my favourite dishes, gaeng gati puu (whole brown crab in coconut milk curry) at Thai restaurant Plaza Khao Gaeng in London, is so sloppy it comes with a pink apron, gloves and a finger bowl. Adopting the personal protective gear is as much part of the experience as cracking the bones and slurping up the broth. Even more embarrassing than stains is food in one’s teeth – especially spinach – which draws unwelcome attention to the mouth. “Orifices are out of bounds,” says Oxford psychology professor Charles Spence on why this might be considered shameful. “Eating with your mouth open is [the epitome of] messy eating.” In the UK, old-school dining etiquette has historically required cutlery for anything but finger food, but modern protocols have evolved. British journalist CE Humphry stated in her 1897 book Manners for Men that only “bread, biscuits, olives, asparagus, celery and bonbons” may be touched with one’s fingers. In 2012, etiquette expert Debrett’s relaxed its guidelines to include pizza, chicken wings and spare ribs. Finger-licking was still deemed bad form. The hyper-aestheticisation of food starting with nouvelle cuisine and culminating in gastroporn on social media has led to a backlash in favour of messiness. “Now messy presentation almost draws attention to the fact that, if it looks unpleasant, it must be tasty,” says Spence. “I went to St John last month and had the Middle White pig with a side of spinach that looked like the student vomit I see outside my house in Oxford. Surely not accidental.” The proliferation of food content has also favoured dishes that ooze, drip and spill, such as burgers, super-sized sandwiches and sloppy joes. “Things in motion capture our attention,” says Spence. In an age of GLP-1s and restraint, there’s something freeing about gnawing on a rib and getting sauce all over one’s face. Or at least watching someone else do that on YouTube. The use of a knife and fork is discouraged with such foods, though there have been exceptions. In 2017, McDonald’s France introduced cutlery for use with its gourmet Signature burgers in a bid to realign itself with more upscale food chains. Eating with one’s hands has various socio-cultural connotations. Consider “macaroni-eaters”, the 17th-century slur used to describe the Neapolitan working class who ate long strands of pasta with their bare hands. The term later became a point of pride. “You can dress a salad so much better with your hands,” says Kenedy. “You also get a deeper connection to your food.” (If you are planning to eat with your hands, make sure you wash them: for the past few weeks a deadly intestinal infection known as cyclosporiasis, spread by contaminated water and food, has been ripping through America.) On a recent trip to Hon’s BBQ in Hackney Wick, formerly a pop-up serving Chinese-Texan barbecue on metal trays that is now a more elevated restaurant, I was unsure given the surroundings whether to tackle the Sichuan peppercorn beef short ribs with cutlery, chopsticks or my hands. The latter turned out to be a hot mess but undeniably more fun. And isn’t that point? “The other day, I had a bunch of guests to dinner including a very lovely two-year-old,” says Kenedy. “She rubbed the food all over her face while everyone at the table watched with delight. I wonder if that came from a desire to get back the freedom we lost as adults.” Do we really all long to smear food on our faces and sling plates in a food fight? If so, it’s worth acknowledging the fact that making a mess is easy – but clearing it up is not. Lead image: Sevilla-Serie No. 6, Nachtisch, Heimberger-Anker-Geschirr, 1991, by Daniel Spoerri © VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn, 2025. Courtesy Galerie LEVY/Dirk Maasbaum Comments

item.title: Chicago: the ultimate insider addresses
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 2.09
Chicago: the ultimate insider addresses Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Chicago When I say Chicago isn’t a celebrity town, that cuts both ways. We have limited tolerance for Instagram culture, we roll our eyes at round-the-block queues and, for most of us, the very notion of $20 trend smoothies triggers an allergic reaction. On the other hand, we can be provincial. At a recent concert at the Jay Pritzker Pavilion in Millennium Park, the Jumbotron cycled through drone footage of American skylines. At the sight of Chicago’s, the crowd exploded. At all others, including a glimmering and handsome New York City? Crickets. Chicagoans have a funny relationship to fame. Seeing a celebrity out and about is not just another Tuesday for us: it’s day-derailing. We’ll ignore the cardinal rule imparted by our peers on the coast and bug the hell out of them, then spend the rest of the day calling our cousins’ cousins. We keep our local celebrities close but feel inordinately stung when they decamp for another city. To better understand this hot-and-cold city, we spoke to eight cultural insiders who know it better than most. Some were forged in Chicago. Others enthusiastically adopted it. And many of them still choose to live here, even when New York and LA beckon. Jump straight to . . . Sandra Cisneros, writer and author of ‘The House on Mango Street’ (born and raised in Chicago; based in San Miguel de Allende, Mexico) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The Aon Center. After going to a concert downtown in Grant Park, we would walk over to what was the Standard Oil Building, now the Aon Center, on East Randolph Street. In the plaza’s sunken garden is the most fabulous treasure: wind sculptures by Harry Bertoia. They look like reeds, and at the dedication ceremony in 1972, the artist climbed inside the installation and “played” them. Bertoia was a furniture designer, too. When his sculptures were displayed at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1975, it was the first and only time I’d seen a sign that said, “Please touch.” I like the idea that he thought about the poetics of these sculptures moving and making these wonderful sounds. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Hot dogs. If you haven’t had a Chicago hot dog, you haven’t had a hot dog. You have to have a bun with little poppy seeds on it, it has to be bundled in waxed paper and the french fries have to be good. Now, there are even vegan hot dogs. Recently, my family and I got some at Portillo’s late at night, and they were really good — I was surprised! One more thing I didn’t realise until two years ago that the flowers in Chicago’s public parks were so much a part of the city. To me, lilacs, peonies and lilies of the valley are the quintessential flowers of Chicago. Jeff Tweedy, musician and lead vocalist/guitarist of Wilco (based in Chicago) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The parks. If you want to soak up what the city and culture are really like, I’d pick any of the Chicago Park District parks, like Independence in Irving Park or Gompers in North Park. Have a picnic and see how Chicagoans really recreate. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand “Dibs”. The concept of saving your parking spot, especially in heavy snow. Technically not legal, but ultimately, pretty fair and moral. If you’re the one who broke your ass shovelling snow, you should get to keep that spot for at least a day or so. What Chicago teaches you When you grow up in a smaller town like I did, there’s a belief that it’s a kinder way to live and that you can’t get that in a city. It’s not true. When I moved to Chicago, I knew more people in my neighbourhood than I did growing up — it’s all about block parties and meeting up with neighbours. Chicago has problems like everywhere else, but it’s a city that facilitates community. Rick Bayless, chef and restaurateur (based in Chicago) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The National Museum of Mexican Art. Rather than establishing the museum downtown, the founders chose Pilsen — a predominantly Latino neighbourhood — and they chose to keep this world-class collection free to all. NMMA is not only one of our city’s best museums but an integral player in this vibrant community. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Storefront theatre. Yes, we have grand old theatres that host Broadway touring companies, and yes, we have the internationally acclaimed Steppenwolf, Goodman and Chicago Shakespeare companies. But Chicago is a city of neighbourhoods, and most of them are home to a host of storefront theatres. One of the best is TimeLine Theatre Company, which does historical pieces that have contemporary relevance. Hungry yet? Forty years ago, when we opened Frontera Grill, farmers’ markets hadn’t taken off in Chicago. Today, with local chefs championing local products, there are over 40 and growing. Now communities are hosting “alternative” farmers’ markets that start at 3pm or 4pm and sell until around 7pm on specific weekdays, rather than weekend mornings. Eve L Ewing, author, scholar and co-owner of Build Coffee & Books in Woodlawn (based in Chicago) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The South Shore Nature Sanctuary and Montrose Point Bird Sanctuary. Our city motto is urbs in horto — city in a garden. Away from all the noise and the hubbub, the marshlands and prairie are also part of our identity. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Community. The city is famously corrupt, but there’s a more generous way to understand the “you scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours” way we do things, which is that Chicagoans look out for each other and take care of one another. If you’re my neighbour’s cousin’s pick-up basketball buddy, you’re in the circle and I’ve got to take care of you. The hill she’ll die on Everyone likes to share their (mostly ill-informed) opinions on Chicago pizza, but through and through we’re a taco city. Our ratio of great tacos per capita is off the charts. I grew up going to El Cid, a Mexican restaurant in Logan Square, while El Milagro in Pilsen both sells tacos and manufactures the best tortillas and chips. Enrique Mazzola, conductor and music director of the Lyric Opera of Chicago (divides time between Chicago and Paris) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The Driehaus Museum. This small museum just off the Magnificent Mile focuses on the art, architecture and design of the American Gilded Age and the Art Nouveau period. Inside is a magnificent auditorium with interesting and diverse programming. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand The walks. One of my favourites goes from downtown along the Lakefront Trail to Lincoln Park. Only a true Chicagoan can understand how beautiful this itinerary is. In general, I love walking around the city — I even walk to work at the Lyric Opera of Chicago and enjoy following the Chicago River every day. Bonus recommendation Wander around the boutique shops and cafés in the North Side neighbourhood of Andersonville. You’re still in Chicago but removed from the tourist areas and high-rises of downtown. Isaiah Collier, saxophonist and composer (divides time between Chicago and New York) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago 63rd Street Beach. The city has its madness, but it also has its tranquillity, usually by the water. Cats will get together here for drum circles — they’ve been doing it for decades. It’s therapeutic and uniquely ethnic. The overview of the city that you see from down there is kind of mythical, very cinematic. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Concerts at Pritzker Pavilion. No matter where you’re from in the city, I think we can all agree there’s something special about being able to witness a proper concert at Pritzker Pavilion. Not amateur stuff, but a full production from start to finish. It’s one hell of a location. A brutal truth We’re the most segregated major city in America. That residual effect has made people feel there are not enough opportunities. It can be disheartening for creatives. Grant Achatz, chef/creative director and co-owner of Chicago’s Alinea restaurant Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago Primitive on Jefferson Street. It’s a massive showroom packed with rare antiquities from all over the world. I’m into medieval and Egyptian history, so for me it’s a rabbit hole I can lose an afternoon in. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand The grit. When I showed up in 2001 with this weird, modernist way of cooking, this city embraced the risk and let me build. People here get that ambition runs quiet, that the winters bond everybody together, that nobody’s impressed with you until you’ve put in the work. You can’t feel any of that from a postcard. You’ve got to live here a while. Tasha, singer-songwriter and poet (born and raised in Chicago, based in New York) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago Promontory Point. We just call it The Point. I don’t think people who aren’t from Chicago really know the secret, stunning beauty it has, especially on the South Side. There is nothing more romantic than jumping from the rocks at sunset on a sticky, hot summer day, the sky pink behind the city skyline, cicadas buzzing. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Being from the city proper. I love the way we bond over that. Not the suburbs. Not the surrounding counties. Definitely not Indiana. A love letter No matter where I end up in the world, Chicago will always be my home, the place I return to, the place that understands me, that holds my whole family and first gave me courage. Chicago forever. What do you love most about Chicago? Tell us in the comments below. And find more of our Chicago guide here Follow us on Instagram at @FTGlobetrotter Cities with the FT FT Globetrotter, our insider guides to some of the world’s greatest cities, offers expert advice on eating and drinking, exercise, art and culture — and much more Find us in Chicago, London, Washington DC, Los Angeles, Tokyo, New York, Paris, Lagos, Rome, Frankfurt, Singapore, Hong Kong, Miami, Toronto, Madrid, Melbourne, Copenhagen, Zürich, Milan, Vancouver, Edinburgh, Venice and Istanbul Comments

item.title: Affordable Alternatives to Japan's Most Crowded Destinations
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 8.00
Japan welcomed more visitors in 2025 than ever before, and most walked the same ten streets. The crowding is real but concentrated: a few temples, villages, and viewpoints absorb most of it, while places offering the same experience sit half empty a valley away. Budget travelers hear a tempting promise: quieter must mean cheaper. Sometimes it does. Sometimes the quiet option adds a shinkansen leg or a rural bus that erases every yen saved on admission. The only way to know is to do the math, so this article does it for four popular swaps using prices checked in August 2026 from official sources. That timing matters: JR East raised fares on March 14, 2026, and Kyoto doubled its accommodation tax two weeks earlier, so numbers from older guides are quietly wrong. The pairings come from the Crowd-Free Japan Index, which matches 40 of Japan's most-visited places with curated quieter alternatives. Kanazawa Instead of Kyoto: The Savings Are on the Ground, Not the Rails Kanazawa is often called "little Kyoto," which annoys both cities, but the comparison holds where it counts. The Higashi Chaya geisha district is a smaller, calmer Gion where the teahouses actually let you in: Ochaya Shima charges ¥500 to walk through a working 1820s interior. In contrast, most Gion teahouses remain entirely closed to casual visitors. Omicho Market delivers the seafood-breakfast experience of Tokyo's Tsukiji Outer Market, with locals still doing their shopping there, and entry to Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens, costs ¥320, compared with ¥500 for Kinkaku-ji or ¥500 for Kiyomizu-dera, each ticketed separately. The biggest savings come from where you sleep. Kyoto's average hotel rate hit a record ¥20,195 per night in 2024. Since March 1, 2026, the city has charged a ¥1,000 per-person-per-night accommodation tax on rooms priced at ¥20,000-49,999, double the previous rate. Kanazawa's tax on the same room is ¥500. | Cost item (August 2026) | Kyoto | Kanazawa | | Shinkansen from Tokyo, one way | ¥14,170 | ¥14,600 | | City bus, single ride | ¥230 | ¥220 | | Transit day pass | ¥1,100 | ¥800 | | Headline garden or temple | ¥500 | ¥320 | | Accommodation tax, per person | ¥1,000 p.p. per night | ¥500 p.p. per night | Note the first row: The train from Tokyo to Kanazawa costs slightly more than the train to Kyoto. The swap pays off in everything after you arrive and compounds with every night you stay. Shima Onsen Instead of Ginzan Onsen: The Clearest Budget Win in Japan Ginzan Onsen's gaslit street has become so popular that the town now meters its own visitors. In winter, day visitors park two kilometers out and ride a shuttle; evening entry requires a paid reservation (¥1,150 in the first season, capped at 100 people per hour), and after 8 pm the street closes to everyone but overnight guests. Those overnight stays start at roughly ¥25,000 per person with meals, and reaching the town from Tokyo costs about ¥13,000 by the Yamagata Shinkansen, plus a ¥1,000 bus that takes cash only. Shima Onsen, tucked in a Gunma river gorge, offers the same Taisho-era wooden-ryokan romance with none of the metering. Sekizenkan's main building dates to 1691, making it Japan's oldest hot-spring inn building, and it is often said to have inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away; its budget rooms start at ¥10,450 per person. The riverside cave bath Kawara-no-yu is open to day visitors from 9:00 to 15:00 without charge. Best of all, a direct highway bus runs from Tokyo Station for ¥3,500 one way and ¥6,300 round trip, about three and a half hours. | Cost item (August 2026) | Ginzan Onsen | Shima Onsen | | Transport from Tokyo, one way | ~¥14,000 (shinkansen + bus) | ¥3,500 (direct bus) | | Night in a heritage ryokan | From ~¥25,000 p.p. with meals | From ¥10,450 p.p. at Sekizenkan | | Soaking without staying | Winter evenings ticketed | Free cave bath, 9:00–15:00 | One honest caveat: the bus runs once daily each way and must be reserved by 4 pm the day before. If you miss it, the rail route via Nakanojo costs more and takes longer. Book the seat, then relax. Ainokura Instead of Shirakawa-go: Let Your Routing Decide Shirakawa-go itself is not the budget problem; walking the village is free, the Wada House costs ¥400, and the viewpoint shuttle costs ¥300. The problem is that everyone arrives on the same reservation-only buses (¥2,800 one way from either Kanazawa or Takayama) and shares the lanes with them. Ainokura, a village of twenty thatched gassho-zukuri farmhouses on a mountainside in neighboring Gokayama, is listed as a World Heritage site with a fraction of the foot traffic. It is also free to enter on foot, and the World Heritage Bus from Takaoka or Shin-Takaoka costs ¥1,100, less than half the Shirakawa-go fare. Whether that saves you money depends entirely on your routing. Traveling the Hokuriku Shinkansen anyway? Step off at Shin-Takaoka and Ainokura is the cheaper, quieter choice. Based in Kanazawa or Takayama with no plans northward? The extra rail leg to Takaoka eats the difference, so the direct ¥2,800 bus to Shirakawa-go wins. The best-value option for seeing both: the ¥4,000 two-day unlimited pass covers Ainokura, Suganuma, and Shirakawa-go on one ticket, and costs less than buying a single round trip separately. Related: Travelers looking beyond Tokyo and Kyoto can find more ideas in Go Backpacking's guide to Japan's Chubu region. Naoshima and Teshima Instead of teamLab: When Quieter Costs More Honesty requires one counterexample, because quiet does not automatically mean cheap. Tokyo's teamLab Planets charges from ¥3,600, with date-based pricing. The contemplative alternatives are Naoshima and Teshima, neighboring art islands in the Seto Inland Sea: the Chichu Art Museum costs ¥2,500-3,000 with timed reservations that cap visitors. The Teshima Art Museum costs ¥1,800-2,000. The direct ferry from Uno Port to Naoshima costs ¥370, while the ferry to Teshima costs ¥780. Per ticket, the islands undercut teamLab. Per trip, they usually don't: Uno Port is a Shinkansen ride and two local connections from Tokyo, and that transport dwarfs the admission savings. The swap only makes financial sense when Setouchi is already on your route, say between Osaka and Hiroshima. If it is, take it without hesitation; if not, this is the case where the crowded option is genuinely the affordable one. The Cheapest Alternative: Don't Leave the City You're In The most expensive way to escape a crowd is to cross half of Honshu. A same-day dash from Tokyo to Kyoto for Fushimi Inari's torii gates costs over ¥28,000 in return shinkansen fares before you have eaten anything. Meanwhile, Nezu Shrine, one of Tokyo's oldest, has its own tunnel of vermilion torii at the Otome Inari sub-shrine, costs nothing to enter, and sits a ¥180 metro ride from central Tokyo. The same logic covers bamboo. Kamakura's Hokoku-ji temple has a grove where you can sit with matcha for ¥400 admission plus ¥600 for the tea. The Great Buddha at Kotoku-in across town charges ¥300, and the train from Tokyo costs ¥1,040. That makes a full bamboo-and-Buddha day out possible for under ¥5,000, compared with visiting Arashiyama's grove at the far end of a ¥28,000 round trip. Even garden-hopping scales down: Kiyosumi Garden charges ¥150 for stone-hopping across carp ponds that Shinjuku Gyoen crowds pay ¥500 for. Altitude works the same way. Shibuya Sky's rooftop charges ¥2,700 online for daytime entry and ¥3,400 for sunset slots, and shares the deck with everyone else who booked the same golden hour. Sunshine 60's Tenbou-Park observatory in Ikebukuro shows a comparable skyline for ¥700 on weekdays, and the free 26th-floor observation lobby of Carrot Tower in Sangenjaya, a few minutes from Shibuya on the Den-en-toshi line, faces Mount Fuji at sunset and charges nothing at all. Four Rules Before You Swap - Price the final leg first. Rural alternatives live or die by the last bus or ferry: its fare and, above all, its schedule. One missed daily departure can force a taxi that costs more than the whole day. - Admission is rarely the problem. Japanese entry fees are modest: ¥150-800 covers most of the attractions in this article. Accommodation and intercity trains decide your budget, so compare hotel rates and lodging taxes before temple tickets. For a broader breakdown of travel costs, read Go Backpacking's guide to backpacking Japan on a budget. - Some crowded icons are free. Fushimi Inari charges nothing; Shirakawa-go's lanes charge nothing. Swapping away from them buys you a better experience, not a cheaper one. Know which reward you're paying for. - Recheck prices from 2026 onward. The March 2026 JR East fare rise and Kyoto's doubled accommodation tax made many older budget guides inaccurate. The official links above reflect August 2026 prices. Quiet and cheap usually travel together in Japan, but not always, and never automatically. Run the numbers for your own route, and you'll often find the lesser-known option costs less and gives more. When it doesn't, at least you'll know before the bus timetable tells you.

item.title: Kilimanjaro Routes Compared: Which Should You Choose?
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.58
Seven official routes lead up Kilimanjaro, and most people narrow their choice to two or three within an hour of reading about them. Machame is the popular one, Lemosho the scenic one, Marangu the one where you sleep in huts instead of tents. Those labels are accurate but don't affect whether you reach the summit. Kilimanjaro is 5,895 m (19,341 ft) high. Its standard trekking routes do not require technical climbing equipment (ropes, an ice axe), but the extreme altitude makes acclimatization essential. The number of days on the mountain matters. Five-day itineraries leave less time for acclimatization, while some operators report summit success rates around 95% on eight-day climbs. These are operator-reported figures, not mountain-wide averages. The takeaway is simple: allow your body more time to adapt before summit night. How the Routes Actually Work Seven official ascent routes exist, but they don't stay separate all the way up. Every climb has three phases, and the route you choose changes each of them differently. The approach (the first four to six days) is where the routes differ. Lemosho starts in quiet rainforest on the western flank. Rongai comes from the dry northern side near the Kenyan border. Machame and Marangu climb from the busy south. For four to six days, you circle toward Kibo, the main volcanic cone, gaining altitude through rainforest, moorland, and alpine desert. This is where you acclimatize, so the number of days here matters most. Summit night. The approaches converge toward Kibo, with most standard itineraries using one of two main summit routes. If you came via Machame, Lemosho, Shira, or Umbwe, you leave Barafu Camp around midnight, climb to Stella Point, then walk the crater rim to Uhuru Peak. Marangu and Rongai climbers leave Kibo Hut, and their route to Gilman's Point takes longer because much of it runs over loose volcanic scree. Either way, you gain about 1,200 meters in the dark. The Western Breach is another summit route, but rockfall and unstable ice make it risky. For that reason, careful operators avoid it. The descent. The park separates uphill and downhill traffic. Routes that summit from Barafu come down the Mweka corridor, a trail used only for going down. Marangu and Rongai climbers walk back down the Marangu trail, sharing it with groups heading up. The Routes, Side by Side | Route | Days | Start from | Sleeping | Traffic | Pick it if | | Machame ("Whiskey") | 7 (or 6) | South | Tents | High | You want the classic climb-high-sleep-low profile and the Barranco Wall, and crowds don't bother you. | | Lemosho | 8 (or 7) | West | Tents | Low early, medium later | It's your first high-altitude climb, and you can spare the extra day. | | Marangu ("Coca-Cola") | 6 (or 5) | Southeast | Wooden huts | High | Sleeping in a tent is not an option for you. | | Rongai | 6 | North | Tents | Low | You want quiet, or you're climbing during the short rains. | | Northern Circuit | 8–9 | West, then north | Tents | Very low | You prioritize extra acclimatization time and a quieter approach. | | Umbwe | 6 | South | Tents | Very low | You're already acclimatized and want a steep, direct route. | | Londorossi (Shira) | 6–8 | West, by vehicle to the plateau | Tents | Very low | You want open views from day one and understand the altitude trade-off. | Route by Route Machame: the "Whiskey Route" (7 days) Machame is the most popular route on the mountain, and the nickname compares it to Marangu, the "Coca-Cola Route." The key differences are that Machame is tougher and steeper, and you sleep in tents. In seven days, you pass through every climate zone Kilimanjaro has, from wet rainforest at 1,800 meters to the frozen crater rim. The third day takes you up to Lava Tower at 4,600 meters and then down to Barranco Camp at 3,900 meters to sleep. That is the "climb high, sleep low" principle built into the route, which is why Machame acclimatizes people so well despite its pace. The next morning you scramble the Barranco Wall, a near-vertical face that needs hands for balance but no rope. The downside is traffic. Machame and Marangu take the lion's share of expeditions, and you will share camps with hundreds of other climbers. The Barranco Wall gives the climb real mountaineering character, and the scenery earns the route its reputation. Still, anyone choosing Machame has to be willing to move in a stream of other groups and share the intermediate camps. The other decision on Machame is between six and seven days. The difference is a single night at Karanga Camp after the Barranco Wall. Drop it, and you go straight from the wall to Barafu and into summit night on the same push, when accumulated fatigue shows up. For example, ALPO runs the Machame Route on the seven-day schedule and keeps that Karanga night for this reason; the company reports 95-97% of its climbers reaching the summit on that version. Its guidance on the six-day option is that the success rate is lower. Lemosho (8 days) Lemosho starts on the remote western flank at Londorossi Gate, about three hours' drive from Moshi. The first two days run through rainforest that the southern routes never touch, and you may not see another group. This is where you are most likely to see colobus monkeys. The route then crosses the Shira Plateau from west to east, one of the highest plateaus on Earth, and on the eight-day version you spend two nights up there, at Shira 1 (3,500 m) and Shira 2 (3,840 m). That slow gain is the whole point. From the plateau, Lemosho joins the Machame trail, so the Lava Tower day, the Barranco Wall, and the summit night are the same. The main decision on Lemosho is whether to do seven or eight days. Dropping to seven means crossing Shira in one long stage and losing a night of adaptation, which helps most. Lemosho also costs more than Machame, partly because of the long drive to a remote trailhead and partly because the extra day adds food and crew wages. For someone whose first real altitude climb is this one, the eight-day Lemosho remains the most balanced option; the gain comes slowly enough that your body has time to catch up. Marangu: the "Coca-Cola Route" (6 days) Marangu is the only route where you sleep in permanent wooden huts instead of tents. The huts are dorm-style, with anywhere from 4 to 20 people per room and shared bathrooms. It is also the historic original route and the one with the gentlest approach gradient, which is how it got its reputation as the easy one. That reputation can be misleading: a gentler trail does not remove altitude challenges. If you prefer hut accommodation, compare daily sleeping altitudes and acclimatization opportunities carefully, and favor the six-day itinerary over the five-day version. Summit night climbs from Kibo Hut toward Gilman's Point, and the route uses the same trail for ascent and descent, so you meet descending groups on your way up. The sensible rule is to choose Marangu in exactly one case, when a tent is physically or psychologically not an option for you, and then to take six days, never five. Rongai (6 days) Rongai approaches from the north, close to the Kenyan border, after a long drive to the trailhead. The northern flank is drier, making Rongai the sensible pick if climbing during the short rains in November. It is also the quietest standard route, with a real chance of larger wildlife on the lower section. The early terrain is less dramatic than on the western routes, and summit night from Kibo Hut is long and monotonous. It is probably the most undervalued route on the mountain: introverted, wild, and worth the trade for silence. Editor's note: For a firsthand perspective, read this account of climbing Kilimanjaro via the Rongai Route, from life at camp to the midnight summit push. Northern Circuit (8-9 days) The Northern Circuit is one of the longest itinerary options, giving you more time to acclimatize. As a result, it has one of the higher summit rates. It starts on the western side, like Lemosho, then swings around the northern face of Kibo on a nearly empty traverse before rejoining the main trails for the summit push. The extra days provide more time to adapt, although individual responses to altitude vary. It is generally among the more expensive options because you are paying for a longer expedition, and it requires solid multi-day trekking endurance. If reliably reaching Uhuru Peak is the goal and time is not the constraint, this is the route. Umbwe and Londorossi (Shira) Umbwe is the steepest line on the mountain and the most direct, climbing a narrow forest ridge that almost no one else uses. Its rapid ascent leaves little time to acclimatize, making it a better option for trekkers who are already acclimatized. Previous altitude experience alone is not a substitute. Londorossi, sometimes called the Shira Route, approaches from the west but begins with a vehicle transfer straight onto the Shira Plateau at 3,400 meters. The views open from day one. You give up the gradual gain that every other route builds in, which is worth considering before you book. What To Weigh Before You Book Days on the mountain. When comparing itineraries, prioritize acclimatization time. Look beyond total trip length to daily sleeping altitudes and acclimatization opportunities. Extra time helps, but fitness and previous altitude experience do not guarantee protection from altitude illness. Follow your guide's safety advice and be prepared to turn around. That is not a guidebook opinion. Yevgen Staroselskiy, co-founder of ALPO Guided Expeditions, is a Master of Sport in Mountaineering and holder of the "Snow Leopard" title (#376), with more than 130 major climbs behind him, including Everest (8,848 m, 29,029 ft) and K2 (8,611 m, 28,251 ft), and 25+ groups guided to the top of Kilimanjaro. His view of the time question is blunt: I've climbed Everest and K2, and I can tell you that no route on Kilimanjaro needs that kind of preparation. What it does need is that you take the altitude seriously. Give your body the days, walk slowly, and almost any physically active person will reach Uhuru Peak. Where I see people fail is when they try to save a day. - Yevgen Staroselskiy, Master of Sport in Mountaineering, co-founder of ALPO Guided Expeditions Everything else on this list is secondary to that number. Tent or hut. A binary question, and it settles Marangu yes-or-no before anything else. Crowds. Machame and Marangu are busy. Rongai and the Northern Circuit are not. Lemosho is quiet for two days and then joins the Machame stream. Summit night profile. From Barafu, the climb to Stella Point is steeper, but you are mostly on firm ground. From Kibo Hut, you spend more hours on scree before you reach Gilman's Point. Season. Compare expected rainfall and trail conditions for your travel dates with your operator. Wetter periods mean muddy trails and reduced visibility; the northern approach is generally drier. Conditions vary, so avoid treating any seasonal window as a guarantee of dry weather. The dry windows are June to early October and mid-December to early April. During the short rains in November, the northern side stays drier, which is a point in Rongai's favor. In April and May, the trails wash out, and clouds hide the views, so no route is worth doing then. A Quick Decision Guide - First high-altitude climb and you can spare eight days: Lemosho. - Seven days, and sharing camp with other groups does not bother you: Machame, on the seven-day schedule rather than six. - You will not sleep in a tent: Marangu, six days, no shorter. - Climbing in November, or you want the mountain mostly to yourself: Rongai. - More time for acclimatization and a quieter approach: Northern Circuit. Whichever route you choose, prioritize an itinerary that allows time to acclimatize rather than booking the shortest option. This article was published in partnership with ALPO Guided Expeditions.

item.title: When Renting a Car in San Diego Makes Sense
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.54
San Diego is often described as easygoing, but the geography tells a practical story. The city is spread out, beaches are miles from business districts, and many useful stops are not connected by a single transit line. That is why mobility matters here. For visitors planning a short break, family holiday, or work trip with meetings across town, reliable transport can make the difference between a smooth day and a frustrating one. That is also where car hire for your stay in San Diego becomes relevant in a very practical sense. A rented vehicle is not only about convenience; it's often the most straightforward way to travel between hotels, the airport, coastal neighborhoods, and inland districts without having to build the itinerary around timetables. When a downtown lunch meeting is followed by a client visit in La Jolla, having flexible transportation can make the day much easier. However, a rental car is not necessary for every itinerary. Visitors staying downtown, in Little Italy, or near a trolley route may find public transit and occasional rideshares easier and less expensive once parking costs are considered. A car makes the strongest case when the itinerary includes several widely separated neighborhoods, substantial luggage, or destinations outside the best-connected areas. San Diego's rhythm rewards people who adapt. Morning fog may give way to warm afternoons. Traffic can change quickly near the waterfront, and weekend crowds shift flow around popular destinations. A transport choice that allows for these changes usually saves time and lessens stress, which matters when a trip has a tight schedule. What Travelers Actually Need on the Road Most trips do not fail because of the destination but because of small gaps in planning. Is there enough time between check-in and the first appointment? Will a late dinner in another neighborhood cause a long wait for a ride? These questions seem minor until they arise at the wrong moment. A vehicle lets travelers control the day rather than react to it. For leisure travelers, that control often means more than one beach stop. A morning near Mission Beach can turn into an afternoon in Balboa Park, and end with dinner in Little Italy, without worrying about carrying bags from one mode of transport to another. For business travelers, it means less time spent coordinating pickups and more time spent preparing for a presentation, which is often the real priority. San Diego also works well for people who mix city time with short escapes. A rental car makes it easier to move beyond central districts and explore places that are otherwise harder to reach efficiently. Even a day trip becomes more realistic when departure times fit the traveler's schedule instead of the other way around. Choosing and Using a Rental Car Thoughtfully Mobility today is no longer only about speed. It is also about how a trip aligns with broader environmental expectations. Electric vehicles, efficient engines, and shared-use models have changed the conversation. Travelers are increasingly aware that how they move matters, especially in regions where road travel is a part of everyday life. In a place like Southern California, that discussion feels especially relevant. Long distances are common, yet so is interest in lower-impact transport. Electric cars, where charging is practical, can reduce local emissions and fit neatly into urban travel patterns. Car sharing also has a role, particularly for residents who need occasional access rather than full-time ownership. The point is not to eliminate driving. It is to make every trip more considered. For visitors, sustainable mobility often starts with simple decisions. Travelers who need a car can limit unnecessary driving by grouping nearby stops, avoiding backtracking, and choosing an appropriately sized or electric vehicle when the route and available charging make that practical. Weekend Routes That Reward a Car Some destinations are easier to enjoy when the schedule is your own. San Diego is full of routes that fit that idea. A drive along the coast gives travelers a sense of the region's scale. Inland neighborhoods show a different side of the city, shaped by local life rather than beachfront traffic. The result is a trip that feels broader and more complete. For a short stay, one sensible approach is to separate the city into clusters. One day can focus on the harbor and downtown, another on the coastal north. A third can be left open for a relaxed outing, perhaps with a stop in a quieter district or a scenic drive without a strict timetable. This structure leaves space for spontaneity, which travelers often remember most. Business travelers can use the same logic. Meetings rarely happen in one place, and even a well-organized agenda may face unexpected changes. A vehicle can turn a complicated day into a manageable one, especially when appointments are spread across the metropolitan area. Time is often the most costly part of a work trip. What Makes a Good Rental Experience People often think of car rental as a simple transaction, but the experience improves when important details are clear from the start. Vehicle size matters in a city where parking varies by district. So does fuel choice, particularly for visitors weighing cost, range, and environmental impact. The best option usually suits the trip, not the other way around. There is value in understanding the local driving environment before setting off. San Diego is generally straightforward, yet it has its own patterns. Morning and evening congestion can build near major corridors, and popular weekend spots may require patience. A calm approach helps. So does checking where parking is available before switching from one stop to the next. For families, comfort matters as much as efficiency. Luggage space, child seats, and room for beach gear can become deciding factors. For solo travelers, compact size may be more useful, especially if the route includes several urban stops. The right choice is not always the biggest or newest but the one that fits the plan without extra work. San Diego as a Model for Practical Travel Travel has become more thoughtful in recent years. People want fewer complications, better use of time, and transport options that correspond with how they live. San Diego reflects that shift well. The city combines leisure, commerce, and everyday movement in a way that makes flexible mobility relevant. A car is not essential for every visitor, but it remains one of the most dependable tools for those who want to see more, manage schedules with less friction, and move between parts of the region at their own pace. That balance between freedom and efficiency is what makes road travel so enduring. It answers a simple question: how do you keep a trip practical without making it feel rigid? In San Diego, the best answer frequently depends on the traveler's goals. A beach weekend, a corporate visit, and a longer holiday may all require a different approach, yet they share the same need for mobility that works quietly in the background. When transportation is well chosen, the city feels more open, and the trip starts to follow its own logic. This article was published in partnership with Europcar.

item.title: How To Turn Frequent Flyer Miles Into a Once-In-A-Lifetime Adventure Trip
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.20
Frequent flyer miles sit unused in millions of loyalty accounts, often because a short weekend trip doesn't feel like enough of a reason to cash them in. Their real value often shows up on itineraries a traveler might otherwise never book, such as long-haul flights in a premium cabin, remote destinations with expensive one-way fares, or multi-country routings that would run into thousands of dollars in cash. Building one big trip from a mile balance usually means treating those miles differently than a smaller redemption. The goal shifts from covering a single flight to opening an itinerary that would otherwise be out of reach financially or logistically. That change affects which loyalty programs are worth prioritizing, when to book, and how far a traveler might be willing to fly out of the way to make the miles stretch. Figure Out What Your Miles Are Actually Worth A mile is not worth a fixed amount, and treating every redemption the same way is the quickest way to waste a balance that could have covered something bigger. Airlines price awards either from a fixed chart or through dynamic pricing that changes by route and season. So the same 60,000 miles might cover a short domestic hop for barely more value than paying cash, or a long-haul business-class seat worth several thousand dollars. The redemptions that tend to deliver the most value share a few traits: - A long-haul flight where the cash fare is already high, especially in a premium cabin. - A route with minimal competition, where few airlines fly, and fares stay high year-round. - Peak season travel dates, when cash prices spike well above their usual range. Working backward from the trip that would strain the budget, rather than forward from the miles in an account, tends to point to a better use of the balance. Aim for the Destinations That Are Hardest To Reach on Points Some destinations are worth targeting with miles because a cash ticket would be brutal, not because the redemption looks exceptional on paper. Patagonia fits that description, since most routings connect through Santiago before a further flight south to Punta Arenas, and cash fares on that leg rarely drop much even in shoulder season. LATAM operates most flights into southern Chile, and although the airline no longer belongs to any of the three global alliances, its partnership with Delta means SkyMiles can sometimes cover part of that routing where a standard alliance search comes up empty. From Punta Arenas, it's a manageable drive to Puerto Natales and the entrance to the national park, where W trekking has become the standard way to see the granite towers, glacier faces, and turquoise lakes without hiring a private guide for every leg. The Patagonia Torres del Paine hike is the route most visitors spend months planning for, since campsite and refugio reservations fill up well before the flights do. Concentrate Your Miles Instead of Scattering Them Spreading airline miles across five or six programs might feel like hedging, but 8,000 miles here and 12,000 there rarely add up to more than a short economy flight. Meaningful redemptions usually start well above 50,000 miles one way. Picking a primary airline, or an alliance that covers regions likely to matter for future trips, means earning from flights and card spending stacks toward one balance instead of several that never clear the threshold for a premium seat. Flexible credit card rewards add another layer to travel hacking because several programs allow points to transfer to multiple airline partners rather than locking a traveler into one carrier's network. That flexibility can help close the gap when an airline-mile balance falls short or when another program offers better award availability. Airline miles generally cannot be transferred between unrelated loyalty programs, so travelers should distinguish them from flexible credit card points. Since credit card transfers are usually one-way, confirm award availability directly with the airline before moving any points.
