item.title: “Bison Belong on This Landscape.” Judge Blocks Federal Order to Remove 1,000 Animals in Montana
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.53
Bison grazing on American Prairie (Photo: Courtesy American Prairie) Nearly 1,000 bison that faced removal from federal land in Montana will be able to continue grazing for now after a judge blocked a Bureau of Land Management (BLM) order seeking to kick the animals out. The lawsuit stems from a BLM order this May that sought to remove the bison from public portions of American Prairie. The nonprofit preserve covers more than 600,000 acres of private land and public grazing leases on Montana’s shortgrass prairie, all of it open to the public, and features camping, wildlife-watching, and hiking. The BLM granted the permits for the animals to graze in 2005. Its new order is rooted in a reinterpretation of the Taylor Grazing Act, which allows the department to issue livestock permits for public grazing. The rewrite seeks to reclassify livestock as “production-oriented.” U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris objected. “No statutory language or judicial precedent exists that requires a livestock operation to focus exclusively on production and entirely ignore conservation, range improvement, preservation, or other values,” he stated in the decision. “Congress recognized livestock grazing and livestock management often includes and considers preservation, improvement, and thoughtful development, hand-in-hand with other uses.” The bison will now remain on American Prairie’s leases while the lawsuit proceeds. The decision will delay the BLM’s original removal order, scheduled for September 30. If that order had taken effect, the preserve would have needed to either cull or remove hundreds of bison from the land, as Beth Saboe, American Prairie’s director of public relations, told Backpacker in May 2026 shortly after the BLM announced the changes. “Worst-case scenario, we potentially would have to get rid of hundreds of animals. We don’t want to see that happen,” Saboe said at the time, adding that the organization planned to appeal any adverse final decision. Besides incurring major costs to American Prairie, Saboe said removing the bison from the public range would have stripped a restorative species of its native habitat. The uncertainty around the herd also led American Prairie to cancel its public bison harvest for 2026. While the permit revocation had support from the Montana Stockgrowers Association and many local ranchers, American Prairie’s tribal partners pushed back. In a January 2026 letter to the Secretary of the Interior, J. Garret Renville, chairman of the Coalition of Large Tribes and Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation, wrote that American Prairie had provided animals to and worked with a number of tribes attempting to grow their own herds, and that the organization’s methods of raising bison were “largely indistinguishable from the practices and techniques employed by tribal herd managers.” In his ruling, Morris wrote that he “struggle[d] to see” how the BLM’s choice to impose the new regulation while ignoring American Prairie’s evidence could be consistent with the law. With its redefinition, the BLM sought to limit grazing to animals “used as part of an operation to provide output for various purposes, such as meat, milk, fiber, or other products and any animals when they are being used to assist with management of other animals in connection with such operations (e.g. horses that are used to assist with cattle management).” The BLM itself concluded in 2022 that bison grazing would improve rangeland productivity and riparian health on the same lands it now seeks to remove the animals from. If American Prairie ultimately loses the right to graze bison on its leases, it could choose to replace them with cattle. There’s evidence that could compromise the land: Cattle herds often heavily graze one small area before moving on. Bison, on the other hand, tend to graze more gradually while constantly moving over the landscape, covering up to 2-3 miles per day. Studies have shown this can increase biodiversity and even drought tolerance on native grasslands. “These are the ungulates that evolved with the prairie landscape,” Saboe said in May. “They’re one of the main keystone species here, and that’s because of how their presence on the landscape improves the rangeland.” The court’s preliminary injunction covers the three federal allotments where American Prairie bison are currently grazing. It did not grant the organization’s request to protect three other tracts where bison do not already graze. “Bison belong on this landscape, and today’s ruling gives them a chance to stay,” said Alison Fox, CEO of American Prairie. “For more than 20 years, our bison have grazed these lands under federal authorization and without grazing violations. The court recognized the concrete harm that removing them would cause, not just to our work, but to our Tribal partners and the broader effort to return bison to their native home.”

item.title: Discover Fall at Its Best in West Virginia’s State Parks
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.02
Fall colors in West Virginia. (Photo: West Virginia Department of Tourism) As autumn sweeps through the gorges, mountains, and valleys of West Virginia, the state’s “Almost Heaven” slogan seems like an understatement. Suddenly, there’s very little “almost” about it. With a kaleidoscope of foliage marching over the rolling hills and complementing the deep greens of the pines, fall in the Mountain State is something to behold. Here’s where—and how—to see the show across West Virginia’s State Parks. With more than 40 waterfalls on the West Virginia Waterfall Trail, visiting one (or several) is a great way to experience the serenity of the season. Each one offers something different, along with the best kinds of similarities—cascading water, stunning foliage, and the feeling of full immersion in nature. See them all, check in, and earn prizes with the West Virginia Waterfall Trail. There’s no better way to end an autumn day than by returning to a forest cabin. And in West Virginia, you hardly even need to leave the trail to find your home away from home—more than 20 state parks have cabin rentals available. One of the best places to lay your head come fall is the scenic Blackwater Falls State Park. There, a day of hiking, biking, or fishing can end at one of 39 fully furnished cabins. Or, for a completely unique cabin experience, head to Coopers Rock State Forest, where you’ll find five stargazing cabins equipped with skylights and floor-to-ceiling windows that let you take in the night sky while enjoying the comforts of home. One of the best ways to experience West Virginia’s colorful fall forests? From above. There are several places to enjoy sweeping mountain views across the state, including the scenic chairlift ride at Canaan Valley Resort State Park and the Aerial Tram at Pipestem Resort State Park. At Pipestem, you even have the unique opportunity to travel over the rim of the Bluestone Gorge and down to the Bluestone River, enjoying the view as you sink into the scenery. As you explore the Mountain State, keep your eyes peeled for West Virginia’s iconic Almost Heaven swings. With more than 50 spread across some of the most scenic state parks, towns, and points of interest in the state, you’re bound to find a spot to pull over, stretch your legs, and commemorate a fall trip done right.

item.title: Paddle, Bike, Run at These Adventurous Multisport Events
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.75
You don't have to swim to compete in a multisport event. These athletes competing in (clockwise from top left) Ski to Sea, Gut Check Cape Cod, The Great American Triathlon, and The Big Hurt get to paddle their way through the water on race day. (Photo: Clockwise from top left: Whatcom Events, Jittipong Rakritikul, Capital Road Race Management, Matt Sagen | Cascadia Films) For most new triathletes, the open-water swim is the most intimidating discipline. If you’re not ready to take the plunge, you can still experience multisport adventures. At most of these unconventional triathlons, the swim leg is replaced by a kayak, canoe, or stand-up paddleboard leg. Ranging from New Jersey to California, these fun adventure races give you a taste of the multisport experience without getting your feet (too) wet. September Nebo, North Carolina North Carolina is home to a number of adventure races, but the Pisgah 12-Hour Adventure Race is truly unique. Unlike a traditional triathlon, athletes will embark on an orienteering adventure with the goal to gather as many punches as possible from checkpoints on the course within the allotted time. The team with the most points in the least amount of time wins. It’s based around Lake James State Park at the edge of Linville Gorge in Nebo, North Carolina, and 2026 will be the seventh time the race has been held in this location. Expect bushwacking, mountain biking on single track, and scenic paddling. You can race solo, but it’s more fun with friends, so create a team of 2-4 people. You’ll need to know how to read a map, use a compass, and even though you paddle, you’ll still get wet, so dress accordingly. Race with a head lamp in the dark and carry fluid and snacks for the duration. It’s the most fun you can have in the woods with a hundred of your newest friends. September Brewster, Massachusetts Gut Check Cape Cod isn’t your typical triathlon. While it definitely falls into the “adventure race” category, this event is more of a point-to-point, outdoor quest. What’s unique is that each year, the course is different, so nobody knows exactly what they’re in for until minutes before the race start. Gut Check began in 2019 and takes place in the 2,000-acre Nickerson State Park. Described as a “unique journey across land and water,” the race includes 1,000 vertical feet of trail running, 1,000 vertical feet of road cycling, and water crossings that can be completed by swimming or paddling. The number of checkpoints is kept a secret until race morning, but there’s an anticipated finish time of 1.5 to 3 hours. There will be no more than four swim segments, and each is a half mile or less. If you choose to paddle, those segments may be a bit longer. How do you prepare for a race like this? Organizers suggest being able to run 4-6 miles on trails, ride 5-10 miles, swim a total of 1,500 yards, and paddle up to 1.5 miles total. This race involves orienteering by map, and you must reach several checkpoints along the way. The objective is to use “your wits and fitness to scramble your way to the last cliff climb.” You can race solo or in a 2-4-person team. In 2025, the race sold out, so don’t wait to sign up for this one. September Lenox, Massachusetts The Great Josh Billings Runaground has a long and storied history (almost 50 years!) in the Berkshires of Western Massachusetts. The race consists of a 27-mile bike ride, 5-mile paddle, and 6.4-mile run. If you think you’re up for the challenge, the first step is to assemble a team. The Tin category consists of two athletes who divide the three legs between themselves. For example, one athlete rides the bike, both paddle, and the second athlete runs. The Iron category is for a single athlete who wants to complete all three legs of the race. The cycling leg marks the start of the event in Great Barrington. Athletes will ride 27 miles through five different towns on the way to Stockbridge Bowl. Expect scenic country roads and rolling hills on this route with five climbs and 1,750 feet of elevation gain. After the ride, the cyclist will hand off a wristband to the next teammate waiting at the lake. That athlete will use a canoe, kayak, or SUP to paddle 5 miles around the lake finishing at Camp Mah-Kee-Nac. After the paddling leg, that athlete must hand the wristband to a runner waiting on the beach. The final leg of the race is a 6.4-mile run around the lake to the finish line at the Tanglewood Main Gate. So, who is Josh Billings? It’s actually the pen name of Henry Wheeler Shaw, a writer and noted humorist from the 19th century. Known as a “cracker-barrel philosopher,” he penned a number of sayings, such as “to finish is to win,” which is the motto of The Great Josh Billings Runaground. This bike-canoe-run triathlon is one of the oldest and largest in the country. It’s fun-loving, eccentric, and a bit wacky, much like its namesake. After the race, stick around for “The Bash” to enjoy live music, a beer tent, massages, food, photo booth, and a kids race. September Bay City, Michigan If you had any doubts about whether or not this race involves swimming, the Bay City Morning Rotary put it right in the title for you. This is a “Driathlon,” which means you won’t get wet (unless you fall out of your kayak). This year marks the 16th annual Driathlon in Bay City, Michigan. Described as a “triathlon with a twist,” the event includes a paddle, bike, and run. It’s a fundraiser for the Bay City Morning Rotary and allows the organization to distribute funds to local charities. Groups of two can compete in either a relay format, in a team format where each athlete does all three events, or you can choose the individual kayak division. Athletes begin the race with a 5K paddle in a kayak or canoe on the Kawkawlin River. The second leg is a 20K, three-loop route on Bangor Township roads. The final leg is a 5K run along the river. The transition area is located at Castaways Bay City where there will be pre-race coffee, donuts, and bagels available. Post-race, you can look forward to ShineWater, water, and fruit, as well as the musical stylings of the race DJ. September Port Angeles, Washington This four-leg adventure race takes athletes from the foothills of the Olympic Mountains to the shores of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Home base is Pebble Beach Park in downtown Port Angeles. Athletes begin their adventure with a 16-mile mountain bike on the Foothills Trail System. Then, they will transfer to a kayak to paddle 2.6 miles in Port Angeles Harbor. Next, hop on the road bike for 30 miles on rural roads in Clallam County. The final leg is a 10K run on the Waterfront Trail. This race can be done solo or in a relay consisting of 2-4 people. With a central transition area, beer garden, and music, this is a very spectator-friendly event. Stick around the next day for The Little Hurt, a youth race for kids pre-K to eighth grade. September Point Pleasant, New Jersey The DQ Treasure Island Sprint Triathlon has something for everyone: a triathlon, duathlon, aquabike, relay, and kayak triathlon. The kayak triathlon consists of a 1.5K paddle, 10.5-mile bike ride, and 3-mile run. Athletes will paddle into the Manasquan River and around Osborn Island before finishing at Maxson Avenue Beach. Then, there’s a four-lap bike ride, followed by an out-and-back run. Because this is part of the DQ Grand Prix and Club Challenge, points accumulate throughout the series. Cash prizes are awarded to overall winners, and awards are presented to age group, Clydesdale/Athena, adaptive category, relay divisions, and more. May Whatcom County, Washington Round up 2-7 of your most adventurous friends to compete in the original team relay race at Ski To Sea. This popular event takes athletes across snow, land, and sea from Mount Baker to Bellingham Bay. It started in 1973 and is held annually on Memorial Day weekend in Whatcom County, Washington. The format involves teams of 3-8 athletes competing in seven different sports to cover a total of 91 miles. In order of event, athletes will complete a cross-country ski (5K), downhill ski/snowboard (4K), run (8 miles), road bike (41 miles), canoe (18.5 miles), cyclocross bike (11 miles), and sea kayak (5 miles). The course takes athletes through Glacier, Maple Falls, Kendall, Everson, Lynden, Ferndale, and finishes in the historic Fairhaven district of Bellingham. Once the final athlete reaches the finish at Marine Park, they will hop out of their kayak, run up the hill, and ring the finisher’s bell. The afterparty includes an awards ceremony, Kulshan Brewing Beer Garden, and food from several local vendors. July Sacramento, California The Great American Triathlon showcases the beauty of the American River Parkway in California’s state capital with a run/bike/paddle. The unique format begins with a 5.8-mile run, followed by a 12.5-mile bike ride, and a 6.1-mile paddle. The entire route travels along the American River Parkway. The run begins at William B. Pond Park in Carmichael and heads downriver to Cal State University, Sacramento. The bike goes from Sacramento to the Sunrise Bridge in Fair Oaks. The paddle leg is a scenic route from the bridge to River Bend Park in Rancho Cordova. You have the option to compete as an individual or part of a team. Space is limited to 250 teams and 600 individual racers. This event raises money to preserve the American River Parkway and benefits local children’s charities.

item.title: Buried in 2 Feet of Snow With No Overnight Gear, a Hike in the Enchantments Just Turned Deadly
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.47
Two people in the Enchantments at the summit of Asgard Pass in the Cascade Mountains (Photo: Tegra Stone Nuess/Getty Images) An Oklahoma woman died of hypothermia while attempting a thru-hike of the Enchantments, a renowned high-alpine region in Washington state’s Cascade Mountain Range. Sybil Claborn, 45, was hiking with her husband on September 13 when an early-season snowstorm struck the trail, according to the Chelan County Sheriff’s Office (CCSO). Several feet of snow buried the couple, both of whom suffered severe hypothermia. Claborn succumbed to the cold. “The area the couple was at is approximately 7,000 to 8,000 feet in elevation, with either trailhead approximately eight to ten miles away,” CCSO Chief Ryan Moody said in a statement sent to Outside. “Storms had persisted throughout the day, producing significant snowfall in the area. The male reported that both individuals’ clothing was soaked and that they did not have overnight gear.” Authorities have not released the man’s name, age, or condition. The Enchantments is a coveted alpine hiking area known for mountain goats, turquoise lakes, and jagged peaks. The Washington Trail Association (WTA) categorizes the 18-mile one-way hike as being “hard,” with 4,500 feet of elevation gain and a high point of 7,800 feet. The couple was in the so-called “core zone” of the Enchantments, which is a high plateau filled with lakes, authorities say. A high-alpine basin forms the centerpiece of the Enchantments traverse. Camping along the Enchantments traverse is only allowed by securing a competitive permit. Some hikers will attempt the entire trek in a day to avoid one, but weather conditions can turn violent quickly, especially at high elevations, putting unprepared mountaineers at an extreme risk of rapid hypothermia. Although large amounts of snow don’t typically accumulate until November, variable weather is common through these alpine peaks. “Those undertaking the Enchantments thru-traverse in September should be aware of variable conditions brought by the onset of autumn in the alpine,” WTA writes on its website. “Conditions can vary greatly this time of year—it is not uncommon for 30-plus degree temperature swings to occur in a single day.” September 13, 5:30 P.M. The husband placed the initial SOS call, reporting his wife was unable to move. 5:50 P.M. A second call confirmed the couple was buried in one to two feet of snow under an emergency blanket. Air rescue was grounded due to severe weather. 8:00 to 10:50 P.M. Army helicopter pilots make multiple attempts from Yakima, Washington, to reach the couple but fail due to storm conditions. September 14, 3:30 A.M. Ground rescuers from Chelan County Mountain Rescue reach the site on foot, finding Claborn deceased and her husband suffering from severe hypothermia. 9:00 A.M. Air evacuation clears, transporting the surviving hiker to Cascade Medical Center in Leavenworth. CCSO provided Outside with a detailed timeline of the rescue. Just before 5:30 P.M. on September 13, authorities say they received an initial emergency call from a man who reported his wife was unable to move, and that he couldn’t carry her out on the trail. Twenty minutes later, the man called again to say the woman was under an emergency blanket and the couple was buried between one and two feet of snow. Weather conditions were quickly deteriorating, and responders determined that it wasn’t safe to fly a helicopter in to evacuate the couple. “At that point, the only other option was to get a ground team in as quickly as possible to try to warm her up,” Moody said. “A ground rescue team was requested from Chelan County Mountain Rescue (CCMR). They provide the quickest ground response possible.” CCSO requested a hoist-capable helicopter before 7 P.M. if weather conditions improved. An hour later, an Army helicopter launched from Yakima, Washington, located about 100 miles away. Weather again prevented responders from reaching the pair. Throughout the evening, CCSO said that the man continued to communicate about his wife’s condition and the possibility that she may die. The Army again tried to fly a helicopter into the area at 10:50 P.M., but the weather was still too dangerous. At 3:30 A.M. on September 14, two CCMR personnel reached the couple on foot. At this point, the woman had died, and the man was suffering from severe hypothermia. Responders warmed the man in a tent rescuers brought, the Sheriff’s office said. Later that morning, a helicopter arrived to transport the man and two CCMR rescuers. They landed at the Leavenworth Fish Hatchery, about ten miles from the trailhead, around 9:00 A.M. Officials transported the man by ambulance to Cascade Medical Center in Leavenworth for treatment. By 10 A.M., the sheriff’s office sent in a recovery flight to recover the deceased woman. She was transported to the Chelan County Coroner’s office Additional information regarding the cause and manner of her death is under investigation, authorities say.

item.title: 5 Workouts to Build Serious Uphill Hiking Strength
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.69
(Photo: Peter Amend/Getty) The first time I ever went backpacking abroad, I was so unprepared for the climbs that I couldn’t complete my planned itinerary. The route in question should have been a dream loop through the Italian Dolomites. But instead of frolicking through alpine passes, I found myself two days in, on the verge of tears, staring down yet another 6,000-foot climb. The sun was about to set, and my quads were Jell-O. I couldn’t do it. I booked a room in an inn I couldn’t afford, climbed the pass the next morning, and then took a bus to my endpoint. While there’s no shame in calling a trip early, it’s a bummer to miss out on miles of beauty just because your hiking fitness isn’t where you thought it was. And while it’s relatively easy to train for a route if you have similar terrain close to home, it can be tough to prep for truly enormous climbs—like the kind you’ll find in the Colorado Rockies, the Italian Dolomites, or the French Alps. “It’s especially hard to train in America for stuff like the Alps or the Dolomites because those mountains are so steep,” explains Alexa Hasman, a mountain athlete, personal trainer, and founder of Rise Ultra Coaching. The trick, she says, is to combine endurance training with hill repeats and gym time to build serious muscular power. Here are a few of her favorite hill workouts. Your first order of business is to build a strong endurance base. For this, Hasman recommends finding the longest hill you can (or setting your treadmill to its maximum incline) and climbing at a consistent pace for one to two hours. Ideally, you’ll carry a little weight: Hasman suggests starting with ten percent of your bodyweight and hiking for 60 minutes. Add 15 minutes each week. You can also play with weight, adding about five pounds per week until you’re at 20 percent of your bodyweight. Hasman cautions against carrying any more than that. Upwards of 20 percent, the likelihood of injury outweighs the diminishing strength gains. (Also avoid increasing weight and distance in the same week—up one or the other, but not both.) Throughout, stick to a pace that’s engaged but sustainable. “You should be conversational,” Hasman says. “If you can say three sentences at a time without gasping for breath, that’s where I want you.” A single long hike is great, but it doesn’t quite simulate the back-to-back days of serious vert that you’ll encounter on a backpacking trip. To prepare, Hasman recommends doing two endurance workouts per week on consecutive days. “Cumulative fatigue is really important there,” Hasman says. “It teaches your body to work on tired legs. You might feel stiff, sore, or heavy the next day, but that’s normal. This is just as much about mental training as it is physical.” Once you have a strong endurance base—i.e., you can reliably hike uphill for 90 to 120 minutes while carrying 15 to 20 percent of your bodyweight—it’s time to start building speed and power. Find a steep hill and charge up it at close to your max effort for ten seconds. Walk slowly down to the base of the hill, then do it again. Your goal is four total reps. Over time, build up to reps of 30 seconds, then 60 seconds, then two minutes, then three minutes. If you live near a hill that’s long enough for a three-minute interval, great. If not, do this on a treadmill at its maximum incline setting. “If you’re an uphill athlete, then you’re also by nature a downhill athlete,” Hasman says. And if you’ve ever done a long descent with weight on your back, you’re probably aware that downhills are the real quad-killers. To avoid jellified quads during your trip, Hasman recommends training downhills specifically. One way to do this is to reverse the above workout. Walk slowly up a hill, then charge down it as fast as you can go without being reckless. Do this for four reps. You can also combine these two workouts: Book it up the hill, then book it down, and take your rest at the bottom. Welcome to the least-fun workout on this list—but perhaps the most effective. “Wall sits are my secret sauce for downhill,” Hasman says. They’re great because they hold you in an exaggerated, active downhill-hiking position for an extended period. “I start my athletes with one-minute wall sits a couple of times a week. After a few weeks, we go until failure. Then we add weight.” Once you can sit with a ten-pound plate on your lap for a minute or two, you’re ready for boss level: single-leg wall sits. “Most people can only hold them for a second or two—it’s almost like marching while sitting against a wall,” Hasman says. “If you can hold it for 30 seconds, you’re an absolute beast.” Nothing beats single-leg exercises for building uphill strength and stability. To this end, Hasman recommends getting into the gym at least twice a week during the meat of your training. Focus on your glutes, quads, hamstrings, and core. While there are tons of relevant exercises, Hasman says step-ups are a particular must-do. “Do 15 to 30 reps on one leg, then switch,” she recommends. Start with three sets. Every week, either add a set or add five pounds of additional weight to make it harder. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: He Fell 120 Feet on Oregon’s Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain. A Bystanding Doctor Came to His Rescue.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.51
Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain is a roughly two-mile-long volcanic ridge southwest of Government Camp (Photo: Ahorica) Just before 3 P.M. on September 15, a 33-year-old man fell 100 feet off a ledge on the second peak of Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain—a jagged, multi-summit ridge above Government Camp in Oregon’s Mount Hood National Forest. The man tumbled while filming a movie, according to the Clackamas County Sheriff’s Office (CCSO). After his initial free fall, he slid 15 to 20 feet down the steep slope. Authorities have not released the man’s name or extent of injuries. “It’s hard to tell exactly what caused it, but at some point he lost his footing and fell from the top of the cliff band,” Sergeant Adam Peterson, a supervisor with the CCSO search-and-rescue team who responded to the incident, told Outside. Peterson added that the man had rigged ropes to capture a shot. “They were filming with a drone, just a couple of guys, making some sort of an indie film.” After the accident, witnesses told CCSO that the man was lying on his side with visible injuries, breathing but not moving. Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain is a roughly two-mile-long volcanic ridge located 55 miles southeast of Portland, with three peaks rising to around 5,070 feet. Internet lore holds that early guides named the range after the idiom “every Tom, Dick, and Harry,” loosely meaning a random assortment of ordinary people. For decades, the peak was known simply as Tom Dick Mountain. In 1969, the U.S. Board on Geographic Names—a government agency not usually known for its sense of humor—added “Harry” to the mountain’s official name. Don’t confuse it with Georgia’s Big John Dick Mountain, Bloody Dick Peak in Montana, or Maine’s double-whammy: Tumbledown Dick Mountain and Tumbledown Dick Head. The name may be a punchline, but the mountain itself is no joke. Trails in the lower Mirror Lake area are popular with casual day hikers, but the upper ridgelines are steep, exposed, and loose near the summits, according to the U.S. Forest Service. Roughly half an hour after the incident, two people helped the man—one of whom was a medical doctor. The duo worked to keep him from rolling further down the hillside and applied direct pressure and tourniquets to control his bleeding, according to the CCSO report. During this time, they relayed details of his condition to rescuers, helping them prepare the appropriate response measures. “[The doctor] was able to control bleeding and handle essentially shock symptoms on the scene,” Peterson said. “That was very helpful due to the level of trauma.” Search-and-rescue coordinators activated a full rescue operation, with an Oregon National Guard helicopter crew and a paramedic reaching the man by 5 P.M. Within 30 minutes, responders strapped the man to a backboard, airlifted him into a helicopter, and flew him to a nearby hospital. Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain keep rescuers busy, Peterson said. It sits directly above the popular Mirror Lake trail and next to a ski area, drawing countless hikers and an ongoing stream of minor-injury reports. “Usually it’s a lot more of your ankle sprains, things like that, for hikers over there,” he said. Just across the highway, though, is the south face of Mount Hood itself, where serious falls are far more common.

item.title: Diving with Giant Manta Rays in Mexico’s Remote Revillagigedo Islands
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.75
(Photo: Jay Clue) My dive watch shows I am 78 feet deep. Even though this is my 17th dive in four days, I feel my heart race and nerves bubble up as we descend into plankton blooms, which are not affording us the crystal-clear diving conditions we’ve experienced in days prior. With nothing to focus my gaze on in these hazy waters, my mind is flooded with thoughts I’ve pushed away this week, including just how far out in the Pacific Ocean I am. Suddenly, I see the now-familiar silhouette of a massive winged creature emerging from the blue. As it gets closer, I stay still—a tip that’s provided me with numerous close encounters this week. It circles me, so close I can see its depthless purple eye, the size of a tennis ball, watching me. And then comes another. A giant oceanic manta ray (Mobula birostris) with a wingspan of 20 feet appears out of the abyss. A handful of other divers quickly kick over, camera rigs pointed forward like shields. Before they reach us, my giant friend hovers a mere four feet above me. I hang motionless. Time seems to slow as the manta reveals its chevron belly, unfurling its scars. And then it’s gone. An immense wave of awe washes over me; my eyes water behind my mask. We are 250 nautical miles—more than 24 hours by boat—from Cabo San Lucas, on the southern tip of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula. That’s the closest civilization, so to speak, from us in the ultra-remote Revillagigedo archipelago. Uninhabited by humans, these four volcanic islands are often referred to as the “Galápagos of Mexico” due to their dramatic underwater pinnacles, exceptional biodiversity, and waters teeming with large pelagic species like giant manta rays, sharks, and whales. In 2016, UNESCO declared the islands a World Heritage Site, and in 2017, it became the largest marine protected area in North America. The only way to visit these remote islands is via a liveaboard boat. And while a Mexican Navy base houses roughly 250 caretakers and their families for this protected area, regular tourists aren’t allowed to step foot on the islands—permits are almost exclusively given for scientific research. But everyone’s here for what’s below the surface: hammerhead sharks galore, singing humpbacks, 20-ton polka-dotted whale sharks, and the islands’ biggest attraction—friendly manta rays that can reach up to 22 feet long. Conditions can be challenging this far out, and out of the group of 20 divers on our seven-day liveaboard trip, I’m the least experienced arriving with only 45 dives. In comparison, some of my fellow divers have several thousand under their belt. Our guide is Jay Clue, the owner and founder of Dive Ninja Expeditions, the first designated PADI Eco Center in Mexico and one of the first in the world. Dive Ninja leads eco-minded big marine animal diving expeditions all over the world. An award-winning photographer, Clue has a deep passion for marine conservation and sustainable tourism that proves these manta rays (and other endangered species) are more valuable alive than dead. On this particular trip, there are many aspiring Clues who want to hone their underwater photography skills. So while my fellow divers are kitted out with the best and biggest camera rigs, I have chosen to dive without even a GoPro. With strong currents and sustained depths, a camera would be one more thing I’d have to think about. This camera-free choice affords me closer encounters, too—apparently, mantas want to look into our eyes, not our lenses. Research suggests mantas are some of the most intelligent fish on our planet. They have massive brains, can recognize themselves in mirrors, and can recognize us, too, it seems. “I was unexpectedly greeted by two familiar faces once,” says Clue, who has led more than 20 trips to these islands in the last decade. “A few mantas I’ve spent time photographing on past trips swam directly up to me, then proceeded to unroll their cephalic fins as they glided, motionless, eye-to-eye only a few feet away.” Almost as if they were saying hello to an old friend, says Clue. “Is this just a rare coincidence my human brain is trying to turn into something it isn’t,” he wonders, “or could it be something more?” Robert Rubin, PhD, the region’s foremost expert on these “flying carpets of ebony silk,” as he calls them, has been studying gigantic oceanic manta rays in Mexico for more than three decades. The founder and director of the Pacific Manta Research Group, he believes manta rays are sentient, intelligent creatures that merit protection. Inspired by Rubin’s research, Clue set out to create dive trips that combine awe-inspiring marine encounters with conservation education and citizen science. “You can dive with manta rays all over the world, but here they have a different behavior than we see anywhere else. They seem to seek out interactions with divers. You can see their eyes tracking you. It feels like they want to have a conversation with us,” says Clue. Several evenings on the trip, he gives presentations on Rubin’s research and Pacific Manta Research Group’s manta identification effort, which is a citizen science project anyone can get involved in. “Whether you have a tiny GoPro or a $10,000 camera, it doesn’t really matter. Anyone can take photos of the mantas’ bellies and submit them,” says Clue. This crowdsourced data helps researchers identify specific individuals to track migrations and protect critical aggregation sites. Today, the biggest threats to mantas are overtourism (in mainland Mexico and worldwide) and boat strikes, both around the islands and on their migratory travels. “As Revillagigedo is a remote location, technically protected by both a national park and the World Heritage Site, it’s largely a safe space for these animals,” says Karey Kumli, project manager at Pacific Manta Research Group. Responsible tourism, however, plays a powerful role in protecting the manta rays. “It wasn’t until all the tourist boats came [to Revillagigedo] that the fishing [ban] really was enforced. So it’s crucial that there’s tourists there,” says Cody Sheehy, director of The Last Dive, a new film about these islands and the mantas making its way across festival circuits this year. “The money and the jobs brought to those islands showed the Mexican government could justify their position on keeping it in the national park and [staving off] fishing,” he adds. Individual mantas have been tracked through photo identification for up to 33 years—the worldwide age record for the oceanic (giant) mantas. When they look back at photo sets taken 10 to 40 years ago, 95 percent of those animals have made at least two appearances, says Kumli. Our dive trip alone added 44 new mantas to the research database. I added a manta to the database and named her Artemis. Inspired from the 2026 Artemis II historic lunar flyby where a crew traveled farther from Earth than any humans in history. It seemed a fitting name, as this dive trip felt like it was the closest I’d ever get to floating weightlessness in space. After each dive at different islands throughout the week, we’d find ourselves elated, rehashing all our incredible encounters on the top deck at sunset. Gina, a veteran diver from Florida, said it best: “My version of heaven is where all questions are answered. Including what the mantas are thinking.” Diving this far out, deep in the blue, felt like a spiritual, mysterious realm to me. And while we haven’t found out what mantas are thinking just yet, the fact that these creatures still trust us in this world feels like heaven enough. This article is from the Summer 2026 issue of Outside magazine. To receive the print magazine, become an Outside+ member here.

item.title: The iPhone 18 Pro’s Camera is Old School. We Couldn’t Be Happier.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.55
The new iPhone 18 Pro has the widest aperture ever on an iPhone, letting in more light when needed. (Photo: Jakob Schiller) All traditional cameras, except for the simplest point-and-shoot, have always come with a mechanical aperture to control the amount of light that reaches the film or sensor. Phone cameras, on the other hand, have never incorporated one because of size restraints. That changes with the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Both come with a physical iris on the main 48-megapixel, 24-millimeter lens that can be manually controlled to let in more or less light. The shutter is still digital, but it can also be manually controlled for the first time. It feels odd to be celebrating something as basic as an adjustable aperture and manual camera options—like we’re going backwards in time. But, having tested it, I’m excited to have more control over how I make photos. After opening the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera app and choosing the main lens, you can peg the aperture and shutter controls to the top of the screen. Tapping these controls brings up a menu that lets you dial in your preferences. For aperture, you can choose from f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. That’s a limited range, but there’s a reason. The sensor inside the iPhone is much smaller and closer to the lens than what you’d find in a DSLR or full-frame mirrorless, so at f/4 you actually get a near-infinite field of focus and there’s little need to go higher. On the other end, Apple stopped at f/1.48 because anything wider would have necessitated a larger lens and compromised how it fits in your pocket. Note: The f-stop control on recent iPhones makes it seem like you can select f/1.4 to f/16, but the aperture is actually fixed. The illusion of changing the aperture and depth of field is created by the software digitally blurring or sharpening the background. Until now, you could not actually change the amount of light the lens let in. Using the iPhone 18 Pro’s f/1.48 aperture, the widest ever on an iPhone, you can now let in a lot more light. Anyone who’s shot a full-frame mirrorless camera knows that f/1.48 creates a razor-thin depth of field and helps you practically see in the dark. On the iPhone 18 Pro, the depth of field and light-gathering ability aren’t quite as powerful but are still significantly better than what you get with the fixed f/1.78 aperture on the main lens of the iPhone 17. I found the manual aperture control super useful. When I wanted to capture a scene with multiple people but emphasize just one, for example, I opened the aperture control, dialed down the depth of field, and was able to send the viewer’s eye to a specific part of the frame. In darker situations, I widened the aperture to allow light into the sensor, rather than having the phone compensate by dialing up the ISO, which can cause the photo to fall apart digitally (Note: the camera will still adjust the ISO whenever the light is too low for the widest aperture). Whenever I selected the aperture manually, the phone adjusted the shutter speed to ensure the correct exposure, just like the aperture-priority mode on traditional cameras. When I wanted a fast shutter speed to freeze fast-moving subjects, I selected the manual shutter control and the phone adjusted the aperture to create the correct exposure. In this setting, the phone acts like the shutter-priority mode on DSLRs and mirrorless cameras. In a lower-light panning situation, where I followed moving vehicles to keep them in focus but blurred the background, I selected manual control for both aperture and shutter. I was able to tell the iPhone to set the aperture at f/4 to allow in less light, which enabled me to slow down the shutter speed. I soon, however, discovered the limitations of the small aperture range, as even using the narrowest setting of f/4, the image got blown out with light whenever I slowed the shutter past 1/30th of a second. I still, however, was able to shoot better motion shots than on any previous iPhone. The 18 Pro is the first iPhone to get subject tracking, a feature photographers love on DSLRs and mirrorless cameras. It works by tapping a subject in the frame, which tells the camera to lock onto that person no matter where they move. This took some getting used to, but was helpful while photographing my son during a soccer game. Also new is a manual focus setting in which sliding one way on a digital dial tells the camera to focus whatever is closest to the lens, and sliding the other way focuses on the background. I found it a bit difficult to quickly identify where the focal plane was, but luckily there’s focus peaking, where whatever is in focus gets outlined in white as a visual cue. I found it nearly impossible to access any of these manual controls one-handed while holding the phone vertically, so I usually shot horizontally. Two hands made it much easier to tap the aperture or shutter speed feature, swipe to the setting I wanted, and click the shutter. The process was much slower than what I could do on a mirrorless camera, but with practice I had a well-organized workflow. I’ve long recommended the iPhone to Outside readers because it has a powerful camera that fits in your pocket and is great for adventuring. Thanks to upgrades like larger sensors and smart software, all the recent iPhones take damn nice photos. The inclusion of an adjustable aperture and more manual controls on the 18 Pro make it significantly more useful than the 17 Pro. Whether you should buy comes down to how you plan to use the camera and what other gear you already have in the closet. If you own a DSLR or mirrorless camera and don’t mind hauling it in your backpack, that’s still a better option. If you have an iPhone 16 or 17 Pro and don’t care that much about manual controls, don’t upgrade because your photo quality will be similar. If, however, you’re a photo geek like me and adventure a lot but don’t want to haul along a bigger camera, the iPhone 18 Pro is an attractive option.

item.title: How to Clean, Sanitize, and Store a Water Filter in the Off-season
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 3.93
It's important to clean and sanitize your backcountry water filter or purifier before storing it during the off-season and winter months. A simple three-stage process involves cleaning the filter to improve flow rate, sanitizing it to kill microorganisms, and drying it before storing it until you're ready to use it again. Step 1: Backflush Your Water Filter or Purifier Many backcountry water filters and purifiers can be backflushed, meaning you reverse the normal flow of water through the filter element. This unclogs debris or contaminants stuck in the filter, flushes them out, and improves the filter's flow rate. Many filters and purifiers come with a hose or a syringe, like the Sawyer Squeeze that you can use to perform this backflushing operation. to clean it. If you've used your water filter or purifier recently, you only need to backflush/clean it a few times. If you haven't used it recently and the filter element is “dry”, it's best to run water through the filter in the normal direction to wet it out before commencing the backflushing operation. Try not to apply extra pressure when you backflush the filter element because it can rip or deform the internal element, which may be paper, depending on the product you use. Sawyer claims their filters are pretty tough, but others are not, and I think it's prudent to be firm but gentle during the backflushing process. Step 2: Sanitize the Filter Element In this next stage, you need to sanitize the filter/purification element and kill any microorganisms that may remain inside. You don't want these to keep growing over the winter because they can permanently clog or damage the filter element. Different manufacturers suggest slightly different procedures, so check their website recommendations. The two most common ways people sanitize their water filter/purification element are to flush it with a diluted bleach solution made with one capful of fragrance-free bleach per Liter of tap water. A few liters should do the trick. Filter these as you would in the field with raw water. Once finished, filter a quart or two of plain tap water through to remove any remaining chemicals so you don't get a mouthful when you start using the filter next season. Alternatively, you can treat a liter or two of water with Aquamira drops or Katadyn Micropur tablets to sanitize your filter. These contain chlorine dioxide, which is an ultralight way to purify backcountry water sources without filtering. If you use one, you don't need to rinse your filter afterward, as the water you'll backflush or clean your filter with is completely potable. In fact, many city and town water supplies use chlorine dioxide to treat their tap water. Step 3: Drying and Storage Let your filter/purifier dry slowly and naturally by placing it in a warm, well-ventilated location, out of direct sunlight. After a week, move it to a drawer or closet in the heated part of your home. Come next season, it will be ready to use. Note: Some manufacturers suggest slightly different procedures, so check their website recommendations. For instance, rather than letting your filter dry, some recommend storing it wet after sanitizing. That's all there is to it! Updated September 2026. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. Some municipalities have enough metals in their water that flushing with your tap water as a final step may lead to a stubborn clog in the spring. It generally requires some sort of acidic flush to get those minerals about. Citric acid is recommended by some manufacturers for this.

item.title: 10 Best Down Jackets for Backpacking | 2026 Recomendations
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 3.15
A down jacket has multiple uses on a hiking or backpacking gear list. It can be used as an insulating midlayer on its own or under a shell, as a warm outer jacket when you're less active in camp, or as an adjunct to your sleeping bag/quilt at night. For hiking or backpacking, some down jackets better meet hikers' needs than others in terms of warmth-to-weight ratio, hood design, durability, and cost. With these factors in mind, here are the best three-season down jackets that we recommend across a variety of price points. Be sure to check out our feature recommendations below, so you can choose the right jacket for your needs. | Make / Model | Gender | Weight | Fill Power | |---|---|---|---| | Patagonia Down Sweater Hoodie | M \| F | 14.8 oz/420g | 800 | | Feathered Friends EOS Jacket | M \| F | 11.8 oz/335g | 900 | | Arcteryx Cerium Down Hoodie | M \| F | 11.9 oz/335g | 850 | | Katabatic Gear Tarn Jacket | M \| F | 10.6 oz/303g | 850 | | REI Magma 850 Down Hoodie | M \| F | 13.1 oz/354g | 850 | | Mtn Hardware Ghost Whisperer | M \| F | 8.8 oz/249g | 800 | | Outdoor Research Helium Down Hoodie | M \| F | 15.4 oz/459g | 800 | | Montbell Ex Light Down Anorak | Unisex | 7.6 oz/215g | 900 | | LL Bean UL 850 Down Jacket | M \| F | 16 oz/450g | 850 | | Cotopaxi Fuego Hooded Down Jacket | M \| F | 13 oz/367g | 800 | 1. Patagonia Down Sweater Hoodie 2. Feathered Friends EOS Jacket 3. Arc’teryx Cerium Down Hoodie 4. Katabatic Gear Tarn Jacket 5. REI Magma 850 Down Hoodie 6. Mountain Hardwear Ghost Whisperer Down Hoody 7. Outdoor Research Helium Down Hoodie 8. Montbell Ex Light Down Anorak 9. LL Bean UL 850 Down Jacket 10. Cotopaxi Fuego Hooded Down Jacket Down Hoodie and Jacket Buying Guide Down Hoodies, Jackets, Sweaters, Anoraks, and Parkas Manufacturer product names are applied inconsistently to lighter-weight down hoodies and jackets. In general, hoodies, sweaters, and anoraks weigh under one pound. Look for ones with hoods, as they provide the most head and neck insulation. When it comes to jackets, some are lightweight and some are heavier, designed for winter use in harsh conditions. You really have to look at the overall jacket weight to determine which is which. Anything up to or slightly over 16 oz will be good for transitional weather in spring or autumn down to freezing by itself or layered under a shell, while heavier jackets will be more appropriate for winter use. Parkas are almost always intended for very cold winter conditions and are too warm for active use when hiking. Sewn Thru vs Baffled Construction With very few exceptions, lightweight down jackets and hoodies use sewn-through construction rather than box-baffled construction because it is less expensive and labor-intensive to manufacture. With sewn-through construction, the front and back of the jacket are sewn together, creating a pocket that prevents the down insulation from shifting. However, warm air can leak through the needle holes, making the jacket slightly cooler. This is not the case with a box-baffled design, which is more prevalent on premium down parkas intended for colder temperatures. Hood Adjustment The hoods on many lightweight or ultralight down hoodies and jackets are quite rudimentary, with elasticized hood openings that may be too large to prevent cold drafts from entering around your ears. It depends on your head size and the specific jacket. Hoods that are 1-way adjustable have volume controls in the back that let you shrink the size of the hood to provide a better fit. Hoods with 2-way adjustability go a step further and add neck cords that let you size the opening to fit your face and block out drafts. Two-way adjustability is pretty rare on lightweight down jackets and hoodies, but it's a premium feature worth looking for. Down Fill Power Down fill powers, such as 700, 800, 850, or 900, measure the effectiveness and compressibility of down insulation – the higher the better. Now, 900- or 950-fill-power down is primo stuff and can add a lot of cost to a jacket while keeping it very lightweight, since it takes less down by weight to keep you warm. You can get the same warmth with a lower grade of down, like 800 or 850, but it takes more of it to keep you warm and adds a bit of weight to the jacket. However, don't dismiss 700 fill-power down jackets, especially if they include synthetic insulation in moisture-prone areas. The warmth difference isn't that significant, and while they'll be a bit heavier, they're ideal in wet climates. Down Fill Weight The fill weight of a down jacket or hoodie measures the amount of down it has, by weight. While this can be informative, a jacket's actual warmth depends on both the amount of insulation and its design, which makes it hard to compare jackets with different styles. Most lightweight jacket manufacturers don't document the amount of down in their jackets, which can make it hard to tell which will be warmer in active use. Waterproof Down Some manufacturers use down in their jackets that has been coated with a chemical formulation, called DownTek or Nikwax, to make it more moisture-resistant and help it dry faster when it gets damp or wet. Honestly, the jury is still out on whether these treatments make any difference to the insulation performance of the down. Some manufacturers believe it degrades insulation value, and others use it because it's considered a desirable feature by prospective customers. I wish it were a bit warmer sitting around at camp when it gets down to 20-30F. Is there a jacket you think would perform better for those situations? I think the REI magma 850, the Katabatic gear Tarn of FF Eos will get you down to 20. Thanks, Philip. Those are ones that seemed like they might fit the bill from warmth standpoint to me. FF and Katabatic are impossible to try on without ordering. I’m on the husky side. The EOS seems like it might be too athletic cut for me. I’ve tried on a Magma. 2XL is a bit big, but XL is snug. It looks like the Tarn XXL might be kind of in between from the size charts. Does that sound about right based on your experience I’m a large – no idea about how those other sizes fit

item.title: A taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroes
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 4.79
‘It’s a magical place, and not just because of the hotel.” Standing outside the greenhouses at Högbo Brukshotell, two hours north of Stockholm, Stefan Johansson is talking about far more than hospitality. The former head chef, now responsible for sustainability at Högbo, has spent much of the past decade helping reshape the way this corner of Sweden grows, cooks and thinks about food. The catalyst was disarmingly simple. Years ago, a journalist asked Johansson why he was cooking the food he was cooking. Like many ambitious Swedish chefs, Stefan trained in Stockholm’s top restaurants, where ingredients from around the world were only a phone call away. The question lingered long after the interview ended. “Before, I wanted food to be spectacular; I didn’t really care where it came from,” he says. “Then I closed the window of where we source from down to the region. It was the best thing I’ve ever done.” Instead of looking farther afield for inspiration, he began looking closer to home. Högbo Brukshotell sits in the former Högbo ironworks, a quiet pocket of forest, waterways and historic buildings north of Sandviken. The area’s industrial past is still visible in its old manor houses, smithies and mill buildings, but since the factories fell silent in the mid-19th century, the woods have reclaimed their place. Walking, cycling and cross-country ski trails now lead into the forest, while the old bruk buildings house cafes, workshops and small businesses. Ingredients that once arrived at Högbo from far away are now grown here. The Made in Högbo project began with lamb, with animal rearing and butchery brought in-house. Vegetable production followed. Now greenhouses sit alongside kitchen gardens, producing ingredients for the restaurant and creating opportunities for people who might otherwise struggle to find work. Refugees from Myanmar helped establish some of the early growing projects. New arrivals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo have joined the initiative, splitting their time between Swedish language classes and work placements, their influence visible in the rows of papaya, bananas and other plants rarely associated with Sweden. There are plans for an aquaponics system that will combine greenhouse cultivation with tilapia fish farming. In farm buildings there are now also a bakery making sourdough and cakes, a microbrewery run by one of the chefs, a dairy making fresh cheeses, and an excellent deli. Högbo isn’t the only place asking these questions about food provenance. Over several days travelling through Gästrikland and neighbouring Hälsingland in eastern Sweden, I discover a network of millers, fishers, distillers, cheese makers and chefs connected by a shared idea: that food should reflect the place it comes from. At Gammelstilla, an old ironworks has become a small whisky distillery. In the village of Gästrike-Hammarby, The Old Mill is now an award-winning restaurant run by Bogdan Ioan Gheorghe and Ellinor Andersson, with a tasting menu that features a roll-call of local producers alongside surprising ingredients such as the invasive species Japanese knotweed. At Bergmans Fisk, in Norrsundet, low islands scatter across the bay and the Baltic stretches east towards Finland beyond the wooden smokehouses. The business is run by a seventh-generation fishing family whose connection to these waters stretches back more than a century. Inside the smokehouses, salmon hangs in neat rows, a slow process, refined over generations. But for traditions – and the business – to survive, they have to evolve and diversify, Dennis Bergman explains. In 2020, the family opened a waterfront restaurant overlooking the bay where much of their fish is caught. We enjoy a smorgasbord of smoked salmon and böckling (hot smoked herring) piled on dark rye crispbreads. The family also operates a travelling fish van serving coastal communities and is planning a small hotel: new ventures that will help secure the future of old skills. Driving north through the deep pine forests and lush fields of Hälsingland, I keep spotting hand-painted signs for potatoes, eggs and strawberries. Outside red-painted farm buildings, honesty boxes sit beside stacks of produce. At Teve Kvarn, a mill south of Järvsö, I meet Anna Larsson, a seventh-generation miller. She sources grain from roughly a 150km (93-mile) radius, selling seed to farmers and then buying back the grain to ensure high-quality flour production. Only a handful of mills of this type remain in Sweden. Anna points out her newest machine – it was installed in 1930. Beside the traditional wooden mill, shiny stills are visible in a tall glass building. This is the Tevsjö distillery run by Anna’s husband, Jonas, producing vodka, gin and aquavit using grain from the mill. The distillery runs on hydroelectric power generated from the nearby stream, and has already increased its production capacity more than 10 times on the strength of the products’ popularity – while creating 10 new local jobs. At nearby Järvsö Lanthandel, I meet chef Tobias Annerhult who runs the general store and restaurant. For Annerhult, local sourcing isn’t just desirable, it’s his entire food philosophy. “I only buy salt, pepper, sugar and oil,” he tells me. “I don’t use stabilisers. Nothing gets thrown away; that feeds the creative process. Our philosophy is to grow through limitations.” In a climate where vegetables arrive in abundance for only part of the year, preserving is essential. Annerhult pickles, cures and ferments local produce, including meat for charcuterie. Tonight, we too have to work for our dinner, taking a cooking class that Tobias offers for private group bookings. We have brought produce collected across the region: flour from the centuries-old mill; cheese and potatoes from honesty boxes; fish from a family that has worked the same waters for generations; and vegetables from local greenhouses. Together, we make fermented pea pancakes with sweet preserved apple and salty local goat’s cheese; bouncy fresh pasta using Anna’s wheat and eggs from Tobias’s chickens, served simply with burrata-style cheese, brown butter and garden herbs; and warm cake with the first of the season’s rhubarb. It’s a meal that tastes all the better for knowing the stories and people behind it. Combining preserved and fermented ingredients with the season’s freshest produce harks back to traditional approaches to cooking and eating. Today’s chefs are reclaiming that philosophy, and the results are delicious. It perhaps helps answer the question that changed Stefan’s career all those years ago. Why cook this food, in this place? Because when food truly belongs somewhere, it becomes a way of understanding that place too. The trip was provided by Visit Sweden. For more information visit gastrikland.se and destinationhalsingland.se. Högbo Brukshotell has doubles from 1,995 Swedish kronor (£155) B&B Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: The other side of Croatia: ‘a landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany’
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.96
‘You’re going to Samobor? You must try kremšnita,” my Dubrovnik friends told me before I set off on my trip north. “But I’ve already had kremšnita in Zagreb,” I told them. They do it better in Samobor, they insisted. I wasn’t about to get embroiled in a battle of the cream cakes in a region where Croatians, Slovenes and Austrians all like to celebrate their own versions of this decadently thick, fat custard slice topped with puff pastry and icing sugar. But I was more than willing – happy, even – to follow everyone’s suggestions to try kremšnita in Hotel Livadić’s Kavana Livadić, in Samobor’s main King Tomislav Square, a mere half-hour drive west of Zagreb. It lived up to the hype – delicately rich, creamy and with a light touch. After spending a few weeks in sun-bleached Venetian Dalmatia, amid the scrubby, limestone Dinaric Alps, I had swapped empires and was firmly in Habsburg Croatia. Here, in Zagreb County’s prettiest town, handsome baroque houses in pastel shades of buttery yellow, apricot and pistachio, festooned with stucco, line narrow King Tomislav Square, whose umbrella-shaded cafe terraces were filled with Croatians getting their morning fix of coffee and chatter. The lush green Samobor Hills overlook the medieval town, through which the Gradna – part river, part stream – flows and ripples under wooden bridges adorned with flowers. One of these bridges led to the onion-domed church of Saint Anastasia; another, with a fairytale wooden roof, took me to one of Samobor’s many green spaces, dotted with free red deckchairs, which had the slogan “Volim Samobor” (“I love Samobor”) written in white. In front of them, the stately former home (now the town’s museum) of one of Croatia’s foremost 19th-century composers, Ferdo Livadić, added to the air of gentle refinement, of culture worn lightly. It was easy to visualise Livadić entertaining his artistic friends, including Franz Liszt, in this august setting. As well as the graceful architectural legacy of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, this rolling green landscape is crisscrossed with forested trails, particularly within the Žumberak nature park, about 16 miles (26km) west of Samobor, where weekenders from Zagreb come to hike and bike in woods of hornbeam, oak and beech with bubbling waterfalls. Not having time for a full-on hike, I could still drive to Potočna dolina Slapnica, near the Vranjak waterfalls, and scramble up the path beside a series of cascades each more impressive than the last. Closer to Samobor, the hilltop ruins of Okić castle rose to nearly 500m above sea level, one of the best-preserved romanesque fortifications in the country. The Mongols couldn’t defeat it, nor could the Ottoman Turks. Sadly, it defeated me when I attempted to hike to the top. Not realising there was a newer, easier path, I ended up on one that was little else but vertical tree roots. With a newly healed ankle and no phone signal, I thought it unwise to continue. But it’s on my list for next time. A much easier path to take was along the Plešivica wine road, where more than three dozen wineries were scattered on a heart-shaped route between the village of Plešivica (10 miles south-west of Samobor) and the town of Jastrebarsko. In a harmonious landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany, vineyards clung to steep slopes between forested hills, many producing the sparkling wine Plešivica is renowned for. I met Martina and Krešimir Ivančić, whose ancestors were given a noble title and coat of arms by the Austrian empress Maria Theresa in 1759. The griffin on the family crest inspired the name of the Griffin Winery, which came about when a Hungarian count gave them a licence to plant a vineyard in 1773. Martina took me to the covered patio of a wooden hut above the vineyards, a suitably bucolic place to taste an elegant and lightly fruity sparkling rose made from red portugieser grapes. We carried on in the extremely stylish tasting room, where plates of cured meats and cheeses accompanied glasses of full-bodied chardonnay. I was also offered copanjek, a thin savoury pastry pie of cheese and greens. “They’re very portable, so workers would take them to the vineyard,” Martina told me. This looked like the winemaker’s version of rudarska greblica, which I had tasted that morning in the village of Rude, about a 10-minute drive west of Samobor, and liked so much I had to have two. Filled with cheese and walnuts, carrots or greens, these used to be made by the wives of Rude’s long-gone miners. They’re such an integral part of the region that they have their own festival every July and have been given EU protected status. At Pekarnica Nikl, in Rude, I met Jelena and Andrejas Nikl, the only authorised bakers of this much adored speciality. Jelena acknowledged the responsibility of keeping up this tradition of rudarska greblica, especially with the paperwork that came with legal protection – but, she said, it was worth it. All around the Samobor Hills, people were holding fast to their heritage and infusing it with life. The Korak family is one of the most illustrious, with its Michelin-starred Korak winery and restaurant in Plešivica. Not a whiff of Michelin stuffiness or pretentiousness here, just the fourth and fifth generations of a family producing superb wine and making beautiful food in a serene setting facing the vineyards. Brother Bernard is chef (and has worked with Massimo Bottura of Italy’s Osteria Francescana and Ana Roš of Slovenia’s Hiša Franko); sister Vera is front of house; and parents Velimir and Mirjana tend the vines – even the siblings’ grandparents are still making cheese and pršut (prosciutto) for the restaurant. Bernard grows as much as he can – the rest comes from local producers, including the farmer whose pigs are fed on scraps from Bernard’s kitchen. And if it’s not in season, it’s not on the plate. My June visit rewarded me with a truffle tagliatelle, and clams and green beans in a caviar sauce, among other delicious dishes in a five-course tasting menu at €118 (a very reasonable price, and in keeping with the region’s overall lower prices). I could only imagine what delights autumn will bring, especially during the annual Wine Days festival in Jastrebarsko from 25-27 September. The Samobor Hills will be teeming with autumn truffles and mushrooms, and welcoming the change in season the best way they know – on the plate.
